A LOOK. I saw it pass from eye to eye, A subtle flash of fine emotion, That bore from each to each the pledge Of the whole heart's life-long devotion. What wealth was there! what boundless store For all the needs of coming years! The noble sympathy in j )y! The priceless balm for pain and tears! Just that one look—and straight was sealed The dearest bond that love supplies; Lips may deceive, but perfect truth Finds glorious speech in honest eyes, Jane C. Simpson, in Good Words for March.

WHAT BECAME OF POLLY'S NOSE? [We all know how the wicked blackbird "nipped off her nose ;" but it is something new to know how it was put on again. "Chirps for the Chicks" (published by Seeley, Jack- son, and Co., London,) gives that very desirable piece of infor- mation.] They quickly caught the wicked bid, And brought him to the King; His little feet were pinioned with A tiny silver ring. The King said, "Mister Blackbird, For taking off this nose, ILou have a very good excuse To offer, I suppose ?" - The Blackbird said, "I'm one of those The Maid put in the pie; If maids make pies or blackbirds, Now please to tell me why The blackbirds can't make pies of maids ?" "Oh. shocking 1" cried the King, " You naughty little blackbird, That is quite another thing." And here the Maiden sadly wept "What will become of me? A husband I shall never get, An old maid I must be. I don't believe I'll meet the man, No—not in all my life— Who'll take a girl without a nose To be his wedded wife. The King replied, "Come, dry your eyes; Don't cry, my pretty dear; For I must find a man for you— That's really very clear. Here, Mister Blackbird, you're to blame, So take the Maiden's hand, For you must be her husband now, I beg you'll understand." The Blackbird cried, "Your Majesty. I dare not take her hand; What would the people say to her At home, in Blackbird's Land? I'il go and get her precious nose— My cook's not made the pie— And r will stick it on again. At least, my lord, I'll try.". Away he flew to get the nose, And brought it in his beak; And soon he stitched it on again So very nice and neat. A dose of cooling medicine, A piece of sticking plaster, Soon took away all marks of this Poor maiden's sad disaster.

Tai s RgLISG rASiliVS.—Not twenty miles from Brandon there died a miner who had passed the whole of his lifttiote as a cockfighter, b)wler, and an inveterate gimbler. To- wards the close of his last illnese; the colliery doctor called In to see him. At the same time a few of the neighbours were anxious to hear the doctor's opinion of the dying man, when one of them asked how long he thought the poor man would live. The doctor replied that he thought about nine o'clock would try bin, when the patient, whsm everybody thought was speechless, heard what was said, he cried out, " Aa'il tyake six to fowr aa live till ten." UNHAPPINESS AT HOME.—No unhappiness in life is equal to unhappiness at home. All other personal miseries can be better borne than the terrible misfortune of domestic disunion, and none so completely demoralises the nature. The anguish of disease itself is modified, ameliorated, even rendered blessed, by the tender touch, the dear presence of the sympathetic beloved; and loss of fortune is not loss of happiness where family love is left. But the want of that love is not to be supplied by anything else on earth. Health, fortune, success, nothing has its fall savour when the home is unhappy; and the greatest triumphs out of doors are of no avail to cheer the sinking heart when the misery within has to be encountered. A common juryman applied to Mr. Justice Hannen, who was presiding at the Glamorganshire Assizes, for permission to he excused from attending as a juror on the following day. "Upon what grounds ?" asked his Lordship. "Oh, my Lord, I am exceedingly desirous of being able to attend a funeral to-morrow, and cannot do so unless your Lordship gives me permission to be absent," replied the applicant. Mr. Justice Hannen, anxious to oblige the juror upon such an occasion, immediately gave the required permission. Upon leaving the court, his Lordship was informed by the Under-Sheriff that the juror who had just obtained a day's leave of absence was an undertaker. OLD MEN'S FANCIER.—Mr. cildtdstorte's early friendship for Lord Stratford de Redebffe was maintained through the varying chances of the times. Once when the ex-Premier called upon the ex-Minister to Turkey, a common friend, bent upog the same errand, met the right hon. gentlemen on the staircase. " How is his lordship this morning?" said the second caller. "He looks very well considering his age; but ah !" Mr. Gladstone continued, tapping his fore- head significantly," I am afraid he is not quite so strong here as he used to be. Good morning." The second caller being admitted into the presence of Lord Stratford de Red- cliffe, observed," I see Gladstone has just left you. He is looking very well." "Yes," said Lord Stratford de Red- cliffs; "but ah!" touching his forehead significantly, "I am afraid he is not so strong here as he used to le." COBDEN'S START IN BUSINESS LIFE.—I begets business in partnership with two other young men, and we only mustered £l,OOO amongst us, and more than half of it was borrowed. We all got on the " Peveril of the Peak" coach, and went from London to Manchester in the, at that day (September, 1828), marvellously short space of 20 hours. We were literally so ignorant of Manchester houses that we called for a directory at the hotel, and turned to the list of calico printers, theirs being the business with which we were acquainted, and they being the people from whom we felt confident we could obtain credit. And why? Because we knew we should be able to satisfy them that we had ad- vantages from our large connection?' our knowledge of the best branch of the business in London, and our superior taste in design, which would insure success. We introduced ourselvet to Fort Bros. and Co., a r;ch house, honestly con- cealing nothing. In less than two years we owed them £40,000 for goods which they had sent to us in Watling- street, upon no other security than our characters and knowledge of our business. I frequently talked with them in later times upon the great confidence they showed in men who avowed that they were not possessed of £2OO each. Their answer was that they were not possessed of £2OO each. Their answer was that they would always prefer to trust young men with connections and with a knowledge of their trade, if they knew them to possess character and ability, to those who started with capital without these ad- vantages, and that that they had acted on this principle successfully in all parts of the world.—Textile Manufac- turer.

_ LOCAL NicKrumEs.—Nicknames are peculiar to every time and place, and, of course, certain towns of the county palatine have come in for remembrance in this respect. "Proud Preston" is a well-known epithet; but we have al- ways failed to find a reason for it. We know of others that are not described in the same faultless language. In many instances it is the inhabitants of a town generally that are designated ; and some wide distinctions, not on the whole complimentary, occur in the following six lines : Whitfield dobbers, Bury bull dogs, Owdham rough•yeds, Bowton trotters, Manchester men, Liverpool gentlemen. The saying varies; in some instances a "Rachda felly';or a "Wigan chap," or both, being introduced. It is ratiier hard on Bury and Oldham, yet it is comforting to know that the distinction may be transposed, and perhaps applied with equal force to those whose characteristics are described in less objectionable terms. Many attempts have been made to trace the origin of these distinctions, and recently a writer in the North British Advertiser accounted for it in the following note :—" Old Herbert, amember of the firm of Jones and Herbert, of Chester, was driver and part owner of the coach between Chester and Birkenhead. One day in the summer of 1838, or thereabouts, on his return from Birken- head, he pulled up, as usual, at Backford, about two and a half miles from Chester, and went into the inn. He was asked by someone in the back parlour whom he had with him. He replied that ha h 4 four of 'em—a gentleman from Liverpool, a man from Manchester, a felly from Wigan, and a chap from Bowton.' " The writer doubts whether Herbert did more than put a string of current local terms into neat collocation, and in this opinion we decidedly con cur. Manchester men and Liverpool gentlemen were cer- tainly current colloquialisms, long before the date of Old Her...:tr,'s ready speech. ROriAL AGRICULTURAL COLLEGE, CIRENCESTER.—The chair of agriculture, vacant at the close of this session by the resignation of Professor Scott, has been offered to and accepted by Mr. E. Herbert J. Little, of Coldham Hall, Wisbech. _

A contract for buildirg a lailway tunnel under the St. Lawrence at Montreal has been awarded. The amount of the contract is 3,500,000 dole., including drainage and light- ing. The tunnel is to be completed by 1885. Upon the island of Euboal fossil human remains are re- ported to have been recently discovered. The Greek Go- vernment has had the objects in question conveyed to Athens, where their scientifie examination is now ordered. The telephone has been applied to Dolcoath copper mine, near Cambome, Cornwall, between the surface and the ex- treme depth of 350 fathoms. This is the deepest metal mine in this country, and Capt. Josiah Thomas pronounces the result to be in every way most satisfactory. Mr. Wild's excavations at Cairo have resulted in the dis- covery of a monolith belonging to Apries, the Pharaoh Hophra of the Old Testament, and bearing the inscription— " The beloved of Ttah of Memphis, giving life for ever, the good god Ra-aa-ah, lord of the two lands, Apries." THE POWER OF ICE TO FRACTURE ROCKS. —ln a recent number of Naturen Herr Bergh has drawn atten- tion to the powerful agency exert, d by ice in severing rocks, of which he gives a striking instance occurring on the Aalesund in West Norway, where a low ledge rising out of the fjord is all that remains of a once extensive fjacid promontory, which in the year 1717 was suddenly blown up and precipitated into the water by the force of the ice within the interstices of the stone. The winter had been mild, and during a rapid that/ p, coosl4er4hle stream had welled ep from the iCe,e6Vered snmmit of the fjoald, add carried RS waters into every crevice of the rock, when a sudden change of wind brought about a sharp frost, which tax ned the de- scending waters of the newly-formed stream into ice, arrest- ing their course within the interstices of the rock. The result was the explosion of the entire mass of the flmld below the outbreak of the stream, and its projection from a height of more than 1,500 feet into the neighbouring fjold, which engalphed the whole of the promontory, with its cultivated fields and farmstead. Simultaneously with the disappearance of the land below the surface of the fjord, a huge mass of waters was propelled against the opposite shore, carrying with it rusty anchors, boat rafters, and numerous other objects which had long lain at the bottom. The disturbance extended a mile beyond the point at which the land was submerged, and the waters in retreating car- ried with them a wooden church which had stood fifty feet above the fjord, besides sweeping away all the fishing boats for a distance of two and a half miles. Before this occur- rence, which was attended by loss of life to about a score of persons, the headland had been much resorted to on account of the halibut which abounded in the neighbourhood; but since that period the fish has never returned, a circumstance which, according to local popular belief, is due to the cover- ing and springs frequented by the fish. REMARKABLE DISCOVERIES IN GUNNERY.—The power of great guns has been developed to an extent hitherto un- precedented in the course of experiments at the Royal Arsenal proof-butts this week. The attention of artillerists has been directed to the air-spacing of cartridges as the pro- bable key to the secret of high velocities, and some of the private manufacturers Wave devised methods of introducing the air, and regulating its precise quantity, which Methods they have jealously guarded against imitations. At the Royal Gan Factories, the superintendent, Colonel Maitland, R.A., has taken a new departure by giving up air-spacing. Having found by repeated trials the description of slow- burning powder best adapted to his requirements, he has designed a contrivance for retaining it in the chamber of the gun until the powder is sufficiently fired to set up a pressare of about two tons per square inch upon the bass of the shot, which then starts at a bound the speed of which is accelerated by the pursuit of the powder gases until it leaves the muzzle. The retention of the shot is accom- plished by a ring of metal fixed around it near the base, and so regulated as to size that it will, when placed in the breach, be a trifle larger than the bore through which it has to pass. According to the resistance which it affords will be the period of retention. It has been demonstreted by experiments with fired gunpcwder that in a very strong ves- sel the powder may be ignited and converted eeto gas, but yet held under subjection for an unlimited thew? The re- tention ring is made of each strength that it will surrender at a givetl j;:essure: and the reinisite conditiM for the At. tainglent: Maxtinitn velot;.i..es taus appear to have been realised. With the 10 4in. gun a 4621 b. shot has been fired at a muzzle velocity of 2.275 feet per second, the equivalent of which in energy is 16,500 foot tons, but as the powder charge was somewhat in excess of the service allowance it is fair to reduce the velocity by 100 feet. It will even then be far in advance of the speed attained under former con- ditions. The improvement has had a stronger illustration in a competitive trial betgeen the two experimental 45-ton guns —that of Els wick manufacture, with the air-spaced chamber, and that of Woolwich, with the retention-ring. The former, with 3501 b. of powder (rather above its service charge), discharging a 7001 b. projectile at a velocity of 1,900 feet per second; the latter, crammed with 400 lb. of powder and the same shot, recorded a speed of 2,120 feet. These figures represent in energy respectively 17,500 and 20,800 tons per foot, and the advantage in an attack upon armour-plates may be assumed in the same proportion. The discovery has created great satisfaction in the Government deptrtments, and is expected to lead to even more import- ant results.

Woams IN MANURE.—These should be got rid of, par- ticularly if the manure is intended for potting purposes. The best way to effect this is to tarn the manure, and add to it while doing so a few bushels of gas lime, that is, lime from the purifiers through which gas has passed, and which will consequently be of a greenish colour. This will im- prove the quality of the manure as a fertiliser, and quickly free it from worms, large and small. Whether it kills them or drives them away, we are unable to say, bat at all events they disappear. A similar result may be obtained by well watering the heap with strong lime water, but gas lime, if it can be obtained, is best. A story is in the Pewsey Vale that a certain sturdy mil- ler, who until recently was a supporter of fox-hunting, being much annoyed at the depredations of a fox, deters mined, if possible, to put Reynard out of existence; and it is said one day, whilst haymaking, he espied the varmint in some garden ground. Now was the opportunity, thought the miller; BO bidding those who were with him "bide quiet," he quick as possible fetched his gun, and was de- lighted to find that "the brute" had not moved. Bang, bang, went both barrels of the ,guns over went the fox, and With the remark, "I've got 'un, he'll never do no more Mfg- ' chief," up rushed the miller, to find that the animal he had shot was his neighbour's fox, which had been Miffed frit 20 years, put out to scare the birds. A curious example of the inflaance of sire and dam in the crossing' of two distinct breeds was noticed in passing over the Maybanks pastures. A little black cow, of unstated origin, but in personal appearance suggestive of the Princi- pality as her birthplace, was brought in among some extra stock, and, as she proved a good milker, retained for the dairy. She bred at Maybanks, to pure Sussex bulls, six calves, mate and female alternately. All the ball calves were red, all the heifer calves black; the balls, however, having black noses, but in other respects resembling their Sussex sires. Mr. Ernest Braby is rearing as a steer one which I understood to be of the second generation, i.e., by a Sussex bull from the black cow by a Sussex bull, grand- ' dam a Welsh cow. It is 'scarcely distinguishable from its pare Sussex companions, and has a nearly clear huff nose, not a stain in the colour of its hair. TURNIP CULTIVATION ON CLAY LAND.—My experience and observation is that to keep such land in order it is ne- cessary to have a bare fallow at least every other rotation— that is, that it may be sown down with a second corn crop one term, but mast be fallowed the next; and this means to turn up the land as often as possible during the summer, at least three times. Too much must not be counted on oat straw unless cat very green, and then you lose the oats. As to the best manures, this is also a difficult matter; but don't lay out money on bones expecting a return some fa- tare day. A welhrotted clang heap or compost harrowed in (not ploughed in) is the most effectual. It is also against such land to allow it to lie ere it grows soar with rushes ; two years, or at most three, is all the good it does in grass. I am sorry I cannot be more definite, on account of so many failures trying to follow scientific men.—A. It., Kirkcaldy. THE RATING OF COUNTRY HOUSES.—Some interesting illustrations of our last week's article upon the rating of country houses come to us from Scotland. The Lord Lieutenant of Inverness-shire, with a rent roll of over £25,000, is rated on Beaufort Castle at £BO a year. The Lord Lientenant of Ross.shire, with a rent roll of £lO,OOO a year, pays £6O a-year in the shape of rates upon his house, and nothing upon his shootings. It is calculated that Mr. Matheson, M.P., of Ardross, spent at least £30,000 on the erection of his castle at Ardross ; but he is rated on that and a grouse-moor, which is said to be worth at least £l,OOO a year, at £l5O. In one case where a deer-forest was let at £3,500, a redaction of £1,400 was allowed by the assessor for the wages of eight gardeners, eight keepers, household servants and their keep, and the keep of the proprietor's horses. Well may sheep-farmers ask why they are not , allowed similar deductions. The increase of deer-forests in 1 geOtland render! the question one o! steacldy-increasiog irn- portinee.—Land. • • • INJURIOUS INSECII..-A lctdr On injurious insects, de- livered at the Royal Agricultural College, Cirencester, by Eleanor A. Omerod, F.M.S., &s., has been published in pamphlet form. " What we need," says Miss Oaserod, "is such a knowledge of the main divisions and habits of insect life as will help us to know in case of attack what it is that is injuring us, and also what general principles of insect and of plant life jointly to work on. The knowledge of the life-history of our common injurious insects is needed by all who grow the crops that are food. plants to these destroyers as well as to ourselves, for thus' in some cases, we are warned betimes, and in others we know (however threaten- ing it may look) that the attack is only a passing evil which extra food will carry the temporarily weakened plants over." This is a simple statement of the kind of knowledge that is required, and any one who procures this pamphlet will not only have the kind of knowledge which he thus requires mapped out to him In a still more elaborate way, but he will, we are certain, resign himself with great satisfaction to Miss Omerod's fuller teaching; and, becoming one of her pupils, by studying her annual reports of agricultural ex- perience in this department, will ultimately, we doubt not, take rank among the company of observers who annually co.operate with her in the extension of useful knowledge on the subject. TIIE NOEMAN-PERCHERON HORSE.-'--In New York and Chicago the Percheron-Normans eclipse all the other breeds as favourites among the dealers. Those who buy' their horses to wear out greatly prefer the Percheron-Normans to any other breed, because they are more compactly and powerfully built, are more enduring, having better feet to stand the bard wear of the city pavements; have better dispositions and are willing workers; are easier keepers, and generally give the best satisfaction. The Clydesdales were frequently criticised as being slim-waisted, coarsely coupled, and generally having had feet. These grade Percheron- Normans bring from $5O to $75 more than any of the other breeds of same weigtit and condition. In Chicago, Mr. I. H. Dahlman, the most extensive horse dealer in America, said—" I handle between 9,000 and 10,000 horses annually on my own account. Of the draught horses I handle, nearly all are Norman-Percheron horses. These Norenan-Percheron horses are docile, intelligent, broad between the eyes, and have some brain. They are easily broken, and are steady in harness—meaning that they won't fret when they do their work. They are powerful horses, and compactly built —short in the back, deep in the body, and broad in the chest. This gives them what we call a good dinner-baeket. They have the best feet of any horses in America. They have a high cup foot. Their feet will stand work on the pavement better than those of any other breed. They are short-coated and thin-skinned, and stand the hot weather the best iff any breed." AMERICAN CONSUMPTION or BUTTER AND CHEESE.— Some figures, of no little interest to dairy farmers in these days when cheese and butter are having somewhat more at- tention given to them than of yore, come to hand in an American Contemporary. Taking the returns of receipts at, and exports from, the single but by far most important port of New York, it is at least instructive to observe that while the number of packages of batter which the American farmers sent into that city, stands almost at the highest point—one year only of the past seven exceeding 1881— the exports sent abroad from New York were only about two-thirds what they were in 1880, and only half the ex- port of 1879. The actual figures are these:—ln 1874 and 1875 a million was about the total number of butter pack- ages received, and somewhat over 4,000,0001b5. in all was annually exported. While barely a third was added to the aggregate supplies in the next three years, 1876 8, the ex- ports sprung up with rapid bounds- to 10,000,000, to 20,000,000, and to 23,000,0001b5. respectively. In 1879 the supply was advanced to over a million and a half of packages, and no less than 36,000,0001b5. of butter were sent abroad from the port of New York. This year, with rather under a million and a half of packages, the export stands at 18,628,0001b5. only. There is surely very significant evi- dence here of the way in which American home consump- tion is gaining, in one commodity at all events', on American agricultural production. The cuss of cheese does not show anything like the same marked growth of home demands, bat it does unquestionably show some progress in the same direstion. The New 'York export of the bygone year was 127,000,0001b5., while it was 123,000,0001b5. in 1880, 130,000,0001b5, in 1879, and 136,000,0001b5. in 1878. The _ _

A writer on school discipline says—" Without a liberal use of the rod it is impossible to make boys smart." An eccentric old gentleman in Paisley, having had a tea party, his servant in removing the tea equipage let the tray fall, by which much of it was broken. Her master having rebuked her, she assured him it was in vain to find fault with her on account of the accident, for "if it had not been fore-ordeened, it would not bae come to pass." "That was fore-ordeened too, then," replied he, lending her a hearty slap. Hum.. —Modern Hull can hardly be styled an architec- turally beautiful city. Money has been spent without stint, but not in " reithetic " improvement. But the place is well and strongly built, with tall, fine houses in narrow but well-paved regular streets. Many of these preserve quaint, old-fashioned titles to this day. Whitefriargate and Mytongate remain, the latter being the name of the lordship which, with the town of Wyk°, or Wyke-upon-Hull, was sold to Edward I. by the Abbot of Meaux. Near these is the "Lard of Green Ginger," a name still applied seriously and officially to a street in the busiest part of the town, the words being printed in ful!. at the head of letter paper, and the locality- being occupied by solicitors and merchants of the highest repute. Not far off, again, is " Bolaly," an obvious degeneration of Bowl Alley, as the street is termed in ancient maps of the town. Blanket-row, Dagger-lane, the Revery, Postern-gate, are other thoroughfares also, marked traces of which still remain; and there is in Hull a Paragon-street, a title not unknown elsewhere, as at Bath and one or two other towns.—The Art Journal.

How TO STIMULATE AN AUTHOR.—The Abbe Delille NTIS an author of some note In his day. One evening, when his ab3ence was remarked, Malouet and Lally went to his lolg- ings to look for him. They found him in bed, and asked anxiously if he was ill. He answered in the negative, throwing at the same time significant glances at a lady in the room. In explanation of this scene, Montlosier relates that the jady, who on the Abbe's return to England passed for his niece, had recently assumed the name and duties of a wife, and was notoriously ruling him with a rod of iron The story went that, on her flinging a quarto volume at his head, he submissively asked whether she could not have rested satisfied with an octavo. He had entered into a con- tract with his publishers at Paris for the completion of a poem within a given time, and they had come to an agree- ment with the lady to allow a percentage for helping him at work. It was his habit to compose in bed, and she required him to compose thirty lines every morning before getting up. Her mode of insuring the performance of the task was simple enough. "There is a little garment which the French have coarsely named 'culotte,' but which the Eng. lish ladies term the little garment 'small-cloth' (sic). When the Abbe had composed his thirty lines, she brought him his little garment, and he might get up, bet not otherwise." On the day when he was missed at Chateaubriand's he had been lazy or not in the vein, and the indispensable garment was withheld until the arrival of Malouet and Lally, by whose intervention, late in the evening, it was brought to him.—Quarterly Review.

TH E EX ANITNE-R, SATURDAY, MATCH 4,1882. r* • THE LAND QUESTION. I ILLUSTRIOUS IRISHNFN. We have in England and Wales, according to the official' returns as compiled in Mr. Brodrick's admirable work, 6' English Land and English Landlords," no less than 1,524,624 acres of waste land, of which 64,305 acres are stated to be in Lancashire, and 6,707 acres in Cheshire. How far these figures are inclusive or exclusive of commons, the writer has not been able to ascertain, as the statistics are often confusing and misleading. We will consider the subject of commons first, on which the exhaustive essay by the Right Hon. G. Shaw-Lefevre, M.P., in the Contemporary Review of January, 1879, supplies the bulk of the information. In times long anterior to the Norman Conquest, there was no individual ownership of land, which belonged to the community. That part which was suited to cultivation was enclosed and divided into three great fields for a three- coarse system of agriculture, of which one was always fallow; and each field was divided into a number of equal parts, which were distributed by lot every year among the heads of families constituting the community. Small plots were attached as gardens to the houses, and considered as Private property. The remaining land was open to the cattle of all. Such was the system introduced by the Saxons, who had inherited it from their Teutonic ancestors, and such was the early origin of our common lands, which was called foie land, or the people's land, and the villagers, whether owners of land or not, had the right of turning out their cattle there, and of cutting turf, or gorse, Or wood, for feel. Under the Norman feudal system the feudal lord claimed the freehold of this common land, subject to these rights of grazing, turf and fuel getting, on the part of the larger free tenants of the manor, which rights came to be regarded as privileges. In the reign of Henry 111., A.D. 1235, it was decided by the statute of Merton that the lords of the manors should have the power to enclose parts of the com- mon land for their own private use and benefit so long as they left sufficient pasture for the freehold tenants of the manor. At that time a large proportion of England was un- enclosed. In process of time, as mentioned in a previous article, the serfs of these manors became freemen, but the Courts of Law would not recognise their right to pasturage, ' &c., on the common lands, which was still limited to the comparatively few original freehold tenants, and by a Judicial decision given in 1603 in Lincolnshire in a disputed claim of this sort, a precedent was established which has re- sulted in the destructioo and extinction in thousands of cases of ancient rights and customs on the part of villagers with respect to commons. The lords of manors in very many cases found means to enclose with the consent of the few tenants who were legally recognised, with little or no compensation to the inhabitants generally, for this conver- sion of public property into private property. These rights of pasturage on the common waste were of great value to the small copyholders, as their own holdings were of ten too small to maintain a family, and in the 15th century these enclosures began to cause great discontent. The small yeo- men (the ancestors of our present agricultural labourers) could not hold on, and were easily bought out cheaply, and their cultivated land turned into pasture. They were too poor to commence the expensive legal proceedings necessary to protect themselves from the rapacity of their rich and powerful neighbours, who, like Ahab of old. coveted Naboth's vineyard, and the Judges of these times, unlike their successors of to-day, leaned to the big purses. Bacon, in his history of Henry VII., says—" Inclosures at this time began to be more frequent, whereby arable lands, which could not be manured without people and families, were turned into pasture, which was easily rid by a few herds- men, and tenancies for years, for lives, and at will, where- upon much of the yeomanry lived, were turned into demesnes. This bred a decay of people." In 1549 Bishop Latimer, preaching before Edward VI, and his Court, reproached the nobles as " inclosere, grazers, and rent raisers." Sir Thomas More complained that "noblemen, gentlemen, and even abbots, in their eagerness to swell their revenues, leave no ground for tillage. They enclose all into pasture, they throw down houses, they pluck down towns, and leave nothing standing. . . . Tenants are got rid of by force or fraud, or tired out by repeated injuries, into parting with their property," In +2l.i, iZ:gn o Ci seen Anne encioSuie begiin to be effected under private and local Acts of Parliament. In 1700 Lord Macaulay estimates that only one-half of England and Wales was under cultivation, but from that year down to 1845 no less than 7,175,000 acres were enclosed under about 4,000 separate Enclosure Acts or Enclosure Awards. The consent of three-fourths of the freeholders and copyholders of the manor was necessary as a preliminary, and the en- closed common was divided among them in proportion to their holdings, the lord of the manor usually taking one. sixteenth, in respect of his manorial interest, and taking another share in proportion to his right of common in re- spect of his demesne. He had, however, a veto on such en- closure, and as he possessed the sole right of sporting over the waste he semetimes exercised such veto, in preference to parting with his game. While this great amount of enclosure has doubtless been of great benefit to the nation at large, and the landowners in particular, it has been one of the chief means of "snuffing out" the small yeomen, who were dependent on grazing rights. In 1845 what is known as the General Enclosure Act was raesed providing that local enquiry should be first made, so as to ascertain the views of the small commoners, and preventing the great injustice which had previously oeen the custom. As Lord Lincoln said on introducing the Bill, "in nineteen cases out of twenty, Committees on Enclosure Bills in the House of Commons had neglected the rights of the poor." The effect of this Act of Parliament has been far from perfect. Between 1845 and 1869 614,800 acres of common land were enclosed. Of this only 3,962 acres were set apart for public purposes, viz., 1,742 acres for recreation grounds, and 2,220 acres for garden allotments for the pocr. "As a general rule the plots selected for garden allotments or recre- ation were the least suitable for the purpose, and remote from the villages. No regard was had for public interests. Commons were enclosed which were in no way suitable for cultivation, and which in their natural state were far more valuable to the nation, many of them being within easy reach of large populations." The enclosure of all these commons has had an injurious effect on the labouring population in their respective neighbourhoods. William Cobbett, in his well known Rural Rides," referred to this, for having spoken "of the great advantages formerly possessed by the cottagers from the cows, pigs, geese, and poultry, which they were able to keep on the waste, over which they had right," he contrasts "the dismal and miserable state of those districts where every inch of land is appropriated to large terms. No com- mons, no grassy lanes, the labourer has not a stick of wood, and no place for a pig or cow to graze on." In 1868 the Report of the Royal Commission on the Employment of Women and Children in Agriculture stated that "the agri- cultural labourers have lost opportunities and means of bettering their dondition which belonged to their class in former times," by two c eines. 1. The enclosure of waste lands; and 2. The absorption of small farms in large farms; "the second cause being undoubtedly dependent to a great extent on the first." In 1869 Mr. Fawcett, on these grounds, opposed the General Enclosure Bill for that year, whirls proposed to en- close 6,900 acres of common land in different parts of the country, of which three acres only were to be reserved as recreation grounds for the public, and six acres only as allot- ment gardens for the labouring poor. From that time until 1876 no further enclosuzes were sanctioned by the House of Commons, and in consequence of discussion on the subject there is no likelihood of any common being now enclosed with the eepproval of Parliament, unless there be some real advantage to the public. It appears, according to a Report of the Enclosure Commissioners in 1874, that there are still 2,632.000 acres of common or commonable land in England and Wales, of which but a small proportion is in the lowland districts, and by far the greater part is in the mountains of Wales and Carnberland, a very small part only being suit- able for arable cultivation. It would seem, therefore, that the extent of common land which can he enclosed with real advantage to the public is not considerable, and the necessity of preserving the few commons still left in the vicinity of populous districts all the more important., There are a number of members of Palliament deeply interested in the subject of these commons. "The interests of agricultural labourers in respect of numerous allotments of land under old enclosure awards, have been watched and defended; and the sale and misappropriation of such land have been pre- vented." There will still for some time to come be every occasion for watchfulness to prevent unauthorised and sur- reptitious enclosure. There is, hewever, doubtless in different parts of the country a considerable extent of waste land in private lands which is capable of being cultivated, or at least made far more productive than at present. Many of the present owners being merely life tenants, are not in a position to sick the necessary capital. Surely if the present owner is not able, from want of means, to develop such land, it is no reason why he should be allowed to follow the dog in the manger policy and prevent anyone else; nor would there be injustice if the Government or some duly authorised com- pany were to buy him out compulsorily at a fair price. Mountain sides will produce timber, while extensive bogs, when subjected to a proper system of arterial and other drainage, can be profitably reclaimed. The Bedford Level, embracing the Fens of Northampton, Huntingdon, Cam- bridge, Lincoln, Norfolk, and Suffolk, or an area of about 450,000 acres, has been converted from flat marshy land, by artificial drainage involving hundrees of thousands of pounds, into splendid highly productive farms. There are bogs in Lan- cashireand Cheshire, such as Chatmoss, Carrington Moss, and many others, which need similar treatment. Again, as an extreme instance of what can be done, it is worth while to remember that the Pays de Wals district in Belgium, al- though the soil is as pure sand as the sandhills of the Lan- cashire coast, and the climate no better, has been made pro- ductive by industry and manure, and now supports a con- siderable population. It cannot certainly be denounced as a revolutionary pro- posal that all lands now uncultivated, and not devoted to public purposes, and which can be cultivated with profit, shall be cultivated. On failure to cultivate by the present owner within a certain specified time, let the State take possession, paying the late owner a fair price, and then let it to tenant cultivators on terms dependent on the improve- ments covenanted to be made by the tenant, the rent payable to the; State to operate like the repayments of a Building Society's mortgage, i.e., gradually clearing off both prin- cipal and interest, and finally conferring on the tenant the freehold ownership. This country is too densely populated, there is too much capital wanting investment, and labour needing profitable employment, we purchase too much food from abroad of a class we could produce ourselves, to tolerate the continued existence of waste land at our own doors, meeting the re- quirements of such circumstances.
No. IX.—JOHN PHILPOT CURRAN. He knew no more of fear than one who dw ells
Beneath the tropics knows of icicles.—Anon.

From the period which Mr. Curran emerged from the irst struggles of an unfriended man, labouring up the steps of a jealous profession, his history forms a part of the annals of ria country. Once upon the surface, his light was always before the eye. It never sank, and was never outshone. The period in which he lived afforded to his forensic talents their most melancholy but most splendid occasions of exer- tion, for the distracted condition of the country gave rise to a series of historical trials, to the political interest of which his eloquence has now imparted an additional interest. _ . _ _

In 1794 Hamilton Rowan, a Frotestant gentleman of large fortune and of a most amiable and chivalrous character, was indicted by the law officers of the Crown for libel. The libel itself was published in 1792, and was in the form of an address to the Irish Volunteers, setting forth the dangers with which the country was threatened from foreign and 41:gestic foes, gag inviting them to rewne their arms for the preservatiCm of the generai tranquillity. Bat though this addresa was published in 1792, it was not till 1794 that it was prosecuted as a seditious libel and as dangerous to the public peace. Mr. Curran was selected by Mr. Rowan to conduct his defence, and it was no mean proof of the ad- vocate's courage that he undertook this defence. When Lord Carleton hinted that in holding a brief against 'the I Crown he ran the risk of losing his gown, 11;0:Drid and witty answer was, "Well, my lord, tt,y may take the silk, but most leave the staff," It was at this celebrated trial that Curran made A speech never to be forgotten in Ireland, and parts of which furnish specimens of oratory more widely diffused in England and America, and more frequently cited than any passage in the appeal of orators dead or living. The speech itself has been generally considered as one of Mr. Carran's ablest efforts at the bar. Lord Brougham, in Ms defence of Hunt, styled it the most eloquent speech ever delivered at the bar. It is one of the few that has been cor- rectly reported, and to this circumstance must be attributed its apparent superiority. It is well known that Mr. Curran thought more highly of some of his other forensic efforts than even this masterpiece of eloquence. After stating the case and commentiag on its law at some length, Mr. Curran referred to that part of the publication which proposed complete emancipation to persons of every religious persuasion, and expressed himself in a passage which is better remembered and more greatly admired than any separate portion of an address ever delivered at the bar in Ireland or in England :—" Do you think it wise or humane," inquired the Advocate, "at this moment to insult them (the Catholics) by sticking up in the pillory the man who dared to stand forth as their advocate? I put it to your oaths; do you think that a blessing of that kind, that a victory obtained by justice over bigotry and oppression, I should have a stigma cast upon it by an ignominious sen- tence upon men bold and honest enough to propose that measure? to propose the redeeming of religion from the abuses of the Church, the reclaiming of three millions of men from bondage, and giving liberty to all who had a right to demand it? giving, I say, in the so much censured words of this paper—giving 'Univetsal Emancipation ?' " "I speak in the spirit of the British law, which makes liberty commensurate with, and inseparable from, British coil; which proclaims even to the stranger and sojourner tha moment he puts his foot upon British earth, that the ground on which he treads is holy, and consecrated by the genias of Universal Emancipation.' No matter in what language his doom may have been pronounced, no matter wilat complexion incompatible with freedom, an Indian or an African sun may have burnt upon him—no matter in what disastrous battle his liberty may have been cloven down—no matter with what solemnities he may have been devoted upon the altar of slavery—the first moment he touches the sacred soil of Britain the altar and the God sink together in the dust; his soul walks abroad in her own majesty; his body swells beyond the measure of his chains that burst from around him; and he stAnds redeemed: re- generated, and disenthrallat by the irresistible genius of un,iversa/ Emancipation." .1 • - - took the whole Court by surprise. The crowd burst into a cry of admiration. The Bench, and the Bar, and the people were alike under the spell of the ad- vocate's wondrous eloquence. Silence being at length re- stored, Curran proceeded with singular grace and touching delicacy :—" Gentlemen, I am not such a fool as to attribute any effusion of this sort to any merit of mine. It is the mighty theme, and not the inconsiderable advocate, which can alone excite interest in the hearer. This is but the tes- timony which Nature bears to her own character—it is the effusion of her gratitude to that power which stamped that character upon her." Speaking of the means by which the liberty of nations may be subverted, he referred to the power of the Press. That power, he maintained, was the great antidote to tyranny —the instinctive power by which the voice of the people penetrates the doors of Cabinets and reaches the steps of thrones. " What remains," he exclaims "the liberty of the Press only—that sacred palladium which no influence, no power, no Minister, no Government, which nothing but the depravity, or folly, or corruption of a Jury can ever destroy." He then finely contrasted the national calamities that must follow on the restrictions of the Press, and the advantages to good government of that openness which ex- poses all secret machioations to the public -view. ". I will tell you, gentlemen, what they are saved from, and what the Government is saved from. I will tell you, also "to what both are exposed by shutting up that comeattnication. In one case sedition sneaks aloud and walks abroad. The demagogue goes fordi—the public eye is upon him—he frets his busy hoar upon the etage; but soon either weari- ness, or bribe, or punishment, or disappointment, bear him down, or drive him ca, and. he appears no more. In the other case, how does the work of sedition go forward? Night after night the muffled rebel steals forth in the dark, and casts another and another brand upon the pile, to which, when the hour of fatal maturity shall arrive, he will apply the flame. . . . In that awful moment of a nation's travail—of the last gasp of tyranny and the first breath of freedom how pregnant is the example? The Press ex- tinguished, the people enslaved, and the Prince undone. As the advocate of society, therefore, of peace, of domestic liberty, and the lasting union of the two countries, I conjure you to guard the liberty of the Press, that great sentinel of the State, that grand detector of public imposture—guard it—because when it sinks there sinks with it in one common grave the liberty of ;he subject and the security of the Crown." He then, in his own inimitable manner, directed the at- tention of the Jury to the character of the accused. "I will venture to say," exclaimed the bold advocate, "there is not a man in this nation more known than the gentleman who is the subject of this prosecution, not only by the part he has taken in public concerns, and which he has taken in common with many, but still more so by that extraordinary sympathy for human affliction, which a am sorry to think he shares with so small a number. There is not a day that you hear the cribs of your starving manufacturers in your streets, that you do not also see the advocate of their suffer- ings—his honest and manly figure, with uncovered head, so- liciting for their relief, searching the frozen heart of charity for every string that could be touched by compassion; and urging the force of every argument and every motive save that which his modesty suppresses—the authority of his own generous example. Or if you see him not there, you may trace his steps to the private abode of disease, and famine, and despair • the messenger of heaven, bearing with himfood, and medicine, and consolation. Are these the materials of which you suppose anarchy and public rapine to be formed? Is this the man on whom to fasten the abominable charge of goading on a frantic populace to mutiny and bloodshed? Is this the man likely to aposta- tise from every principle that can bind him to the State, his birth, his property, his education, his character, and his children ?"

In concluding his appeal t 3 the Jury Mr. Curran made one of those fine Scriptural allusions, of which he made such frequent and successful use. "I will not relinquish the confidence," he went on to say, "that this day will be the period of his sufferina • and however mercilessly he has been hitherto pursued, that your verdict will send him home to the arms of his family and the wishes of his country. But if (which Heaven forbid) it hath still been unfortunately determined that, because he has not bent to power and authority, berme be would not bow down before the golden calf and worship it, he is to be bound and cast into the furnace, I do trust in God that there is a redeeming spirit in the Constitution which will be seen to walk with the sufferer through the flames, and to preserve him unhurt by the conflagration." At the close of his speech the audience once more burst into acclamation, and on his leaving the Court the people took the horses from his carriage, and drew him in triumph home.

Yet notwithstanding this public homage to his talents, the most grateful reward of his exertions was wanting. The Jury, of whose purity very general suspicions were enter- tained, found a verdict against his client. Rowan was sen- tenced to two years' imprisonment and a fine of £5OO. After a short imprisonment Mr. Rowan effected his escape from prison and tied to France. After a long exile and many wanderings, he was permitted to return to his country, where he resided till the day of his death. It may be interesting for the reader to know that in the month of June, 1794, Dr. William Drennan was prosecuted for the publication of the same libel. He was defended by Mr. Curran and acquitted, not, however, on the merits of the imputed libel, but on failure of proof that Dr. Drennan had published it.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.
At a special meeting of the Durham Miners' Association, on Saturday, a resolution was passed requesting the Federation Board to ask the coalowners for au advance of wages.

The Cleveland Ironmasters' A ssociation held a meeting at Middlesborough, on Saturday, and resolved to continue the restriction of the make of the Cleveland pig iron 12. - per cent. until the end of September next. At an important meeting held in Manchester, on Tuesday the cotton manufacturers of North and North-East Lanca- shire resolved, in consequence of the depressed state of trade, to reduce production to the extent of two weeks' work before the 12th April next. Definite promises to run short time had previously been received from manufacturers represent- ing over 60,000 looms.

-PRESTON PAINTERS—The wages agitation among the painters, decorators, and paperhangers of Preston was settled on Tuesday night. 'The employers received a deputation from the men, ani.l by mutual concession the question was settled, the employers giving a halfpenny per hour advance,: commencing on Wednesday. The workmen's association applied ftrf the advance six months ago. The properties of the Darlaston Steel and and Iron Com- pany were offered for sale, at Wednesbury, on Monday, and out of thirty-six lots twenty-five were not sold, the other eleven producing £21,055. Among the unsold lots were the steel works, the sheet mill, the blast furnaces (Nos. 2 and 3), and almost all the lots of building land. The forges and mills, upon which more than £25,000 had been expended, were knocked down for £3,750. The question of a strike or DO strike for an advance of 5 per cent, in the wages of the Bolton spinners, was submitted on Saturday to the arbitrament of the ballot, which was now employed for the first time amongst these operatives. The votes for leaving work numbered 327, and those against leaving work 1,103, so that the demand for an advance will be withdrawn. Nearly 1,000 members of the Spinners' Union did not vote. It is interesting to observe that—con- trary to the advice of the Council—a meeting of delegates on the previous evening was in favour of a strike. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE: Manchester, Wednesday. —The business doing in the iron market continues very limited in extent, and although quoted prices are without any material alteration from last week, to effect sales con- cessions upon current rates are in most cases necessary. For pig-iron the inquiry continues extremely small. Makers of both local and district brands are open to offers at 40s. to 505., less al-, for forge and foundry qualities, delivered equal to Manchester, but they are booking very few new orders at these figures, and there are sellers in some cases at less money. Hematites are also easier in price, and can now be bought at ss. per ton under late rates, foundry qualities de- livered equal to Manchester averaging 70s. per ton. Finished iron makers are still generally holding for £7 per ton for bars delivered into the "Manchester district, but good specifications *might in some cases be placed at 2s. GI under current rates, and mlrclaants are sellers at £6 15s. The engineering branches of trade continue generally well employed.

THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE: Manchester, Wednesday. —The coal trade continues very depressed, and with the commencement of the month a pretty general reduction in the price of house coal has come into operation. In the ! Manchester district the leading firms have reduced their delivered rates to consumers 10d. per ton on house coal and sd. per ton on burgy, but other classes of fuel are without change. In the West Lancashire districts prices have b3en gradually receding for soma time past, and this mouth there is a giving way more or less general of about 6d. per ton upon the previously quoted prices: for the better classes of round coal at the pit mouth. The average prices at which coal can now be bought at the pit may be given at about Bs. 6d. to Os. for the better qualities for house-fire purposes, Gs. 6d. to 7s. for seconds ss. to Gs. for common coal, 4s. Gd. to ss. for burgy, and is. dd. to 4s. 3d. per ton for good slack. The amount of business doing during the week has been very limited. In the shipping trade rather more activity !s in smite caqeS reported, but generally business is dull, and low prices are taken. THE CORN TRADE.---The MA: Lane Express says : " The weather in the Englih counties for the past week has been for the most part dull and mild down to Saturday, when a gale of wind and rain set in and continued during Monday. The rainfall, however, has been slight, and the temperature has not fallen. The growing crops remain in a most favourable position, and spring sowing is pro- gressing in a rapid and satisfactory manner. The position of the grain trade is anything but satisfactory. Prices for the best samples of native wheat are weaker, and . occa- sionally lower, whilst inferior samples are practically un- saleable. Flour has been irregularly cheaper during the week, at the close of which all breadstuffs met a very de- pressed trade and a very limited inquiry. With the excep- tion of grinding barleys being occasionally cheaper, there has been no alteration in the value of other native produce. ! The trade for foreign breadstuffs off stands lapsed into a state of extreme depression at the close of the week in the principal markets of England. There is no fresh cause for this, but the Ono which has been influencing the market for' some weeks past is now becoming intensified."

div.head: EMPRESS OP AUSTRIA.
div.p: THE EMPRESS OP AUSTRIA.

The Empress of Austria hunted with Sir Watkin Wyma's hounds on Saturday. Inc meet was at Edge Greeti, a eouple ' of miles from Alalpas, and about ten from Combermere Abbey. The weather was unfavourable. All the covers about E]ge were drawn blank, and unfortunately this was the case at Lowcross, Grafton Larges, and Clutton's Gorses. The field then trotted to Duckington Wood, on the hills, where three or four foxes were soon on foot. One crossed the road and went into the open; another, which the hounds hunted, ran on to the hills at the back of Broxton Station, where after dodging about for some time he was lost, and at 3-30 the hounds were ordered home. On Monday the Empress hunted with Sir Watkin Wynn's hounds. The meet was at Holt, in Flintshire. The hounds were taken to Carden Cliff, where a grand fox was speedly on foot. Breaking away at a capital pace, he Ivent down the hill to the park lodge gate, then turning to the left, ran past the Hooks straight on to Edge Park; through the park up the hill to Overton Scar, over which he went past Cluttou's Gorse ; leading which to the left, he bore,to the right over the road to Lowcross; past Edge Hall, alongside the Chester and Whitchurch railway, past the Hooks again, down nearly to Carden, being eventually lost close to the lodge gate, after a grand run over a rough and heavy country of an hour and a quarter. Rain had fallen more or less the whole time, and as there was no appearance of it ceasing her Majesty proceeded to Carden Hall, and, having stayed there a short time, she and her suite left in their broughams for Combermere Abbey, a dozen miles away. The Empress put in a long day with the South Cheshire hounds on Tuestay. The meet was at Wilkesley. After drawing Kent's Rough and Adderley Wood in vain, the hounds were taken to Shavington, which yielded a fox. He ran half way round the park, then beaded towards Wilkesley and Brooke's Mill, where the scent being indifferent he was given up. The hounds were subsequently put into Mr. Poole's gorse adjoining Combermere, where a brace of foxes were found. Tbe hounds got on line of one, which ran through part of Combermere Woods, then hearing to the left went down nearly to the railway, as if for Marley Moss, but turning to the right he crossed the road and was making back towards Combermere, when suddenly he made to the right arrd ran nearly to the railway bridge by IVrenbury Station ; he then crossed the two roads and went near Sineaton farm, over the Wrenbury brook and canal, and eventually ran them out of scent near to the Veld, after a lengthy and most enjoyable run over a beautiful country. Her Majesty fully intended hunting with the North Staf- ford hounds, which met at Adderley on :Wednesday, but the morning was so very threatening, and the previous heavy day having somewhat fatigued her, she decided to liave a quiet day of it. This was a great disappointment to Mr. Corbet and a large party who were present to meet her. Prince Lichtenstein and Major Bulkeley were present. It being the special wish of the Prince of Wales to have an interview with the Empress before she leaves England, her Imperial Majesty has made arrangements to stop half an hour at Kensington, on her way from Windsor Castle to Dover, on Monday next.

The adventuress's goods were sold by auction, under power of a bill of sale, at Liverpool, on Friday. The lots were of an ordinary description, and brought the usual prices. Amongst other items sold was a quantity of jewellery, which displayed all a lady's lore of ornament, notwithstanding Miss Furneaux's great ambition was to be thought a man. It consisted of a lady's gold Geneva watch, a 15-carat dress ring (corals and pearls), a half-hoop ditto, a half-hoop diamond ring, and a heavy gold albert chain. There was also among the lots a plated telescope drinking cup, a railway travelling lamp, and several opera glasses, which latter articles be- tokened her predilection for theatrical spectacles. Euterpe was represented by a cottage pianoforte by Ajello, a har- monium by Schiedmayer, and several musical instruments. Among her collection of hooks was the Bible, which showed that the possessor sometimes, at least, had more serious thoughts than that of personating a defunct nobleman. The works of Josephus were also amongst the number. Besides these she had the "Clergy Directory of 1879," the latter no doubt proving useful as a reference in case of need. For moments of relaxation she bad several works of pure fiction. Amongst the novels were " Asmodeus," "Heritage of Lucy Dale," "The 'Two Destinies," "Alice Lorraine," "Horace Templeton," "Heartsease," "Lady Betty," " Juck Thurlow and I," 'The Parisians," "Constance Mordaunt," Charles Lever," " Mortenby's Estate," rSzc. There were among the rots several engravings, amongst which may be mentioned "Incidents in the Life of Lord Beaconsfield," and "Funeral of the Earl of Beaconsfield ;" also a splendid photograph of the same celebrated statesman, evidently showing the lady's predilection for Conservatism, coupled, it may be, with an aspiration that whatever mutations took place in this change- ful world "our old nobility" might be left to us. Notwith- standing that the auctioneer appealed to the company "to recollect the memories connected with the different articles" which he offered, only ordinary prices were obtained for the goods, which were all sold.

FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

Prince Henry of Prussia has arrived safely at Jerusalem. A despatch from Ismailia reports that the block of shipping in the Suez Canal has now ceased. It is reported from Berne that the new commercial treaty between Switzerland and France has been signed. The Dominion House of Commons has passed the second reading of. the Marriage with the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill. _ _ _ _
There are renewed rumours in influential quarters as to an approaching reconciliation between Germany and the Vatican.
From St. Petersburg we bear that the Trans-Caspian rail- way scheme has obtained the support of all classes of the community, and that its construction is now only a matter of time. _ _

_ While Kin..' su Alphonso and his ite were out hunting the other day, in Andalusia, the King's horse was wounded by a wild boar. His Majesty dismounted forthwith, and killed the animal with his hunting knife. • From Berlin we learn that the Nihilist teal at St. Peters- burg is concluded. Ten of the prisoners, Including one woman, have been sentenced to death, and the others to various terms of imprisonment. The bill for the establishment of a new mail steamship service between America and England, and authorising the appropriation of the sum of $2500,000 for thlt purpose, has been reported back to the House of Representatives. News received in Plymouth by the China mail states that piracy is still rampant in the Canton river, u passenger and a cargo boat having both been attacked. The pirates, after securing the cargo and passengers' clothing, made their escape. The bill establishing the mist favoured nation clause between France and England, passed the Chamber of Depu- ties on Saturday without discussion; and an opinion was expressed that negotiations for an Anglo-French treaty should be resumed.

The Canadian Budget was presented in the Dominion House of Commons on Saturday. Sir S. L. Tilley stated that at no period of the history of the country had the finances been in as good a position, credit so high, or the people 90 prosperous. Sad accounts have reached us from Waslington of the disastrous effects of the floods in the Mississipi valley. The country inundated is 150 miles long and 40 wide. In one locality, it is stated, 1,000 negroes are starving, and that from 50,000 to 75,000 labourers are destitute. The Egyptian Ministry have given orders to the new dovernor General of the Soudan to act with vigour against the slave dealers. A special committee has been appointed to assiit in administering the affairs of the province, and they are required to put a stop to "the terrible traffic in human beings which excites the indignation of humanity!' Candahar is quiet, and the Ameer is conciliating the chiefs, but stories are still abroad of Russian advances and of traders from the Russian.camp having already appeared in Herat. The Ameer is said to have had some disagreeable letters from Mahomed Ishak Khan, Governor of Turkes- tan, who complains that his brothers are not treated with consideration.

The French Government have resolved to modify the law of 1849 relating to the exclusion of foreigners from France in the following sense :—That every foreigner who has already been convicted of crime in his own country may be .expelled immediately and without formality, but if he has not been so convicted the case must be brought before the Council of Ministers.

It is now reported, on apparently reliable authority from St. Petersburg, that the recall of General Scobeleff was ordered from head-quarters before he delivered the speech to the Servian students, which has been so much com- mented on, for the reason that he had held personal inter- course, • with apparently ulterior political objects, with Frenchmen who are unconditionally attached to what is known as the "Revenge party." GENERAL GARFIELD'S ATTENDANTS,—The Committee of the United States Congress, which is auditing the expenses connected with General Garfield's illness, has determined to allow the physicians and nurses the following amounts : Dr. Bliss, $25,000; Dr Agnew, $15,000; Dr, Hamilton, $15,000; Dr. Reyburn, $10,000; Dr. Boynton, $10,000; Mrs. Edson, $5,000; Mr. Crump, steward of the White House, is allowed $3,000, and the other White House employ6s are to receive two months' extra pay. Surgeon- General Barnes is to be promoted to be major-general on the the retired list. Surgeon Woodward is to be promoted to be lieutenant-colonel. The Committee also grant Mrs. Gar- field the remainder of the President's salary for the current year. EXTRAORDINARY DESIGN TO ASSASSINATE M. GAMBETTA. —At the Seine assizes, on Monday, Emile Florion' twenty- three, weaver, was sentenced to twenty years' hard labour for firing at a doctor at Neuilly. His original design was to assassinate M. Gambetta as a protest against middle-class ascendancy. He set out on foot from Rhei:ns last October with a revolver, and for three days prowled about the Palais Bourbon; but M. Gambetta not being visible be resolved to shoot the first rich-looking man he met. lie accordingly fired at Dr. Meymar, whom be did not know, but who wore a foreign decoration, and then attempted suicide. Happily, Dr. Meymar's face was merely grazed. The evidence showed that the prisoner had taken part in strikes, read Socialistic papers, had been dismissed by his employers for sullenness or insubordination, and had determined to kill one of those men—M. Gambetta, M. Grevy, or M. Ferry, for instance— whom he described as fattening on the swelt of the masses'. On the sentence being delivered, the prisoner exclaimed, " I quite expected it. You (the jury) arc all bribed. rive la Revolution soeiale !"

VISIT TO THE PITCAIRN ISLANDS —A repert has been made to the Admiralty of a visit paid in April last by H.M.S. Thetis to Pitcairn Island. This far-distant and interesting little colony, founded by the mutineers of the Bounty, was found in a flourishing condition. The whole population, now numbering about 100 souls, turned out en masse to give a welcome to our blue jackets. The only dread the islanders have is that they will be some day forgotten and left entirely cut off from all tidings of the outer world. But this is a fate that is not likely ever to befall them. Her Majesty has shown that she kindly remembers the little speck in the ocean inhabited by these interesting people, and they receive occasional visits from passing vessels. The advent of a British man-cf-war off their coast is an event for great rejoicing, and for interchange of pleasant courtesies. The islanders send off a supply of bananas and limes, for which they decline all payment. They are always glad to receive articles of clothing, prints for the women's dresses and cloth far the men. They do not produce such articles on the island, and they have therefore to trust to outside supplies to prevent them lapsing into primitive modes of attire. An American trader lately left the islanders a supply of cotton seed, and they hope to be able to culti- vate the plant. EXPLOSION IN AN AUSTRIAN MINE: TERRIBLE

div.head: LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: LOSS OF LIFE.

A terrible explosion is reported from Leoben, in Styria. At that place there are some extensive coal mines.belonging to the Alpine Montan-Gesellschaft. At the time of the accident the miners appear to have been almost all at work. The explosion which took place was most destructive. The number of lives lost, so far as could be ascertained, was no less than 150, including tNO of the superintendents. It is only a few weeks ago since the announcement was made that the Alpan Minirg Company had been purchased by M. Bontoux. THE INSURRECTION IN THE HERZEGOVINA. A telegram from Constantinople announces that the Sultan has ordered twelve battalions of troops to be des- patched to Novi-Bazar to occupy the district between that place and the Austrian military line, in order to prevent the passage of insurgent binds and to arrest the Panslavist movement in that direction. The situation of affairs in the Balkan Provinces threatens to become still further complicated. It is announced from Cettinje that several thousand refugees fram Herzegovina have forced their way into Montenegrin territory, impelled thereto by the terrible sufferings they were enduring on the frontier. The Austrian military authorities admit a loss of 116 killed and wounded, including ten officers, in Herz9govina, between the 16th and 28th ult. The rebels persistently re- fuse, says the Austrian General, to come to close quarters with his men—a statement which is curiously confirmed by the admissions of officers engaged in the operations to a corresp indent at Ragusa. A correspondent says that the Austrian force engaged amounts to 60,100 ien, with 123 guns. A Cettinje telegram, dated Tuesday, says :—lntelligence received here through Slavonic sources states that. a severe engagement was fought on the 25th ult., on the Drina, near Foci, between the Austrians and the insurgent leader, Stojan Kovacsevic. Some Austrians battalions left FOca with the object of dislodging Kovacsevic, who defended the passage of the Drina. The attempt was, however, unsuccessful, Kovacsevic maintaining his position. The account asserts that the Austrians lost two or three hundred killed and wounded, while the insurgents had only fifteen killed and thirty wounded. Many BOsnian families are taking refuge at Plajevije.
