div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 4, IEB2.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 4, IEB2.
M I SCEL LANEOUS.

Mr. Sexton has fixed the 13th of March as the day on which he proposes to have a call of the House. Mr. A. Blanchard has engraved in line, and Mr. Lef6vre will shortly publish Messonier's well-known picture the "Connoisseur," exhibited in the Hanover Gallery Exhibition of 1880.

——- - - Admiral Loney, the "father " of the British navy, died at Plymouth, the other day. at the age of 95. He had for the long period of 34 or 35 years been connected with the navy. Mr. Henry Underhill, town clerk of Wolverhampton, died on Monday morning, in the 60th year of his age. He suc- ceeded the late Mr. E. J. Hayes as town clerk of the borough in 1860. The Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh inaugurated the Electrical Exhibition at the Crystal Palace on Saturday. Their Royal Highnesses were accompanied by the Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont. On Saturday the Governor of Norwich Castle received a respite for Henry Stebbings, whose execution had been fixed to take place on Monday for the murder of a girl named Brett in Norfolk. HomicidaVmania is understood to be the ground fot the respite. The exclusive character of the Old Water-colour Society is driving many well-known artists into the New, viz., the Institute of Painters in Water-colours, of which Mr. Keeley Halswelle, Mr. Joseph Knight, Mr. M‘Whirter, A.R.A., ana Mr. Randolph Caklecott have this week been elected members. William and Susannah Wadsworth have been charged at Manchester with having neglected their child, who is about three years of age. The evidence showed that the child was so weak that it could neither sit nor stand. The father was sentenced to six and the mother to three months' im- prisonment. The High Church party propose to make the anniversary of the Rev. S. F. Green's arrest, Sunday, March 19, a day of special intercession for his release from Lancaster Gaol. The recent appeal made to the Wesleyan Methodist ministry by means of a circular letter for the purpose of evoking sympathy and aid in behalf of Mr. Green has turned out an utter failure. On Sunday morning, immediately after the second lesson and the third publication of the banns, at St. Jude's, Hard- wick-street, Liverpool, a mart lege was solemnised, owing to the bridegroom having to sail to America at four o'clock the following morning. lhe vicar gave a sermon in place of the address, explaining why the marriage had taken place at this unusual time. A disastrous fire occurred in Manchester on Tuesday morning a large carpet and general furnishing warehouse, in the occupation of Messrs. Faulkner Brothers, being entirely gutted and the stock destroyed. The building was originally the Olympic Theatre, attached to which was the Olympic Hotel. The damage done by the fire is roughly estimated at £45,000. At Hatfield Park, the seat of the Marquis of Salisbury, the piles to support a coffer-dam across the river Lea have just been successfully driven by the power from a water- wheel situated at a distance, which power was transmitted by two dynamo-machines and a couple of wires to the gear- ing connected with a pile-driver of ordinary construction, and which were erected on a barge floating in the river. The War Office have consented to place three or four of the forts in the neighbourhood of Gosport at the disposal of the commanding officers of the volunteers on Easter Monday, and Colonel Bennett, commandant of Royal Marines, has pro- mised to provide accommodation for 500 men at the Marine Barracks. Provision will thus be made for about 3,000 men, who may arrive on or before Easter Sunday. In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, judgment was given in the case of Bull v. Esquilant, in which the defendant had obtained a rule nisi for a new trial. rhia was an action for libel brought by the Rev. W. Bull, of North Woolwich, against Esquilant for charging him with im- moral conduct. At the trial the jury found for the plaintiff, with £2 damages. Their lordships were of opinion that this verdict should stand, and discharged the rule. The case of the Queen v. Lister, in which Mr. Roberts, who was appointed City Rmiembrancer in 1878, brought a criminal information for libel against the defendant, who was a clerk in the Remembr.ancer's office, was concluded in the Queen's Bench Division on Tuesday. The Attorney- General, who prosecuted, said he was prepared to stop the case if the defendant undertook to withdraw all imputations against the prosecutor's integrity. This was done, and the jury were discharged. An order has been received in Leeds from the Local Gov- ernment Board giving effect to the result of the poll taken last October on the subject of the triennial election of mem- bers of the Board of Guardians. The order states that here- after members of the Board will sit for three years, instead of for one as at present. Leeds is the fourth town in the country which has secured this privilege, which will effect a considerable saving of public money. Sir Charles Dilke has addressed a communication to the Manchester Chamber of Commerce on the subject of the French Treaty negotiations. He says Her Majesty's Government much regret the unsatisfactory termination of the existing treaties and of the recent negotiations, but their deterniination not to be a party to a retrogade treaty has been announced throughout the discussions, and it has met with the concurrence of commercial bodies in the country and with the sanction of Parliament. On Sunday, the Salvation Army visited Oldham for the first time, and met with a stormy reception. At the out- door meeting they were mobbed and hustled off the ,e.round, the Hallelujih young women having to be protected by the police. They adjourned to the skating rink, where thousands ' of roughs assailed them with oaths and curses. Missiles were thrown. Subsequently the army were parsued to their lodgings, stoned, and covered with tilth. In the afternoon the mob broke the widnows and burst the door panels of the rink.

The police at Hall have under investigation a case in which a fisherman named Elijah Richardson has, it is alleged, confessed to having murdered a policeman belong- ing to the Hull force on the 10th September, 1880, by push- ing him into one of the docks and drowning him. A heavy and continuous downfall of rain, lasting for a considerable time, has again caused rivers and their tribu- taries to overflow their banks in Warwickshire and other parts of the Midland counties. Largo tracts of low-lying land are submerged, and in some places footpaths have once more become impassable. Mr. H. C. Raikes, M.P., presided on Tuesday at the half- yearly meeting of the Mersey Railway Company, and in moving the adoption of the report, congratulated the share- holders on the rapid and satisfactory progress which was ' being made with the tunnel works, and the bright prospects a the undertaking generally. Mr. George Leeman, M.P. for York from 1865 to 1880, died at Scarborough at half-past three o'clock on Saturday afternoon. His illness commenced with an attack of

paralysis on Shrove Tuesday of 1880, and a renewal of the attack occurred on the 21st inst, Shrove Tuesday of the present year. He was born in 1809. The Prince of Wales presided on Monday at a meeting in support of the proposed International Fishery Exhibition next year. The Duke of Edinburgh referred to the neglected state of the Irish fisheries, and remarked that they would probably derive some benefit by the attention which the exhibition would draw to the general condition of eur coast fisheries.

At the monthly meeting on Monday the Board of Manage- ment of the Manchester Royal Infirmary was informed that as the result of the late special appeal for funds there had been collected a sum of £33.940. This includes increased subscriptions, contibutions for .a term of years, and dona- tions, whilst in addition legacies have been notified of the value of £34,000. The largest and most remarkable rough diamond that has been received from India for many years is now in England. It is a pure blue-white stone weighing 67 carats, in form nearly a drop, and when cut and polished would be about the shape of the Sancy diamond. Its form would also allow of a perfect round being obtained. The surface is slightly indented, but there are no marks of cleavage, it being a perfectly natural crystal. The estimated value is £35,000. One of the numerous recent" mysterious disappearances" was cleared up at Worship-street Police Court, London, on Saturday. A Mrs. Gillett had stated some time ago that her dAughter Minnie had disappeared since the Ist of the month. Slio,had actually been absent from home since the Ist of January, and was known to be in the vicinity of the mother's house. She bad told several people that she was really turned out. The custody of two orphan children is giving rise to con- siderable interest in Nottingham. They were in a Roman Catholic home, and their relatives desired to remove them, alleging gross neglect and ill-treatment against the priests and nuns; but the priests refused to give them up, as the relatives were Protestants. After an unsuccessful applica- tion to the magistrates the relatives took the children by force, and are now concealing them. They are deseribed as covered with sores and in a filthy condition. Mr. Frith's picture of the Royal Academy " On the Day of the Private View," will, no doubt, be one of the most popular pictures at the forthcoming Royal Academy Exhibi- tion in May. The plates after Toffan'y and Ramberg, with portraits and costumes and pictures in city, have never lost their interest, and it is about time that another should be added to the series. The subject is well fitted to the powers of Mr. Frills, who will prezerve the life and character of the different artists and other personages introduced. In the Lenten pastoral of the Bishop of Salford, read in all the Roman Catholic churches of the diocese on Sunday, it is contended that society has de-Christianised the State, that the State in turn is de-Christianising national educa- tion, and that the present School Board system is the educa- tional peril to Christianity. Dr. Vaughan expressess his regret "that efforts have been made recently, under the School Board system, to interfere with parental rights, and to prevent the opening of Catholic schools, or to close them when opened." A very bad case of defying the cattle diseases regulations was heard at the Carlisle Petty Sessions on Monday. Wm. Johnstone, cattle dealer, was charged with moving cattle from Cumberland into Scotland in contravention of the orders of the Privy Council. In one instance he had altered the figures of a pass to make it carry a larger num- ber of cattle. There were three charges in all, and the defendant pleaded guilty to them. He was fined £3O and costs. The proceedings were taken by direction of the Privy Council. MUNIFICENCE or A LADY.—Mrs. Frances Grant, residing at Rock Ferry, near Liverpool, has placed aside a suns of £lOO,OOO, the interest of which she has directed shall be paid for the relief of the deserving poor, without reference to class or creed. The interest on this munificent gift amounts to about £4,000. annually, and in the distribu- tion of the money Mrs. Grant now takes a lively personal interest. It may be added that Mrs. Grant gave £lO,OOO for the foundation of a chair in connection with the University College of Liverpool. GRANTS TO PROVINCIAL MUSEUITS.--In interesting return has been prepared, showing the capital amount ex- pended upon buildings, fittings, Lc., by the principal towns which have established libraries or galleries of art, or both, under the Free Libraries and Museums Act. From this

A destructive fire occurred on Friday afternoon, at Patri- croft, in a cotton mill worked by Messrs. E. and A. Har- greaves. Commencing in the spinning-room, presumably from the friction of machinery, the fire spread over nearly the whole building, which was reduced to a heap of ruins in spite of strenuous efforts on the part of a number of firemen from the district. The damage, it is stated, cannot be less than £65,000, but this is fully covered by insurances in a number of offices. Five hundred workpeople have been thrown out of employment. William Henry Leonard, aged 46, pleaded guilty, at the Central Criminal Court, London, on Tuesday, to several in- dictments charging him with robbing children of their clothes. The prisoner appeared to have carried on a regular system of accosting children in the street, and under various pretences, inducing them to accompany him to a lonely place, where he stripped them of the greater portion of their eothes, leaving the poor children almost in a state of nudity. He was sentenced to seven years' penal servi- tude.

At a meeting of the Manchester School Board, on Mon- day, a discussion took place as to the advisability of the Board undertaking the duty of removing young children who may, after the bill promoted by the Corporation shall have become law, he found engaged in "casual employ- ment "in the streets after certain hours at night. As the hill stands, this duty will devolve upon the School Board. The Chairman of the Board (Mr. Herbert Birley) and four of his colleagues voted in favour of a motion to c 'et the work upon the Corporation, but the proposal was defeated by a majority of two. AmarrrEn WIFE MURDER.—At Weduesburv, on Tues- day, Edward Meakin, aged 40, a labourer, was remanded for committing a murderous outrage on his wife. Late on Mon- day night, the prisoner went home and had an altercation with his wife. He knocked her down and kicked her until she was imensible. When on the floor he plunged a carving fork into the back of her head, which caused dangerous in. juries. On being detected inflicting further injuriea, prisoner left home, but was subsequently arrested in a public house. He said he knew nothing about the matter. The wife is in a very dangerous condition. Major Marindin has reported to the Board of Trade upon the collision on January 23 at Hornsey Station, on the Great Northern Railway, when three fatalitiee occurred and a large number of persons were injured. The accident occurred in a thick and sudden fog. In his conclusion Major Marindin says although the accident was a consequence of a very sudden and dense fog, the driver of the Moorgate train is g ' greatly to be blamed for having passed the advanced starting signal without ascertaining whether it was against him or otherwise. He ought, also, to have proceeded more cautious- ly. Major Marindin adds that the entire system of fog signalling is a very weak poiet, and requires improvement. - -

TILE PROPOSED NATIONAL COLLEGE OF Music—The Prince of Wales presided on Tuesday over an influential meeting held at St. James's Palace in connection with the movement for establishing a National College of Music. The Dukes of Edinburgh, Albany, Teck, and Canibridge, Mr. Gladstone, Sir Stafford Northcote, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Earl Derby, and Cardinal Manning were amongst those present. The subscriptions at present pro- mised inolude £5OO from the Queen, and amount to about £lO,OOO. The Prince of Wales explained that free educa- tion in music, coupled with the free maintenance of the pupil, would be a distinguishing feature of the institution. They would not exclude paying pupils. Five scholars would be selected by open competition. Arrangements bad been made with the Exhibition Commissioners for a site at Kensington. A charter of incorporation had been prepared, and he had undertaken to be president. On the motion of the Duke of Edinburgh, a resolution was carried approving of the proposed college and pledging the meeting to give it active support. Mr. Gladstone proposed, and Sir" Stafford Northcote seconded, a vote of thanks to the Prince of Wales.

" JUMBO."—The Zoological Gardens were visited on Mon- day by no fewer than 8,571 people, against 674 on the i corresponding day last year, so great is the anxiety shown to take a farewell view of the celebrated elephant. As is usual on the occasion of other public demonstrations of sympathy and interest, those who could not personally attend wrote letters indicative of their concurrence. Six or seven hundreds of signed and anonymous communications have been re- ceived since the "Jumbo " movement began, and some of the writers have given practical expression to their feelinc, by enclosing buns, which have been duly conveyed tc the ject of their delicate attentions. One corresponelent euggested that a looking glass should be placed in the end of the box: I formed to receive the gigantic captive. The elephant, it I, was thought, would, upon reflection, advance towards it. Another writer offered to place the elephant in the box for £10; but made the somewhat ignoble condition that this , sum, together with his travelling expenses to London, should first be remitted to him in the country. The Council of the Zoological Society not been able to accede to this suggestion. The box itself, which had been placed ousido the animal's ' den, has been removed in order teat it may be placed on a lower trolly. It is undergoing considerable alterations, and la ultimately to be only at a height of 6irn from the ground. It seems quite uncertain whether the animal will be shipped to-day. Owing to the wet weather he did not gc out. This lstate of the weather made the great number of visitors stUl more remarkable,.

An anonymous donor has again giYen £2,500 to the Liver- pool medical and other charities. At the Grand Lodge of Freemasons, on Wodneslay-night, the Prince of Wales was again elected Most Worshipful Grand Master. The trial of Dr. Lamson for the murder of Percy John, his

brother-in-law, was on Wednesday fixed for Monday next at the Central Criminal Court. Her Majesty's ships Bacchante and Cleopatra, the former having on board the Princes Albert Victor and George of Wales, arrived at Suez on Wedwsday evening, and were granted free pratique. At the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, John Mowbey was indicted fur the manslaughter of his son, eight years old. The prisoner is one of the Peculiar People, and failed to call in a doctor when his child was ill. He was found guilty, and ordered to come up for judgment when called upon. The Board of Trade has signified its intention to revoke the order giving permission for the use of steam on the Burnley and district tramways. Numerous summonses have been taken out by the police against the Tramways Com- pany. This action was censured at a meeting of the Town Council, on Wednesday, and it was decided to ask the Board of Trade on what grounds it had come to its present decision.

A most audacious and impudent robbery was committed at Coventry, early on Wednesday mprning. A cabowner named Maton, living in Swanswell-street, has stabling and coachyard adjoining his residence. During the night, the premises were entered, and .a valuable horse and cab driven away so noiselessly that no one in the house was disturbed ; the horse rug being torn up and evidently used to muffle the horse's hoofs. The affair has created a great sensation, no clue having yet been obtained of the thief. A meeting of the friends of the Liverpool D:ocesan Board _ _

of Education was held on Wednesday, Bishop Ryle pre- siding. A satisfactory report was read. Archdeacon Bardsley said that the Church of England provided 55 9 per cent, of the school accommodation; the school board system 25-5 per cent.; the British, Wesleyan, and undenominational schools 13-1 per cent.; and the Roman Catholics 5-9 per cent. The "unfortunate nobleman" is now " languishing " at Portsmouth, where he may sometimes be seen sawing wood and unloading timber in the dockyard. The Claimant, al- thouer greatly reduced in bulk, appears to be in good health and quite able to do his work. At the time of his sentence he weighed 25 stone, and lie has now the appearance of being about 16 stone. Castro's daily ration is understood to he about a quarter more than that of a prisoner of ordi- nary size and bulk. He may claim to be a proof of the sufficiency of prison diet. Dr. O'Beilly, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool, presided at the annual meeting of the Catholic Reformatory Association, on Wednesday, when the reports for the train- ing ship Clarence, the Birkdale Reformatory School, and the May-place Girls' Reformatory were submitted. It was stated that 75 per cent, of the boys turned out well, but that the percentage of the '(iris was not s 3 high. The bishop appealed for increased subscriptions. Mr. Raffles said the reports were quite as favourable as those of the Protestant institutions of a similar kind connected with this city. On Wednenday afternoon the premises in Fleet-street, Liverpool, where Conroy's malt coff 473 was being manufac- , tured, were visited by an °Meer of excise, who, eta asking 1 for the proprietor or responsible person, announced his intention of seizing all the stuff in the place. The seizure, as might be expected, came with sudden surprise on all,who saw a complete stop put to their means of subsistence. Explanation was demanded as to this sudden step on the part of the authorities, but no explanation was given. Some tons of the preparation found in the place were immediately put under seizure, in charge of another officer of excise, and a complete stop was put to the works. Lord Hartington was present at the banquet in connee- don with the sittings of the appointed Chambers of Com- merce on Wednesday evening, and, replying to the toast of Her Majesty's Government, made reference to the experi- ment which the Government propose to try of a division of labour in the House of Commons by submitting to a stand- ing committee all measures affecting trade. If the proposal were carried, his lordship said, a committee would be formed representing fairly the political opinions of the House, and composed in the main of those interested in commercial and , industrial pursuits. ' A REASONABLE GRUMBLE. —At the meeting of the Liverpool City Council, on Wednesday, a memorial was presented from some chimney sweeps praying the •Council to obtain a more vigorous police surveillance and prosecu- tion of persons who allowed their chimneys to take fire. The memorialists stated that the practice of householders firing their own chimneys was on the increase, and that not only was the atmosphere of the city thereby fouled, but the sweeps were deprived of their earnings, and consequently of the opportunity of bringing up their families " in the way that every honest chimney-sweeper would wish."—The memorial was referred to the Watch Committee. At the Manchester City Police Court, on Wednesday, Thomas Llewellyn Hodson, John Travis, and Charles Bret- tingham, medical students at Owens College, were charged with having along with others created a riot during the per- formance of the drama "George Barnwell," and the panto- mime "Aladdin," at the Queen's Theatre, Manchester, on Shrove Tuesday. The charge of riot was not established, and as regards the defendant Brettingham, the Stipendiary found that no offence whatever bad been committed. Hodson and Travis, who were shown to have engaged in certain disorderly prkeedings, were bound over to keep the peace for a period of six months, and ordered to pay the Mts. div.head: CONFLICT WITH THE HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: THE CONFLICT WITH THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

The gravity of the political situation respecting the threatened conflict with the House of Lords was empha- sised on Monday by a conference held in Downing-street between the members of the Goverment and their sup- porters in the House of Commons. All manner of wild rumours filled the air as to the purport of this gathering., but these have met with prompt contradiction. Mr. Glad- stone explained to his assembled followers that the meeting had not been summoned because they was anything within the party lines that needed discussion or settlement, or because there was any disagreement that required to be talked over. On the contrary, the Premier declared that he had never known a party more unanimous than the Liberals were at the present moment. Their meeting was, be de- clared, necessitated by a matter entirely distinct from party questions, by a matter of a grave character, imperilling the peace and good government of Ireland. Mr. Gladstone went on to explain the action of the House of Lords with regard to the Land Act, and urged a strong and united opposition to their manoeuvres for the defeat of the operation of that measure. Mr. Gladstone spoke in earnest and emphatic language, and was loudly applauded by all present, amongst whom the most perfect unanimity prevailed. The meeting only occupied about forty minutes. On leaving Downing- street for the House of Commons Mr. Gladstone received a splendid tribute to his popularity, being greeted again and again with cheers from an excited multitude which had been gathered together by the rumours of the serious nature ' of the crisis. A member who was present at the meeting writes—" The reception of Mr. Gladstone was of the most enthusiastic character—the cheering, stamping of feet, and waving of hats lasting more than two minutes. His speech seemed to weld Whigs, Liberals, and R idicals into a thick block of granite against the action of the Lords. At the conclusion of the meeting, Mr. Gladstone, whose face glowed with pride at the demonstration which had been accorded to him, thanked the party for the confidence they bad shown in the ministry at this important juncture."

div.head: DESECRATION OF A TOMB AT
div.p: THE DESECRATION OF A TOMB AT
DUNECIIT.

Quite a sensation was caused in Aberdeen, on Saturday, by a somewhat vague report in the morning papers that at last the authorities had succeeded in establishing a clue to the perpetrators of the outrage at Dunecht and that one or two men had been apprehended in connection with the crime. The confirmation was eagerly awaited, and it came in due course. The mail train which arrived from London in the early morning brought a passenger for whom the authorities at Aberdeen were anxiously waitieg. This pas- senger was Thomas Kirkwood, a servant of the Earl of Crawford and Balcarres, who had been many years in the employ of the family, and was so trusted by the present Earl that, on the occasion of the expedition to the Mauritius to watch the transit of Venus, he was permitted to accom- pany it and carry out such ivork as he, a skilful artisan, was capable of in connection with the mission. Regarding Kbk- wood and others, it appears that certain suspicions have for some time been felt, and it was deemed advisable to send him to London, as he supposed, in connection with some alteration to be carried out at the Earl's laboratory there. The real object, however, was to enable inquiries to be made in his absence touching his alleged connection with the !desecration of the tomb of the late E in. As the result of these inquiries it was deemed advisable to arrest Kirkwood, and but for a question as to jurisdiction, this would have been done in London. The scheme was, however, effected in another way. Kirkwood was sent for, and he, along with Inspector Swanson, of the Scotland Yard detective service, proceeded to Aberdeen, arriving there on Saturday morning. The moment he stepped upon the platform at Aberdeen Kirk- wood was arrested, and charged with complicity in the crime. The Earl of Crawford, who was cognisant of all that was going on, travelled from London by another train. At the same time, the authorities in Aberdeen had been on the out- look in another direction. After dark the previous night several officers were sent to arrest a man named John Philip, who is a messenger in Aberdeen, but who until lately acted as a drill instructor in the Echt district. Philip also was charged with complicity. An Aberdeen correspondent telegraphing on. Monday afternoon says :—This afternoon a private communication was received under the strictest pledge of secresy as to de- tails, from a quarter of undoubted authority, according to which the whole case will assume an entirely new and al!e- gether unexpected aspect. This information is to the effect that a distinct clue has been obtained to the actual instiga- tor of and prime mover in the ou'rage, and that this clue is about to be followed up to what it is believed will be a suc- cessful termination. No indication can at the present stage be given as to the identity of the person upon whom sus- picion rests, but should the supposition referred to be cor- rect, all the theories hitherto entertained as to the scheme of abstracting the body being devised by a foreigner will prove utterly untenable. One anonymous correspondent has, it is said, sent a series of five letters signed "Speculator." He introduced himself as the man who bought the body, and went the length of tabulating the items for its restoration thus :—Sum paid for body, £5,000; expenses of removing, £2,000; and keeping it, ,£3,000; personal expenses, £1,000; interest at 85 per cent., £5,100. In another communication "Speculator" threatens to raise the price if the police are informed of his letters, lie ridicules the idea that the perpetrators were
PEASLEY CROSS CONGREGATIONAL
CHURCH, ST. HELESi.

_ There was a large gathering at the Peasley Cross Sunday School, on Wednesday evening, when the annual congrega- tional tea party was held. An attractive and bright ap- pearance had been imparted to the _room by decorations of wreaths of holly and roses, and conspicuous amongst the mottoes which adorned the wall was "Success to our pastor and schools." About 300 persons sat down to a very enjoy- able tea, and subsequently was held an entertainment presided over by the Mayor of St. Helens (Mr. R. Pilkington). He was supported by the Revs. J. P. Ritchie (pastor), R. J. Ward, Jas. Brown (Presbyterian), Sargeant (United Methodist), Messrs. Gilchrist (deacon), Smith, and Sharpies. The Rev. R. J. Ward having offered up prayer, the pro- ceedings were commenced by the choir singing, under the leadership of Mr. Smith, the anthem "Let the words of my mouth, &c." The choir durinz the evening also sang several other pieces in good style. Mr. Barton sang the song "Sweethearts," and the "Pilgrim of love," for which he was warmly applauded. The trio "0, memory," by Miss Sharpies, Miss Mallinson, and Mr. Barton was also a success. Miss Sharpies accompanied on the piano. The CHAIRMAN delivered a short address in which he con- gratulated Mr. Ritchie upon the large audience which had assembled, which showed what a strong and thorough interest the people took in the Church. At Peasley Cross they were always having some new thing, but be thought there were two things yet wanted. One was a large clock in order that the ministers should not preach too long sermons—(laughter), —and the other was a belfry ' to ring the people to church—because he was not sure they always got there at the proper time: (Applause.) Could Mr. Ritchie have so good a congregation on a Sunday morn- ing as there was that night be would be happy, and it would be a source of satisfaction to the people themselves. The chapel was not so full as it ought to be, but if their numbers were not so strong as they might be, they made amends for it by their energy and good work. They had a minister thoroughly good and earnest, and in proportion as they supported Mr. Ritchie, with downright hearty St. Helens energy and determination, and Peasley Cross and Sutton good will, so would they be able to accomplish honest, useful, good work in Peasley. (Applause.) In a working class neighbourffled like that they must combine together and vie with each other to see how much they could do to forward the work of raising the standard of moral and spiritual life of the inhabitants. It was their ' duty to endeavour to redeem the neighbourhood from its darkness and ignorance, by creating something more intelli- gent. noble—a connection with a being far higher than them ; and he trusted they would assist Mr. Ritchie in that work, and in whatever be pointed out. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. J. P. RITCHIE said it WAS his earnest wish to see the chapel well filled on Sundays, but added that it would be no real success if the people were indifferent and inconsistent, and had no living interest in Divine things. It would, however, be a great help if they bad a congrega- tion strong in faith (hear, hear), and anxious to spend and be spent in the Master's service ; and with such people they would undoubtedly prosper and progress. (Applause.) He had not had the least cross word with any person conntclea with Peasley Cross since he came. He had worked in perfect concord and sympathy with the people, and the more he knew them the more he respected ar.d loved them, and desired to help them. He thought it would be found that the people connected with Peasley Cross were distinguished from their neighbours by the cleanliness of their bonses: the tidinC•°,s of tbt arrangements, their economy, their interest in their chit: dren's welfare, and their respectability and decency as mem- bers of society. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He felt more and more how mach depended upon the minister, and when he saw so much that needed to be done in the neighbour- hood, and realised how little there was being done, he was almost.overpowered by the sense of the responsibility which rested upon him as one who bad come into the neighbour- hood to perform the work of the Lord. It was only the other day that his attenticn was directed to the great spiritual destitution which lay round about them, especially in Sutton district, where there was no chapel in whiell thepeople could attend divine service, and he was urged to open a meeting at that place. His difficulty was in finding someone to con- duct it, and he brought the matter forward at a deacons' meeting at St. Helens. He received a promise at that meet- ing that if the people at Peasley Cross would throw them- selves into the work, they at St. Helens would endeavour to help them. (Applause.) Short and appropriate addresses were afterwards delivered by Mr. Gilchrist, Rev. James Brown, Mr. Smith, Rev. R. J. Ward, Rev. Sergeact,.and Mr. Sharpies. _ _ _ _ _ _
A vote of thanks to the friends who had decorated the schoolronm, prepared the tea, and to the vocalists, &c., con- cluded the meeting.
SP. HELENS BURIAL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Boar I was held on Thursday afternoon, Alderman Harrison presiding, and there were also present Messrs. Moon, Slater, N. Lacey, Windus, Lewis, Canon Carr, Mr. Brewis (clerk), and Mr. Grant (Registrar.)
CANON CARR'S PRIYELEGES.

Mr. SLATER said he gave notice at last meeting that he would ask at the inext meeting upon what terms and con- ditions Canon Carr had a back entrance from his house to the semetery. He simply asked that not only to satisfy himself, but others who like himself were young members of the Board. The knowledge that Canon Carr possessed such right came to him within a short period through a mis- fortune that had happened to one of the pillars near the cemetery. Mr. Grant asked him to look at this pillar, and to ascertain the probable cause of the misfortune. They went and came to the conciusion that it should be repaired at once, and Mr. Brewis acquiesced in that view, because it was one of those things that would not admit of delay. Coming tway from there, he discovered an admission on that road, of whch he was perfectly unaware before, and he remem- bered no entry having come to his notice of any right or privelege being granted to Canon Carr, he thought it was desirable to get some information, and consequently he put the notice at the last meeting. Mr. Brortvzs said that he had gone over the books and he found that a special meeting of the Burial Board was held in August, 1867, when it was resolved that Dr. Carr have the temporary use of that portion of the back road t* the cemetery granted on the understanding that the road be reinstated after the purpose for which the road was granted. Again in 1868 a letter was read from Dr. Carr to the then chairman of the Board, Mr. Gaskell, Taylor asking per- mission to divide his land from the back road to the ceme- tery, the fence to be removed at the pleasure of the Board. 'That was granted. Those were the only two resolutions bearing upon the subject of the road to the cemetery.—Mr. SLATER said that resolution might pass out of their minds, and Canon Carr's successor might come with the impression that he had a full right to use that road. Would it not be better if Canon Carr paid them simply a shilling a year for the use of that road.—Mr. BREIVIS : The ordinary process is to have an acknowledgement of memorandum. I think there ought to be a document signed by Dr. Carr as acknowledge- ment of the privilege—Mr • SLATER : That says we can stop it if we require it, but we can have better security.—Mr. BREIVIS : The right is purely one of suf- ferance.—Mr. SLA.TER : Yes; but the present generation die out, and the conditions die out, too, and Canon Carr's successor might know nothing about the right. The whole thing would be better met if Canon Carr paid a shilling a year, so. that it would become known to all the members year by year.—Mr. BREWIS : But in doing that you will embody these resolutions. I don't suppose Canon Carr will have any objection to paying a shilling a year.—Rev. Canon CARR :. No, not in the least. I use the road for the purpose of getting a small load of hay or straw about once in three months. It appeared from the surmises of some members of the Board that the mischief had been done to the pillar by the men bringing a load of straw, hut I thought it was perfectly impossible, and the carter positively denied it. The load was never more than half a ton, and quite impossible to have touched it. A far more ;reasonable way for account- ing for it is by saying that it has been done by mischief. I believe it has been done by mischievous parties For instance, in the high wall before you get to my gate, there is a hole large enough for a man to pass through. This has been done out of sheer mischief, probably by some colliers amusing themselves on Sunday mornings, as they often do with their pick-axes.—Mr. SLATER: I apprehend Canon Carr has a key to let himself in and out without troubling Mr. Grant.—Mr. GRANT: He never comes to trouble me.— Rev. Canon CARE: I don't know whether I Lave a key or not; if have my man has it.—Mr. SLATER: You don't get your coals in that way ?—Rev. Canon Came: SLATER: Nor ashes ?—Rev. Canon CARR : No, I use it about once in three months.—The subject then dropped.—The Registrar's financial statement showed a btlance in hand from last month, LK 103.; cash received during February, £43 l&t. 7d; total, £O5 4s. sd. The wages and other pay- ments had been £2l 35.; deposited in bank, £2O; leaving a balance in hand of £24 Is. sd. The number of interments for 1882 brought forward from last month was 84; the number of interments during February 97, making a total of 181. The number of interments for the corresponding month of last year was 62, the excessive mortality this month being attributed to the prevalence of measles amongst the children.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A PAIR OF BOOTS AT PRESCOT, —On Tuesday morning, at the Prescot Police Court, before Mr. W. L. Evans, Bridget McGarry, maaried woman, and her son, Robert McGarry, were charged with stealing a pair of boots, value 7s fid, from the shop of Mr. Cox, boot and shoe manufacturer, Eccleston-street, Prescot. About 10 o'clock on the previous Saturday night, the male prisoner, who is only 12 years of age, went to the pawnshop of Mr. Jones, Eccleston-street, and offered the boots in pledge. Suspecting that he had not come by them honestly, Mr. Jones detained him and communicated with the police, who mcertained that the boots had been stolen from Mr. Cox's shop door. The female prisoner, on being charged, ad- mitted having stolen them. Prisoners were remanded to the Petty Sessions on Tuesday.—A man named Patrick Burns. of Rainhill, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk on the previous Saturday night. div.p: DARESBITRY PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall and Robert _ Pierpoint.

DRUNKENNESS. —Frank Hulme bookbinder, Appleton, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Appleton on the 15th ult., and was fine i ss. and Bs. GI. costs-.—A similar penalty was inflicted upon Allen Hewitt, of Apple- ton, for a like offence, committed at the same place, on the 19th ult.—Samuel Littler, bricksetter, Lower IValton, and Joseph Partington, of Hatton, were charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of John Kirkham, Hatton, on the 13th ult.—P.C. Royle said he was on duty at Hatton at a quarter to ten on the night in question, and he heard a " scuffling " in the Red Lion Inn. He went in and found the defendants fighting, and, with the assistance of the landlord, they were ejected'. They were very drunk.—The landlord was celled and said he had turned Partington out of the house before the arrival of the officer. He evinced much reluctance in defining the condition in which the defendants were at the time, but, in reply to the magistrates' clerk, he admitted they were not sober.—Each defendant was fined ss. and costs.

HIGHWAY A FrEnCES —Samuel Thompson, drayman for Messrs. Greenall and Co., was fined 21. (3d. and costa for beim; asleep whilst in charge of a team of horses and cart, at Latchford, on the 16th ult.—For riding on his cart without reins, Thomas Whytch, carter, Norton, was fined Is. and Ca. 61. costs,—The cases were proved by P.C. Morley. CRUELTY TO A DozssEr.—Stephen Mcllroy, a rag-gatherer, living in Warrington, was charged with having, on the 9th ult., at Sutton Oaks, cruelly ill-treated a donkey by working it in an unfit state.—John Bennett was charged with a similar offence in regard to the same animal, committed on the 11th ult. and James Toole, marine store dealer, Foundry-street, Warrington, was charged with allowing it to be worked.—Mr. &.T. Moore defended Toole. Bennett did not appear, and a warrant wai issued for his apprehension. —P. C. Speedsaid he examined the donkey on the 9101 ult, when it was being driven, by Mcllroy. On the left shoulder was a raw wound about the size of half-a-crown, which appeared to give the animal great pain. The collar, which had been padded, was saturated with blood. He also saw it in charge of the man Bennett, at Whitley Superior, on the 11th ult. The wound was much worse than on the previous occasion, and blood was running down the ,leg and breast of the animal.—P.S. Blair gave evidence of the state of the donkey on the 9th, and said it staggered about when walking.—Mr. Moore, in defence,. stated Mcllroy hired the donkey from his client, who was unaware of its state. Bennett had not his authority to work it.—lt was shown that Toole kept the donkey in his st4ole, and he was fined ss. and costs. Mcllroy was mulcted in a similar penalty.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

At the Salford Hundred Intermediate Sessions on Monday, Mr. R. FfaringtOn, Mariebonne, Wigan,:qualitied as a magis- trate for the county. A meeting of the Conservative party was held at Wigan on Monday evening, for the purpose of selecting a candidate in the event of a writ being issued. It was unanimously decided to ask Mr. N. Eckersley, who formerly represented the borough, to stand. ' BURGLARY AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. William Fair- dough, was on Monday brought before the Wigan magis- trates, charged with burglariously entering the Owl Inn, trpholland, on February 6, and stealing therefrom 295. He was also charged with attempting to commit suicide. In consequence of systematic robberies a constable was stationed in the public-house parlour. The prisoner moved the latch of the window, entered the house, and proceeded to the till, which he rifled. The officer, seeing that the prisoner carried a heavy iron bar, struck him down with his fist, and then the prisoner stabbed himself twice in his throat with an open table knife which he had in his left hand. Medical assistance was called in, and the prisoner was removed to the Wigan Infirmary, where he has since remained. The witnesses were cross-examined as to whether prisoner had not simply called for a drink, and then attempted to commit suicide on being chArged with burglary. The bench com- mitted him for trial at the Liverpool assizes. THE ABRAM COLLIERY EXPLOSION: CONDEMNATION OF THE DAVY LAMP.—The inquiry into the cause of the death of two of the men injured by the explosion at the Abram Collieries, who died in the Wigan Infirmary, was resumed on Wednesday, before Mr. Rowbottom, borough coroner. The jury returned the following verdict :—"That John Rigby and Williaae Leese died from the effects of an explosion at Abram Colliery; that a sudden outburst of gas occurred at the weighting of the roof, as explained by the witnesses Westhead and Speakman, but that as to the mode of the firing the evidence is insufficient to enable the jury to form an opinion. The strong suspicion manifested, however, in the reports of the engineers—that the flame had passed the gauze of a Davy lamp—impresses the jury to urge most strongly on colliery proprietors the necessity of some change in the manner of lighting mines in this district ; and they would call particular attention to the further evidence given to-day by Mr. Hall, Her Majesty's Inspector of Mines, as to the superiority of the Meuse! er and Tin-can Davy over those lamps now in use. The jury would also suggest that the authorities should, as recommended by the Inspector of Mines, keep at public fire stations a supply of extincteurs, the use of which at this exploS'ons evi- dence, saved several lives." according to the

It has been said that the Government are acting without precedent, but the records of Parliamentary proce'd are show that is not the case. According to the latest phase of this political crisis it would appear that Earl Cairns has been ap- pointed Chairman of the Lords' Committee, and that the Chief Secretary for Ireland has been invited to give evidence before it. That request the Cabinet of course refuse to comply with. Lord Cairns is now credited with exercising his soothing influence among the members of the Commmittee, who, it is not im- probable, may be induced to adjourn their delibera- tions for an indefinite period. Should this be the case, a conclusion satisfactory to all parties will have been arrived at. It must not, however, be understood the Government fears inquiry; on the contrary, they court it; to the fullest extent ; at the present time it is inopportune. It has been said that the House of Lords is by its own actions "diligently engaged in digging its own grave ;" certain it is that its abolition was never so fre- quently hinted at as it has been during the past few days in the press, and if ever its extinction becomes an accomplished fact, the hereditary legis- lators will have themselves to blame by setting at defiance the will of the people's representatives.

LOCAL NOTES.

Those who saw the announcement made under this column ' last week, to the effect that the Rev. W. Preston, vicar. of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, had been appointed one of the secretaries to the Palestine Exploration Society, will no doubt be much interested by an article which appears in this month's number of Clianthr's Jounzal. This is en- titled "The Great Map of Palestine," and details how the exploration fund was started ten years ago. Six thousand square miles of territory have been minutely surveyed and 'mapped, comprising the whole of Western Palestine from Dan to Beersheba, and from Jordan to the Mediterranean. The expenses of the work during the years 1872-77 were about £3,500 a year, and the total expenses incurred have been about £17,500 in five years. The notice of the map concludes as follows :—" If your tastes are serious, you can linger round Beersheba, see the same wells and surroundings as were familiar to the patriarchs; you can accompany Abraham step by step on his journey to Mount Moriah ; or you can gaze on the surroundings of Machpelah, where he and his repose in peace. You can accompany David in all his wanderings; and in a• manner never before attained, you can realise his various haunts and characteristic escapes. And to crown all, you can follow with reverent foot, David's son in His various journeys; you can see the very well at which He sat wearied with His journey, and, at a glance, talre in the surroundings on which His eye TrnW lay e rested, the glorious Vale of ShecheM, guarded by the historic tbal and Gerizim. You may realize Sated, the city set on a bill'; or wander along the hallowed shores of the Sea of Galilee; and lastly, you can follow the Saviour step by step along His last sad journey to Jerusalem." The half-yearly meeting of the Runcorn Coffee and Cocoa Rooms' Co., held last week, was characterised by much more liveliness than former gatherings of a similar char- acter. The company started under the sunniest of pros- ' piots, as far aa ontwarcl appearances went, but the directors l‘leem to have made an important miscalculation, which 68 landed them in the difficulties by which they are now beset. They imagined—judging. from the remarks of Mr. John Sippson—that they were sure to obtain what was spoken of as first-class custom, and, consequently, fitted up the rooms in a style which was unnecessarily expensive—quite pala- tial, in fact. No doubt it is very pleasant for the eye to feed itself on handsome fittings and magnificent plate."' Windows, bnt these aort of pleaspreP cost. C'..,-aslderable's;uam" of money, as many a poor fellow who nas! tried to imitate his neighbours, who were in a bette,2 position, has found to his cost. He who for the Rake tif showing off lantlei himself in debt, soon fiGds that th?.. creditor is servant to the lender, and that suer people :tre, as the philosophic Franklin says, great observer i!`., set times and seasons. It is a matter for regret that he directors of the concern indulged in any speculative spirit, for such yielding to the day dreams of vivid imaginations are apt to make shareholders who have invested their money under their auspices more straight- forward in their remarks than considerate for the tender feelings of those who have had the management in their own hands. Mr. G. S. Haxlehurst, whe was formerly one of the directors, does not appear to view the action of the gentlemen who at present occupy that position with feelings of unmingled admiration. He seems to be of opinion that several plans might be adopted which would tend to make the rooms a commercial success. Perhaps Mr. George does not know it, but I may inform him that many of his townsmen look /Ton him as a little visionary. Some have -even gone so far as to say he would have Inuit a splendid Swedenborgian, but that he is governed rather too much by his imagination to be thoroughly practical. Whether these statements are correct or not, I will-not stay to discuss, but merely remark that Mr. Haxlohurst is comparatively young, and may become sadly toe practical and hardened in his feelings before he joins the majority. A. suggestion thrown out by him at the meeting was that one of the large front windows belonging to the rooms might be used with great advantage as a sort of con- fectioner's shop. Mr. Hazlehurst argued that there were many people who had shares in the 'concern who would be inclined to give them their support in the matter, and that the general public were often tempted to buy, by seeing tempting viands exposed for sale. This suggestion seems practical enough, and I hope that the directors will not throw it on one side as unworthy of their dignified considera- tion. Now that part of the building has been let off to the Young Men's Christian Association, there seems to be a fair a chance of a dividend in the future. Mr. John Simpson, who has already taken one hundred extra shares in the company, stated at the half-yearly meeting that rather than see the concern collapse he should 'be .quite willing to purchasel another hundred. It is, however, much to, be regretted that the company ever took the extensive premises they now occupy. A wiser plan would have been to commence in a small way, and enlarge as the 'business increased. The Vicar Of Runcorn is determined to have his "pound of flesh," as far as the fees at the cemetery are concerned. It is really wonderful how important the most insignificant person becomes in the discussion of a question like this as soon as he is dead, though during his lifetime there were none so poor as to do him reverence. It ought in justice to the Canon to be stated that he has not the slightest objec- tion to the Rev. Fattier Fennelly or the Rev. E. Williams going through the burial.service on a frightfully wet day— those gentlemen are quite welcome to any honour which may come from such conduct—bui- he has the strongest feeling in the world against a 'Dissenting minister pocketing the fees ! Under such circumstances, the dead body of the poorest parishioner must become an object of the dearest interest to the vicar of the parish—he is almost as deeply concerned on the subject as the Protestant Defence Associa- tien were in poor Ginx's baby, whenrthey discovered the awful fact that its body was being nourished by ladies be- longing to the Catholic Church'! The -question in dispute between the Vicar and the Burial Board is to come before one of Her Majesty's judges, in the-County Court, and the defendant will be Mr. Salkeld, the worthy secretary to that body.

It certainly is rather amusing to read the assertion of Mr. Bullough, the secretary of the Widnes Conservative Associa- tion, to the effect that there is a steady growth of Conserva- tism in the town. Those who know Widnes are not to be led astray by statements of this kind, made by a paid secre- tary, who, I suppose, is bound to make the best of a poor case. If Widnes has ever the honour of political enfran- chisement conferred upon it, it will be seen that the town is a centre of Radicalism. I perceive that poor Mr. Bullough classes Radicals with Republicans and Atheists—he might as well have stigmatised them at once as servants of King Diabolus. After such a wild and untruthful assertion, I shall not be surprised at any other strange thing which the brain of the local Conservative Secretary may bring forth. "'Tis a strange world, my masters."

Your Runcorn readers will be glad to find that the good work which was commenced some time ago in that town by the Wesleyan Methodist circuit ministers, and carried on so successfully since the advent of the Rev. George Hack, is not to be allowed to drop. The battle is to be still further pushed to the gate during the ensuing fortnight, when Mr. Robinson Watson will conduct a ten days' mission in C.;i. Paul's Chapel. The half-yearly report of Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co., which has just been.presented to the shareholders at their meeting in Liverpool, brings to mind the palmy days of the chemical trade, when fortunes were made as if by magic. It is a fact worth pondering, that whilst the chemical trade in Widw s and the neighbourhold is comparatively stagnant, this ve...y modern firm, by the air of their special patents, I suppose, can manage to pay a dividend at the rate of 19 per cent. pdr annum.

PRESENTATION TO MR. THOMAS COOKE, OF RUNCORN. —On the evening of the 24th ultimo, a handsome silver pencil case was presented to Mr. Thomas Cooke, late assis- tant secretary to the Young Men's Christian Association, as a mark of the courteous and able manner. in which he had discharged his duties in the past. Mr. J. E. Longsbaw made the presentaticn, and short speeches were also delivered by Mr. Humphreys and Mr. W. Shaw.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 4, 1882. •
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 4, 1882. •

REVIVAL SERVICES AT WIDNES. The series of revival services in connection with the Primitive Methodist Chapel in Hutchinson-street, Widnes, was continued of Saturday and Sunday, and were well attended. WIDNES OAKLAND-STREET IMPROVEMENT CUSS. -- On W«lnesclay evenilig, at the weekly meeting of this class, Mr. T. Hughes gave an interesting address on "Critics, and the use and abuse of Criticism." An interesting discussion followed.

STAR OF WIDNES LODGE, I.O.G.T.—At the meeting OD Wednesday evening, Bro. H. Hupton, W.C.T., presided, and amongst those who contributed to the entertainment were Bros. Parkinson, Johnson, Turton, Bushell, Carter, Smith, and Sister Rout:edge. SERVICE OF SONG AT RUNCORN.—OR Tuesday evening, the service of song, known by the title " Given in charge," was given in the Camden schoolroom, by the Camden choir. Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst was the reader, and the story was illustrated by dissolving views. The proceeds amounted to about £5, which will be given to the trust fund. BUNCORN BRUNSWICK IMPROVEMENT CLASS. At the weekly meeting on Wednesday night, Mr. Bisbrown pre- sided, and Mr. J. W. Boyle read a paper on "Alcohol and its effects on the system." A discussion followed, in which Mess.rs. Jones. Leathwood, Hopkins, Scott, Coventry, and F. J. Norman (the secretary) took part. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-011 Tuesday evening, Mr. Craig, of the Collegiate School, Runcorn, gave his lecture entitled "Reminiscences of Scottish Life and Character," under the auspices of this society. The Rev. John Lockwood presided. There was a good attendance, and at the close a very hearty vote of thanks was given to the talented lecturer. TEMPERANCE MEETING AT WESTON POINT.—On Tues- day night, a meeting, under the auspices of the Sons (,f Temperance, was held at the Weston Point Wesleyan school- room. Mr. S. Coventry presided. The Weston fife and drum band was in attendance, and played several pieces of music. Addresses were delivered by Mr. J. Parker, Mr. J. W. Boyle, and Mr. Holford. A reaciing, entitled "The Drunkard," was given by Mr. A. Nisley, a recitation, "The Three Angels," by Mr. Rosenberg, and a song" Come home, poor Jack," by Mr. Norman.

HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—On Monday evening, Mr. J. Moss, of Helsby (e-president of the society) read a paper to the members on " deneral Garfield, late President of the United States." The Rev. J. Bateman pre- sided. At the close, Mr. Moss received a ,hearty vote of thanks. There was a very large attendance.

REVIVAL SERVICES AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Robinson Watson, who is very well known amongst the Wesleyan Methodist denomination, will to-morrow (Sunday) commence a series of services, over several days, at St. Paul's Chap!, Run- corn. Those on the week days will take place at noon, and at seven in the evening. Mr. Watson has visited the prin- cipal towns of the kingdo:n for a similar purpose, and he is high3y spoken of as a cultured and popular revival preacher. Further particulars will be found in our adver- tising Columns. BOY DROWNED AT RUNCORN.—On Thursday afternoon, an inquest was held at the Grapes Inn, Halton-road, by Mr, Wasley? deputy coroner, on the body of William Acton Earp, tnanuieVurr, Qf the 64nie thorougllfare, who Was found drowned in the llridgewaier canal on the prevloo evening. The evidence showed that on Wednesday after- noon, about half-past five, the deceased had tea after which be went out to play upon the wharf at the foot of his father's chemical yard, which abuts upon the canal. Shortly before six, a boatman who was passing saw the child's body in the canal, and shouted to a man named George Southerton, a waterman, who rescued deceased, qnite dead, and took him to his own home. The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."

HASTE TO THE RESCUE LODGIi, 1..0.G.T., WIDNES.— The usual weekly session of this lodge was held on Tuesday evening, when there V,TPJ a good attendance of members. Brother Bradshaw, W.C.T., and Brother T. Hughes, L.D., gave a report of the meeting of the South-West Lancashire District Lodge, 1.0.G.T., which took place at Liverpool on Monday, from which it appeared that the capitation was raised 41 per member. The representatives from the Widnes district lodges were Brothers T. Hughes, L.D., and W. Bradshaw, W.C.T.' of the Haste to the P.escue Lodge, and Brother J. Reay, W.C.T., of the Hope of Appleton Lodge. Brothers J. Makin, W.S., and B. Bedggood, W.G-., and Sister R. Hudson, W.V.T., took the district lodge de- grees. It appeared from the report that there was an increase of 166 members over the previous quarter. A vote of thanks was cordially given to Brothers Hughes and Bradshaw for their report of the district lodge session. The usual busi- ness having been transacted, .a programme organized by Brother G. Makin was gone through. It comprised a read- ing by Brother J. Thompson, P.W.C.T.z a song by Brother Johnson; a recitation by Brother Makin, W.G. ; a son, by Brother Thompson, and a reading by Brother Hughes, L.D. The programme was creditably gone through, and the ; .Good Templars spent a pleasant evening. RUNCOnN SCHOOL BoARD.—The Rev. Canon Barclay presided at the montkly meeting of the Board, held at the Board-room, Bridgewater-street, on Wednesday. There were also present the Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. J. Simpson, , P. Briscoe, Richard Lea, J. Pritchard, and F. Rigby (clerk). —The Chairman read a letter from Miss E. Speed, mistress of Mill Brow Board school, tendering her resignation, and stating she, had got the offer of another school which she had long been wishing to obtain.—The resignation was ac- cepted.—A letter was received from Mr. Yarwood, painter, stating that he could not reduce his account for painting at Mill Brow school, as requested by the Board.—The Clerk stated he had seen Mr. Yarwood, who told him the work hadbeen.done, and he could not make any reduction.-141r. Briscoe had also seen Mr. Yarwood, who informed him no rednction could be made, but if the work had not been chine satisfactorily he was quite willing the wall should receive another coat of paint.—The Clerk stated Mr. Yet-wood was a very conscientious tradesman, and he did not know one more so.—lt was decided to pay the account.—Mr. Bowyer, the school attendance officer, reported that during the month of February the certified Government accommoda- tion was 2,323, the number on the rolls 2,341, and the aver- age attendance 2,041.5, against an average attendance for February, 1831, of 1.709.1, and for the year 1874 of 1,252. The accommodation in excess of avenige attendance was 281.4, and the number on the rolls in excess of accommoda- tion was 518. These figures show an increase of 332 4 in the average attendance as comi with the corresponding. period of last year, and an increase of 789'5 as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board. The total number in attendance at private adventure schools under ninepenco per week was 6.—This was all the business.

THE REPRFSENTATION OF WIGAN.—A meeting of the Wigan Liberal Association was held on Thursday night, to consider what stops should be taken, on a writ being issued, to fill the vacancy in the borough. It was unanimously resolved that the seat should be contested on behalf of the Liberal party, and it was decided to request Mr. John Lan- caster to become their candidate. Several other prominent Liberal gentlemen were mentioned as willing to fight the battle, but it was resolved that no action should be taken until the receipt of a reply from Mr. Lancaster to the request of the association. The meeting throughout was most en- thusiastic. Rumour says that in the evetat of Mr. Eckersley declining to contest the seat in the Conservative interest, the party will nominate Mr. Walter ,Mayhew as their candi- date.

THE SAD roATING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—The funeral of the young man Williams took place on Sunday afternoon, and, notwithstanding the very heavy rain, there was a very large concourse of people, which KiLE augmented by ri considerable number of the division of the Sons of 'temperance, which the deceased belonged. The Revs. John Nowell and John Bateman, and Mr. G. S. Hazlet:rust and , Mr. W. J. Shore, superintendents of the Camden Wesleyan Sunday School, walked at the head of the procession. The cofEn was carried by Messrs. B. Crossley, J. Dutton, Geo. Liveslev, Wm. Dutton, Thomas Shiw, James Lea, Thomas Page, ;James Roots, B. Smith, John Moulton, Gibmon, and Stringer, who were followed by friends •and relatives. Hundreds of spectators assembled at the Cemetery, where the concluding por Lion of the burial service was read by the Rev. J. Bateman. The hymn "Safe in the arms of Jesus " was also sung.

BRICK-STREET AND FRIARS' GREEN BAND OP H0P.13 SOCIETY.—The seventh of the winter series of entertain- ments in connection with. this:society was held in the Brick. street schoolroom on Tuesday last. Mr. Wm. Hudson occupied the chair, and was supported on the platform ty Mr. Joseph Garner and Mr. James Shaw. The Chairman, in a short address, endeavoured to show the evil effects whia followed drink, and how they might all he avoided by becoming abstainers. The programme, which was a rather lengthy one, was gone through in a manner that left little to be desired. The recitations and dialogues were inter- spersed with songs by the choir. During the evening Mr. Charles Boardtnan and Miss Betsy Thornber favoured the audience with songs. The former received a - well merited encore, The latter sang "The deep clear spring " very Sweetly.

The adoption of the report, which was considered most satisfactory, was moved by Mr. John Green, and seconded by Mr. Win. Wallington, and after a few observa- tions from the Chairman, Mr. Jeans, and Mr. Joseph Shaw Green, was unanimously carried. The followini officers Were then appointed for the ensuing tmt t—Directors, Messrs. Thomas Morris, Was. Reid, Joseph Shaw Green, John Edward Wright, Thomas Pilklngton, John Andrews, And Elisha Wallington ; auditors, Messrs. Walter Young and Joseph H. Clarke. Votes of thanks to the clash man, retiring directors, and auditors brought the meeting to a conclusion.
