ME SECOND ST. HELENS 350Ti1 STARR-BOWNETT BCILD- ING. SOCIETY.—The first annual meeting of this society was held on Wednesday evening, iii the Assembly Room of the Cocoa Rooms, Market-place. Mr. Sherlock presided, and there was an excellent attendance of members. The following report was read :

The directors, in submitting the first annual bala -ce sheet, certified by the attlitors, congratulate the members on the suc- cess which has attended the working of the society. The mem- bers must feel gratified at the result of the year's working, since it leaves a balance in favour of the soci?ty of £24 19s. 31. The income of the society for the year has bees—From sub- scriptions, £787 18s ; from en'rane3 tees, fines, bank interest, taansfers, premium on transfers of appropriations and for- feitures 2.50 18s. 81d.: from sale of subs,ription and rule books, £lB ss. 6d.; from repayments of appropriation, £l6 ss. 40.; and from profit on sale of appropriatlon by tender, £4 9s. 61, making altogether a total income of £s7s 175. 00. The ex- penditure of the society fur the year has been—For appropria- tions completed. £1300; for the year's working expenses, £62 103. 9d.; for the preliininary expenses incurred in forming the society, £32 13s 31d.; for purchase of deed lyax and official seat. £5 4s. 90 ; for account books and forms, 211 19s. Id.; and for subscription and rule books, £l5 161. 81.; making with £147 us. 90. in the ManchestmCand Salford Bank and 90. in band, a total as per contra. in £375 17s. Old. Five appropriations amounting to £9OO have been made during the year. It will be observed that the hoard put into °petal ion the power vested In them, under rule 21, authorising the purchase and re-sale by tender, of appropriations; the result ot one transaction giving a profit to the society of £4 9s. 6d. after paying the cost in- curred in selling. The directers would respectfully urge upon the member the advisability of their (Ling thei c utmost to aid in btinging new members to the society, in order to complete the list of members and to make the society a still greater success. The following directors retire this year, but are eligible for re-election, viz, ;—Messrs. Sturg.ess, Cliadwick, loydell, and Thomson,

Mr. Sherlock said he .observed that the society was not vet full, there being only 357 members towards the full number of 500. Bearing this in mind, the fact that they had made profit seemed to hint highly creditable to the Board of Management. In considering the expenditure they Should remember in a society of that -kind the expenditure was al- ways lfeavy the first year ; they had all the preliminary expenses to meet, and several things such as the deed box and seal was to be bought, and this was dead stock The preliminary expenses liad been proportionately charged, the remainder being carried to next year, which was a reason- able arrangement. Then the outlay for books was a source of profit, because every book sold was a little to the good, and this would add to the profits of next year. The prac- tice of buying appropriations was a very good one, because it not only benefited the society considerably, but also the members having got an appropriation might not want to use it, and perhaps could not get a customer for it. The recommendation contained in the last paragraph of the report was a very important one, because although Starr-Bowkett's might work and work successfully with a small number of members, still it would always be &ow. He knew that members of those societies sometimes complained that the appropriations did not come fast enough, and sometimes wondered when it would be their turn. The more subscribers there were, and the more money there was coming in, the faster the appropriations would come. And not only that, the more appropriations there were made the more money there would be returning to help to make the appropriations more frequent. If a member wanted his turn to come quick, there were two things to be done: get the club full, and pay subscriptions regularly.—The report was adopted. The retiring directors, Messrs. Sturaeiss, Chadwick, Boyden, and Thomson, were re-elected for the ensuing two years. Messrs. Burgess and Hopwood were re-elected auditors.—On the motion of Mr. Josh. Boydell, seconded by Mr. Foote, both of whom, together with the Chairman, referred in complimen- tary terms to the secretary, it was decided that Mr. Griffin's salary be £3O per annum until 400 members were enrolled; from 400 to 500 at the rate of £35, and when the full com- pliment of members were obtained at the rate of £45 per annum.—The sixth appropriation then took place, the scrutineers being Mr. Barrett and Mr. Fararn, and a boy named William Daft drew the ballot balls. The balloting resulted in No. 51 being drawn, and Mr. Edward Burgess, managing clerk for Mr. Riley, solicitor, was declared en- titled to an advance of 1.200 for 12; years, without interest.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
ATTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE THE QUEEN,

A dastardly attempt to assassinate the Queen was made at the Windsor Railway Station on Thursday evening. Her Majesty had just returned with the Court from London, and had entered her carriage for conveyance to the Palace amid the loyal cheers of a large gathering of on-lookers. At this moment a man standing amid the spectators, pointed a revolver at the Royal carriage and deliberately fired at its occupants. Her Majesty and the Princess Beatrice, by whom she was accompanied, escaped unhurt, and the would- be assassin was at once arrested. His name is Roderick j M`Lean, and he states that he is a clerk in reduced circum- stances, and would not have committed the act if he had not been suffering from hunger. The cowardly miscreant, or half-crazed, half-starved lunatic, had a narrow escape of being lynched on the spot. The news of the diabolical outrage spread like wildfire throughout the country, and created an immense sensation in London and in the provinces, where the news was pub- lished between seven and eight o'clock. Mr. Gladstone receive.' a telegram in the House of Commons from Sir Henry Ponsonhy stating that Her Majesty was in n 6 way suffering from the shock upon the alarming incident. A telegram was subsequently despatched from the Honse by Mr. Gladstone and Sir Stafford Northcote congratulating the Queen ar. her providential esdape. Congratulatory telegrams were received at Windsor from all quarters. Her Majesty's first thought on arriving at the Castle after the outrageovas to send an equerry to discover whether anyone had been injured. It appears, however, that no one was hurt, and before the man had time to fire a second shot the revolver was struck from his hand. It is hardly necessary to state that no political motive what- ever is assigned for the outrage. Though the accounts on the subject are conflicting, the opinion is generally enter- tained that the prisoner is of unsound mind, and not, respon- sible for his actions. There is DO suspicion that 11PLean has any accomplic,!s. He is a man about thirty years of age, and described as very miserable looking and shabbily dressed. No trace has been found of the bullet, and it is consequently surmised that the prisoner may have only fired a blank cartridge. When picked up it was found that two of the chambers of the revolver were loaded with blank cartridges and two with bullets. The correspondent of the Manchester Guardian at Windsor, says :—The dastardly nature of the attempt upon the Sovereign's life naturally created the most intense in- dignation among the spectators. There was a general rush towards the man. Colonel Sir J. C. Genera: Sir H. Ponsonby, and Viscount Bridport, who at the time were

waiting to enter their carriage, ran to the Queen's carriage, and it was ascertained that Her Majesty had received no injury, the shot from the revolver having missed its aim, as the vehicle was being driven rapidly out of the yard. Her Majesty and the Princess continued their progress to tire Palace, followed by the ladies of the suite in the remainder of the carriages. While the royal party were on , their way thither the assassin was conveyed to a fly, which was obtained in Thames-street, by Mr. Inspector Fraser, Chief Superintendent Hayes, Sergeant Jackson, Constable Alexander, and Superintendent Blake, of the county police. This act was not accomplished without some difficulty, owing to the crowd, who manifested • the greatest indignation at the crime. Once in Thames. street the assassin was driven rapidly in the custody of the officers named to the Borough Police Station, where, in the Prf,gnCq 9f Mr. LT, o.lifripSon, one of the justiCes, he SW at (Mee charged by Superintendent Hayes with shooting at Her Majesty the Queen with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. The prisoner, who is 27 years of age, and gave the name of Roderick Maclean, is of medium height and slim build. He is poorly clad, and apparently in reduced circumstances, and he states that he is a grocer's assistant. lle avers that he would not have done the deed had he not been suffering bona hun- ger, and says that he walked from Portsmouth to Windsor, •ss here he has been staying for a week.

The Mayor of Windsor (Mr. Joseph Devereaux), Mr. H. Darylll (town clerk), General Sir H. Ponsonby, Vis- count Bridport, and Colonel Sir J. M'Neiil were present in the clia.rgeroom while the prisoner was being searched. Later on he was examined in the cell by Dr. Holderness who pronounced him sane. After the prisoner bad been searched by Inspector Fraser and Chief Superintendent Hayes, the weapon, a mediem-sized six-chambered Colt's revolver of American make, was examined. It was found that two of the chambers still remained loaded and two had recently been discharged, while the other two were empty A paper containing 14 ball cartridges, several pipers, and several valueless articles were also discovered upon M`Lean, who said he should make no defence, but should reserve what he had to say till his examination. The statement of M‘Lean that he was hungry :fcarcely seems to coincide with the fact of his being ill possession of such a valu- able weapon as the revolver, which is almost new. It seems that M`Lean, when he tried to shoot the Qeeen was slightly in advance of the Royal carriage, and tired the revolver as it was approaching him. His action was perceived by Princess Beatrice, who was much alarmed. It appears that while Chief Superintendent Hayes was near the wicket gate of the station yard he saw the prisoner suddenly raise his right hand, take careful aim at the Qaeen's carriage, and tire deliberately at those in the carriage—the Queen, Princess Beatrice, and the lady in waiting. Dashing upon M`Lean, Superintendent Hayes seized him by the neck. This caused the would-be assissin to drop the revolver in the roadway, whence it was picked up by a young man named Jamee Barnsfield. Inspector Fraser, of the Royal Household Poliee, who is always in attendance upon Her Majesty, ran up at the same moment, and assisted in the capture of the Prisoner. The prisoner when arrested was followed by crowds of people to the station, and throughout the even- ing groups of residents have collected in the streets corn- meEtiug upon the attempted assassination. A Windsor correspondent telegraphing on Thursday night, says :—The carriage occupied by Her Majesty and Princess Beatrice has been examined, but up to the present moment
no mark or indentation has been found upon it. Brown, the

Queen's personal servant, was sitting in the rumble and saw Maclean raise his band and aim the revolver which exploded as the carriage dashed to .vards the prisoner, the bullet from the weapon probably passing Brown and the upper part of the back part of the carriage, and dropping, it is believed, in the station yard. Her Majesty happened to be sitting on the right side of the back seat of the vehicle, the further place from the prisoner, who was to the left of the carriage when he fired the shot. As an instance of the feeling of the people at the moment of the attempt, it may be stated that while Superintendent Hayes and Inspector Fraser were collaring Maclean, an Eton student rushed up to the prisoner and belaboured him in an excited manner over the bead and shoulders with his umbrella. Maclean, since Saturday, has been living at 24, Victoria Cottager., Windsor, where he has had tea, getting his dinner at the Royal Borough Coffee Tavern Inn, Peascod-street. There is reason to believe that there is more in this matter than at present appears upon the surface, and that the vile attempt s the outcome of some plot. When Inspector Fraser seized Maclean the latter exclaimed, "Don't hurt me." Mr. Fraser replied, 'Certainly not," and the prisoner then observed," I have done it through starvation." On inquiry this evening at the Castle, General Sir H. Ponsonb,l,- said that Her Majesty was not at all alarmed by the untoward
occurrence, and remained in very good health and spirits.
• THE QUEEN'S ACCOUNT. A correspondent having called at Marlborough House, is enabled to state that the first news of the dastardly attempt upon the life of Her Majesty seems to have come direct
from the Queen, and therefore any needless alarm as to her safety was fortunately obviated. Shortly after six o'clock 'the following telegram was delivered at Marlborough House:—
"FROM THE QUEEN, WINDSOR CASTLE, TO THE PRINCE OF
WALES, MARLBOROUGH HOUSE. "In case exaggerated report should reach you, I telegraph to say that as I drove from the station here a man shot at
the carriage, but fortunately bit no one. arrested. I am none the worse."
He was instantly
Immediately upon the receipt of this telegram by the Prince, a message as returned to Windsor on behalf of
their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales,
expressive of their thankfulness upon the happy escape of the Queen.
[LATER.] During yesterday the greatest exclemeut prevailed ov,

the attempt upon the life of Her MajQsty. At Buckingilam Palace and Marlborough House there was a constant stream of callers and enquiries after the health of the Queen. I'l the foreign ambassadors and the ministers, both of the late

and present Government, being amongst the numter. Sir W. Harcourt went down to Windsor and saw Her Majesty, who stated that she had suffered no ill effects from the shock. From the provinces telegrams were continually being received, showing the deep sympathy felt throughout the country at the dastardly outrage. FINDING OF THE BULLET.

A most important discovery has been made which settles the question as to whether it was a blank cartridge or a ball which was fired when 111‘Lean directed his revolver at the Royal carriage. Inspector Noble, of tbe Great Western Railway Police, assisted by Inspector Turner, of the Loco- , motive Department at Slough, commenced a strict search yesterday morning, in order to ascertain whether a bullet had really been discharged at her Majesty. Inspector Turner discovered a small ballet embedded in the ground. It was slightly flattened, and bore traces of having struck some object before it lodged in the soil. The spot where it was found exactly coincides with the direction in which the prisoner M'Lean pointed his pistol, and it is conjectured that the bullet must have passed either over the horses or the carriage. Upon an examination of the pistol being made by Mr. Superintendent Hayes, of the Windsor borough police, it has been found that, after the first discharge, the prisoner turned the barrel to a second loaded chamber, but was prevented from discharging it by the revolter being knneked out of his hand.

THE PRISONER'S ANTECEDENTS. Every inquiry as to the antecedents of M‘Lean is, of course, being made, but nothing has yet transpired to con- fleet him in anyway with anything in the nature of a political organisation. INPLean has as yet made no further statement as to his motive in attempting the life of the Queen, but no doubt the letter found upon hi -n, but which the authorities will not publish, will contain a full exposition of his object. Although only lid was found upon him when searched, it is stated that on Wednesday night he was at a public-house close to the station, and openly exhibiting what for him would be a considerable amoeint of silver, which he was freely spending in drink for himself and others. A Pcrts- mouth correspondent says . that M‘Lean left Portsmouth, on February 22nd, to walk to London. He had on the day previous received money from his friends at Croydon, from whom a letter now awaits him at Mr. Hacker's, Cecil- grove, Soutbsea. He told Hackers that his brother had mar- ried the sister of a well-known theatrical celebrity. Hackers fully believes that M`L?an is mad. Physicians_ d:clare him to be quite sane.
The French and English Banking Company was wound up in Chancery yesterday. Summonses have been issued for a Cabinet Council to meet at two o'clock to-day.

Yesterday morning a young man was killed at Worth Village Mills, Keighley, by a hoist falling upon his head.. The electric light apparatus is now being adjusted at the Wharncliffe and Woodman Collieries, near Barnstey,with the view of lighting the pit if found practicable. Ricleout, the driver of the engine which ran into a pas- senger train on Thursday at Chilcompton, died during the night. The others are progressing favourably. Her Majesty's corvette Bacchante, with the Royal Princes on board, arrived at Ismailia late on Thursday night, and their Royal Highnesses landed yesterday morning. Yesterday afternoon Edward Hanlan, of Toronto, and Edward Trickett, of Sydney, were matched to scull over the Thames championship course on May Ist for £5OO aside. At Birr, yesterday, Captain Douglas applied to the magistrates for a summons against the police, who had taken from his pocket copies of Ca/tea _Wand. Till) *I plication wag refusal for want of jurisdiction. A block was caused on the Deyonport and London main, line yesterday afternoon by an engine and tender running off. The traffic was seriously interfered with. This was the second block on the same lino yesterday. Henry Moran, the deaf boy who was charged at Darwen with placing three iron chairs on the Lee on Sunday, was on Thursday taken to the 'union workhouse until arrange- ments can be made to send him to a mute nstitution. A communication was received from the Board of Trade yesterday morning consenting to a continuance of the use of steam power by the Burnley Tramway Company until the let of May, on the understanding that the corporation take the responsibility. The Clitheroe Town Council, on Thursday, after an animated debate, resolved to redace the price of gas 3d. per I,COO feet for domestic purposes, and also 2d. per 1,000 feet for manufacturing purposes, providing manufacturers did not consume less than 150,000 feet.

A 13uter's telegram from St. Petersburg says:—lntellig encc from likutsl: states that Lieutenant Danenhaner has lost the sight of his left eye, while the right is seriously endangered by epthalmic affection produced by the snow- glare. lie is conßquently complltd to postpone his de- pa:.ture.

At the Central Criminal Com t, psterday, Thos. Gallicrs and James Casey were charged with the wilful murder of Frank James Wlllmote, on the Tames embankment, in December last. The charge was afterwards withdrawn, and that of marslaughfer substituted. The tiial was after- wards adjlurned.

Mr. Montague Williams appeared before Justice Hawkins, at the Old Bailey, yesterday, and said that having regard o the number-of cases still remaining to be disposed of, it was not probable that the trial of the prisoner Lamson could commence on Monday. He therefore asked for a postpone- ment until Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Poland and Mr. Justice Hawkins agreed that the trial should be adjourned until Wednesday.

Mr. John Thomas Smalley, manufacturer, of Mello; near Blackburn, wits found dead in Whinney-lane, Mellor, yes- terday morning. Ills horse returned home without him, and Mr. Smalley was afterwatds discovered with a deep wound On the back of his heal and several scars on his face. It is supposed that he had been thrown from his horse when returning home,

About nine o'clock yesterday morning Jatnes Walker, engine driver of the goods train from Preston to Liverpool, met with a frightful accident. When his train reached Croston Station he stepped down before it had. stopped, slipped, and fell between the platform and the wheels of a wagon. His left arm and leg were fearfully crushed. He was taken back at once and conveyed to the Preston Ind.- mary, where the limbs were amputated.

Yesterday, at Wolverhampton Police-court, Samuel Holden, ex-policeman, of Liverpool, was sentenced to six months' hard labour for obtaining money by false pret7lnes from Major Warner and other volunteer officers. The pri- soner represented himself to be a first-class Army Reserve man in indigent circumstances. When arrested he bad a long list of nimes and addresses of military officers from whom he had obtained money.
NORTHAMPTON ELECTION.

The Northampton election has been fought out with great spirit and earnestness on both sides. The nomination took place on Monday at noon. Mr. Bradlaugh was norninatcd by Mr. James Gurney, magistrate, and seconded by Mr. Hobert Del bv, ex-Mayor (Baptist). Mr. Corbett's nominator and seconder are Mr. Thomas Wetherell (Wesleyan and Conservative) and Mr. John Coo (Churchman). Several Dissenters assented to the Conservative nomination. The polling took place on Thursday, and in anticipation of dis- turbances, military were imported into the town. The voting on the whole, however, proceeded quietly. The following is the result :
MR. BRADLAUGH (L) 3,7P6 MR. cORBETI (C) 3,688
Majority 108

_ The succ:?ssful candidate, Mr. Bradlaugh, and Mr. Labouchere lift Northampton for London by the 8 45 p.m. train, for the Hous3 of Commons direct. The pall was heavier than on the last occasion through 500 voters having been added to the register, but the fact that 753 more haw.? voted shows that there were not so many abstentions on th,2 Liberal side as had been expected.
FURNMkUX FRAUDS.
EVIDENGE OF LORD COLERIDGF.-COMMITTAL
OF THE PRISONERS.

The prisoners were again brought before the liiraningbarn magistrates yesterday. The knowledge that Lord Chief Justice Coleridge would appear in the witness-box created a -profound sensation, and the interest taken in the proceedings was intense. The adventuress, since she was brought to the court on Thursday, has prepared a long written statement in which she makes allegations too grave for publication against different persons. She declares that only two occasions has she appeared in male attire, and that those were when she was told that Mr. Powell was hunting at every railway station and every railway carriage for her, and that she could only make her escape in male clothing. The Lord Chief Justice arrived at New-street Station by the quarter past 12 o'clock train from London and was driven by the mayor to the police office, where 1:e arrtved 10 minutes later. The learned judge gave his evidence amidst breathless silence. Having been sworn upon the bench, he Ivas examined by Mr. Pollard: What is your name? John Duke Coleridge, Lord Chief Justice of Eng- land.—Will you be good enough to state do you know either of the prisoners? Not that I am aware of.—Has your lord- ship ever seen either of them with reference to the matter of

• Lord Arthur Clinton? Never in my life that lam aware of: certainly not about Lord Arthur Clinteu.—Handing his lord. shin a document known a "the proclamation" respecting Lord Clinton, Mr. Pollard aslied : Will your lordship be good enough to say whether it is your signature? Lord Coleridge (unhesitatingly): Certainly not.—A second document was put in with the same answer, and a letter purporting to have been writted by his lordship was proncunced by the distinguished witness to bear no resemblance whatever to his handwriting, the same reply being made respecting two other forged letters.—Mr. Pollard: Here is another letter, dated the 9th of August, addressed to Lord Arthur Pelham Clinton. That is not my handwritfig.—Here are four others not previously put in. Do you wish me to read them ?—No, my lord ; simply state whether they bear your , signature. Certainly not. None of these have any re- semblance to my handwriting.—It is alleged that the male Prisoner stated that he had an interview with your lordship at Judges'. Chambers, in 1876 or 1877, with reference to this matter. I certainly never had such an interview, nor could I have had, for I was not at Judges' Chambers during the years 1876 and 1877.—Mr. Pollard: That is all I have to ask you.—Both prisoners were subsequently committed for trial.

- HOUSE OF LORDS. Lord CARLINGFORD, replying to Lord Middleton, said the Government had no power to interfere with the holding of fairs in Ireland, and were net_ prepared to introduce a bill on the subject.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. MR. 13nADLAvan.—Mr. Bradlaugh occupied his usual seat under the Press Gallery at four o'clock; bat the official return to the writ for Northampton not having reached the Speaker, he did cot present himself at the table to take the oath. It is understood be will do so next Tuesday. THE STATE OF IRELAND:—Mr. CALLAN gave notice that on an early day the member for Waterford would cel the attention of the House to the state of Ireland. SENTENCE By A SCOTCH JUDGE.—Sir W. HAncounT re- plying to Mr. Cameron, said he had ha 1 his attention called to a sentence of five years' penal servitude having beets passed on two boys aged 14, by Lord Deas, for stealing letters at Glasgow. He thought penal servitude ought not to be inflicted on such young persons, and Ile had directed the boys to be released after the ordinary imprisonment of six months. THE OUTRAGE ON THE QUEEN.—Sir W. HARCOURT said he had no material facts to communicate relative to the outrage on the Queen. The bullet from the pistol had been found that morning. The Queen had not suffered in health from the outrage. PERSECUTION or THE JEWS.—On the motion for going into Cbmmittee of Supply, BARON DE WORMS moved a reso- lution deploring the persecution of the Jews in Russia, and urging the Government to use their good offices to prevent a recurrence of acts of violence. He detailed horrors per- petrated on the Jews in Russia, and said 201 women had been violated, 56 men had been killed, 20,000 rendered houseless, and £16,000,000 worth of property had been wrecked. He severely condemned the action of the Russian Government, which allowed its troops to perpetrate such horrors, and said that the Government having connived at the outrages were morally responsible for them. He did not wish the Government to intermeddle with foreign affairs. but he did ask that the good offices of the British Govern- ment might be used to prevent a repetition of such horrors in future.—Mr. SLAGG stworted the resolution.—Sergeant SIMON condemned the resolution as an unfortunate mistake. The House had no right to pass censure on foleign govern- ments, and the resolution, if passed, would render the position of the Jews in Russia worse than ever.—Mr. GLADSTONE thought if the resolution was passed it would promote injuries to those whom it was wished to serve, and he did not think the House could move in the matter without doing serious mischief. Anything beyond friendly counsel he thought would be unwise, and suggested withdrawal of the resolution.—Sir STAFFORD NottTHCOTE admitted the delicacy of the position in which the House was placed, and trusted a hostile division would be avoided.—Mr. COHEN objected to the resolution, and thought it would injure the effect of the great meeting held a few days ago.—The discussion was continued by Mr. Bourlie, Mr. Eckroyd, Sir C. Dilke, and Mr. Ashtnead Bartlett.
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Col. McCurquodale presided at the monthly meeting held at the workhouse yesterday. There were also present Messrs. Darbyshire, Cooper, Owen, Gibson, Kilsllall4Houghton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. 11. Gornall (medical officer), IV. Owen (surveyor), and G. Rawling (inspector).

TIIE ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF THE QUEEN. I The CHAIRMAN said before proceeding with the business that morning he felt sure they would join with him in heart- felt gratitude to Almighty God that our most gracious sovereign lady the Queen had beer, saved from the effects of the diabolical attempt that was made upon her life on the previous day. He felt sure that, had a fatal result occurred, which, God be thanked had not been the case, they would have been totally unfitted to discharge their duty that day. (Hear, hear.) lie did not think any one of them would have had nerve to go into the business and attend to their duties that morning. There would have been a gloom caat over the whole length and breadth of the land, and they would have felt as if death had catered into their own houses. He, for one, felt most thankful that the life of of Her Majesty was spared, and he was sure the members would all Join with him in the expression of the hope, that she may long continue to reign ever the happy, loyal, and contented people she had reigned over so long. He believed he was quite correct in stating that we had not had, in the history of our country, another sovereign who had done so rn ch good as the Queen—(hear, hear)—and during whose reign the country, had been so contanted, so happy, and so prosperous. (Hear, hear.) Mr. DARBYSIIIRE felt sure the members agreed with the chairman in the rernaiks he had given expression to that morning, in reference to the attempt which had been made upon the life of Her Majesty the Queen, and also that they all felt grateful that she had escaped. Mr. COOPER also joined with the chairman in showinee his allegiance to the Queen. He said that, as a public body of Englishmen, he thought it was their bounden duty, be- fore proceeding with the business, to join with the chairman in thanking an Allwise Providence for His merciful inter- position in saving the country from the perpetration of the dastardly intention of the coward and villian who had attempted to take her life. From a boy it had always been his duty, next to his allegiance to God, to show his allegiance to the sovereigu of this country, and he hoped, she might long be spared to reign over the country; " The CHAIR/SAN said it was clear they all ri.;',;iced tha+ e Queen had been spared to reign over us ' THE LONGFORD D 17,0„,. The CLERK, referring to th°_. action of the Authority in reference to Longford De_aoot, said' the Deputy Town Clerk had told him they h°,:a visited several works for the disposi- tion of manure ;:n other parts of the country, and that the Corporat i.'2,11 Lad reason to believe that the nuisance corn- 91°.'.ite1 of by the inhabitants of Orford had arisen from the use of what was called the carboniser. !ley propoecd to dispense With the use of the carboniser altogether, and they were full of expectation that the nuisance would Ce deviated. He (the clerk) explained to them that the purpose of the Authority was not to interfere or to pat the slightest diffi- culty in the way of the Corporation removing in the way aey do, the :contents of the privies and ashpits from the densely I)opu!ated districts of the borough, but that what the Authority contended for was that in removing the oee nuisance they should not create another, sedecially if it was possible by any known means to discontinue the nuisan. e. (Hear, hear.) He therefore advised the Authority to wait and hear the result of the proposed work. The Cr- TRMAN siid they must give the Corporation a. little time to make the change, and they must express them- selves very much pleasal that the Corporation were going to do so.

The MEDICAL OFFICER believed the nuisance a isirg from the carts would be remedied. Mr. DAEI3YS/II RE said the Authority should look after the pollution of the streams as well as the pollutlen of the atmosphere.

ALKALI th. WM:KS INSPF.CTOES. A letter was read from the Local Government Board ac- knowledging receipt of the Authority's letter of the 28th January, and informing. Ihem th it the matters referred to in the memorial forwarded therewith had been under considera- tion. With respect to the portion of the memorial which related to the appointment of a separate inspector for each of the districts of Widnes and St Helens, the writer was di- rected to inquire whether the Authority were willing to take advantage of the provision in Section 19 of the Alkali 4:c. Works Regulation Act, 1881, for the appointment of ad- ditional inspectors, or whether they were prepared to unite with any adjoining authorities for the purpose. The CLERK suggested that the proper reply was that, un- fortunately, while the Authority had all this nuisance they had not an increase, but an absolute reduction of the rate- able value of the farm lands surrounding the district, and that it seemed rather hard for the Autherity to he called upon to join in the expanse of their inspectors under these circumstances. The suggestion was adopted. THE NEW RATE. The CLERK presuited the estimate to meet the expendi- ture during the hrlf-year ending Michaelmas, and on the proposition of Mr. DARI3YSIIIRE, it was decided that a rate id. in the £ be laid.

TUE CHAIRMA.N' AND TIIE BOARD. The CuitumA.N said as his engagements for the corning year would prevent him attending the meetings of the Authority, he had to ask them to accept his resignation. He referred to the good feeling that had existed, and ex- pressed the hope that Mr. Dar'byshire would be elected chair- man.

Mr. RYLANDS congratulated the chairman upon his hon- ourable appointment as high sheriff—(applause)—and sug- gested*that at the next meeting the chairman should be re-elected, but that the duties should be discharged by the vice-chairman.
Mr. DARBTSIIIRE and Mr. COOPER bore testimony to the efficient manner in which the chairman lal fulfilled his duties, and hoped he would agree to Mr. Rylands' snggea. tion.
—Ultimately, the chairman said he Would place himself in the hands of the Board of Guardians.
