RUNCORN COFFEE AND COCOA HOUSE CO. Sir,—According to your report of the annual meeting of ' this company, Mr. Geo. Haztehurst stated that "Many poor men who could not afford, had been constrained to put money in the Society, and now they were not getting any dividend." On examining the share list I find that there are only three that I think can be called poor men. One has paid £7 103., another, £l2 103 , and a third, £2 103. A 5 per cent dividend would of coarse be 7s. 61, 123. 61, and 23. 61. on these amounts. I may say that out of £1406 103. capital paid up, £l2Bl 18s. belongs to the original-promoters and their friends, only £124 12 baying been contributed by others, and of this amount £623. 103. is in three hands, and £62 23. in seven others. At the end of the first year (1878), the com- pany paid a dividend of 10 per cent on the 53. per share then paid, and for rBBO one of 21 per cent on 73. 6d. per share. The additional 53. per share called up, was most of it paid towards the close of last year. If the 12.1 per cent paid in dividends, had been spread over the four years, things would not have looked so bad.—Yours respectfully, March Ist, 1882. JOHN SIMPSON.

WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. SATURDAL—Before Alderman Chandley and Alderman Burgess. A WIFE DESERTER.—A puddler named John Bright was charged with running away from the borough and leaving his wife and family chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, said the prisoner's wife applied to the Guardians for aid on the 10th February, stating she was quite destitute, the household goods haying been sold for rent. Her husband, she alleged, could obtain constant employment, but did not often work. Herself and three children were admitted to the workhouse, and the pri- soner was subsequently apprehended at Congleton.—The case was adjourned for a month, to give the prisoner an opportunity of paying the Guardians the expenses they had incurred. • A WIDNES Tram—John William Cawley, a toolmaker, of Widnes, was charged with stealing 11 pounds of tripe from the shop of Thomas Richardson, Market-street, and three tea pots of the value of 35., the property of Thomas Bailey, also of Market-street. —From the Chief Constable's statement, it appeared that about three o'clock on the pre- vious afternoon the prisoner purchased a pennyworth of tripe at Richardson's shop. When he had left the premises Ann Broughton, the shopwornan, discovered that the priso- ner had left a tea pot, and she recalled him. He returned and took the tea pot, and as he was passing through the old market shed he was seen by Mrs. Bailey to take three tea pets from a crate which was standing there. She claimed the articles as her husband's property, but the prisoner ran along Castle-street, dropping the tea pots on his way. One was smashed. At the end of the street he was apprehended by P.C. Bruen, who found opon him 11 pounds of tripe. Mr. Hunt informed the Bench that the prisoners children were in the Warrington workhouse.—Alderman Burgess: How many ?—Prisoner: Six. Up to the previous day he had not been in the town for 15 months, and he was drunk when he committed the theft. He was paying 63 per week • towards his children.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for a month with bard labour. THE Boor ON THE WRONG LEG—John Morgan, a hawker, living at 13, Lord Nelson-street, was brought up on a war- rant charged with assaulting his wife.—Prisoner : Not guilty. 1 think the boot is on the wrong leg this time.— Prosecutrix said the prisoner went home drunk, and accused her of going with a man named Ned Brown. He "ran at her" and struck her, upon which she shouted Murder." The neighbours shouted "shame upon him." Her husband then sent for D±. Cannell to attend to her.—Prisoner said he had given his wife instructions not to visit Brown's house, who was a widower, but she persisted in doing so, saying, "I shall go to Brown's when I like. Brown's adecent man and you are a-- wastrel." She added that she would go and live " tally " with him. He (prisoner) allowed her 30s. per week, and if he bought a little clothing it would be in the pawnshop next day.—The prisoner had been before the Bench seven times previously on various charges, and he was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognisance of £lO. 510:MAL—Before Major Cartwright, Alderman Holmes, and Councillor Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS. Michael Mulkearn (14) and John Butler (15) were charged with playing pitch and toss in Carlisle-street at a quarter-past eleven on Sunday morning. P.S. Bowen proved the case, and the prisoners were each fined 2s 6d and costs.—Two young men named Joseph Shep- herd and James Wilke, glass cutters, were charged with committing a breach of the peace in New-road, Latchford, on the 19th February. P.S. Bowen and P.C. Hitchmough deposed to seeing the defendants exchange blows. A witness named Whitworth stated Wilks did not strike Shepherd. The latter was bound over to keep the peace for six months. Wilke was discharged. WARNING TO "HOT POTATO" DEALERS. James potato dealer, was summoned for obstructing the free passage of Horsemarket-street on the 18th February, by allowing his potato engine to stand there an unreason- able timc.—P.C. Paice said the defendant was standing with his potato engine in front of the Ram's Head from 10 minutes past two until 20 minutes to three. Several shop- keepers complained of the obstruction.—Sergeant Cox cor- roborated.—Defendant said he paid 2s 61 toll, and considered he had a right to stand there.—Mr. Hunt: It is a great nuisance.—Alderman Holmes: It is a great nuisance, cer- tainly; but it is a great convenience.—Major Cartwright said although defendant paid toll he had no right to stand in the street. He paid toll to ha sk.—Defendant : Yes, sir.—Major Cartwright : Very well, then, you must keep on the move.—Mr. Hunt said there were a number of grocers who paid toll, but they delivered their goods and went away.— The defendant was cautioned, and ordered to pay the court fees. THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER THREATENED.— Mary McCohen was charged with using obecene language. —P.S. Bowen said on Monday morning last the defendant used some very bad language towards the school attendance officer, Mr. Riley, and threatened to have his life Mr. Riley hurried away, and the defendant ran after him vowing she would have " satisfaction off that ." It was becom- ing a custom for the women who had been summoned by Mr. Riley to wait for him at the bottom of the steps leading into the court and attack him.—Mr. Riley said the sergeant's statement was true —Major Cartwright remarked that it was becoming an intolerable nuisance for Mr. Riley to do his duty-, and fined the defendant Si. and costs. UNJUST WEIGHTS.—Jane Curry, butcher, 14, Pinner's- brow, was charged with having in her possession for use an unjust 21b. and 11b. weight.—Mr. Place, inspector of • weights and measures, said he visited the defendant's shop on the 17th February, and found a 21b. weight 81 drachms shOrt of its proper weight, and a 11b. weight 3 drachms •• light. There were seven other weights also a little below their full weight. He added he did not believe the defend- ant had allowed the weights to get in that state intention- ally, and the Bench consequently only inflicted the penalty of ss. and costs. A UNION PROSECUTION.—Peter Clough, a file cutter at Messrs. Jolley and Co.'s works, was c' !merged, under a warrant, with neglecting to maintain his wife and family.—Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, said the prisoner's wife applied for relief to the Board of Guardians on the previous Wed- nesday, and she was admitted to the Workhouse. He had visited the home, which was badly furnished and unin- habitable, and was unable to find any food on the premises. The defendant could with ease earn 23a. and 21s, per week. The prisoner contended that he gave his wife sufficient money to live on, remarking that she could "drink as much ale as anybody in England."—P.C. Chantler deposed to apprehending the prisoner in a common lodging house on Town Hill, on Sunday night, when he was under the.in- fluence ref liquor. He (witness) hid always considered the prisoner's wife a respectable woman, and had never seen her drunk.—P.S. Bowen said he had often seen the prisoner drunk, but not his wife.—Prisoner, who had a long list of previous offences against him, was committed to gaol for a month with hard labour. THE SCHOOL COMMITiEE AT WORK —Thomas Randles, soap maker, Bank Quay, was summoned by Mr. Riley, the school attendance inspector, for neglecting to send his child Ellen regularly to school. This was defendant's second ap- pearance, and it was stated that the girl had not passed an examination in her life. She had been absent CO times since Christmas. Fined 55.—Martin Non, of Silver-square, pleaded guilty to neglecting to send his son to school, he haying only attended school six times out of a possible 140. A fine of ss. WAS imposed.—For a similar offence, Samuel Maxfield, of Stamford-street, was mulcted in the sum of 55. —Joseph Davies, of Latchford, was charged with not pro- viding proper schooling for his step-daughter, Maria Fair- hurst. Mr. Riley said the defendant had appeared three times before the School Attendance Committee and twice before the Bench in reference to his step-daughter, who for four successive years had lost the grant to the Roman Catholic school. Since the beginning of January she had only attended school 10 half days. The mother said the girl was 12 years of age and consumptive; and she handed in a certificate from Dr. Richmond, dated Thursday, which stated the girl was a patient at the Infirmary and unable to follow her employment. Mr. Riley maintained that the girl was title to attend echool, and the case was adjourned for a fortnight, so that he might collect some further in- formation.—For not sending his son Aired to school, Alfred Barker, living in Birchall-stree', was fined 59.—A similar penalty was inflicted on Pat Dolby, joiner, Blackhurst- street, who pleaded guilty to neglecting to send his daughter regularly to school.—Pat Glynn Golborne-street, was fined 53. for a similar offence. Mr. Riley stated the defendant's daughter, Mary Ann, 11 years of age, had only passed the Ist standard. A DISHONEST LODGER.—Ceeii Gilbert Peetival, a fitter and draughtsman, was charged with having stolen a silver Geneva watch from the dwelling-house of Thomas Gibson, toolmaker, Tinsley-terrace, Foundry-street.—For the last four ruenths the prisoner had lodged with the prosecutor. After he had left the house on Saturday merning, the watch was missed from the prosecutor's bedroom. Enquiries were instituted by Inspector Berry, w no learned that the prisoner had attempted to pawn the watch, and he was subsequently apprehended in the Corporation beerhouse. In asswer to the charge, he said "Yes, I did."—The prisoner said he had given way to intemperance for the last seven months, and it had been the cause of him sealing the watch.—He was committed to gaol for a month with hard labour. NURSING A SERPENT.—Emma Brocklehurst, an old woman, was charged with having, on the 13th February, stolen a blue bed quilt and a quantity of wearing apparel, of the value of Bs., the property of Robert Shaw, a forgeman, living at 24, Howell-street.—ln November last the prisoner called at the prosecutor's hone°, and narrated so pitiful a tale of her troubles that Mrs. Shaw took compassion upon

her, and from that day "treated her as one of the family." On the 12th February the prisoner suddenly disappeared, and with her had also disappeared a quantity of wearing apparel and a bed quilt. The bed quilt had been offered ill pawn by the prisoner, and on Saturday last she was appre- hended in Congleton.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner had been several times convicted, and was at present under police supervision. She was " gazetted "on September 30, 1880, for having left her place of abode without reporting herself, and was also " wanted " at Stockport on a charge of felony. —The prisoner was committed to Liverpool Sessions for trial. FELONY BY A MARRIED WOMAN.—Mary Ann Miller, wife of John Miller, bandsman in the 2nd Royal Lancashire Militia, was charged with stealing two boots of the value of 85. 6d , the property of Alfred Hollywell.—The prosecutor, who is a boot and shoe dealer at Middleton, occupies a stall in the Warrington Market, and on Saturday night the priso- ner went to his stall, took into her hands a number of boots and inquired their price. She did not make a purchase, but when she departed two odd boots were missed. Subsequently P.S. Cox visited the prisoner's house,- and found there the stolen articles. When charged the prisoner said she found the boots under a stall.—The prisoner's husband asked: the Bench to deal leniently with her, and she was fined L 1 and and £1 Bs. costs, total £2 83. THE DANGERS OF THE STREET.—SAVAGE ATTACK ON A YOUNG Womaar.—A young fellow named John Morrissy, described as a "tramping grinder," living in a common lodging-house in Bank-street, was charged with stealing two shawls, value Os, from the person of Sarah Hansbury, living with her husband in Blackburst-street.— From the evidence, it appeared the prosecutrix was in Dial-street on Saturday night at 11-30 waiting for her husband, when the prisoner approached her, and familiarly accosted her with, " Well, Polly, how are you ?" He accompanied the words with an insulting push, and the prosecutor told him she was a married woman, and wished to have nothing to do with him. Entering a passage the prisoner beckoned the prose- cutrix to go to him, and when she would not, he seized her in a violent manner. In her struggles to release herself, the prosecutrix left her shawls in the hands of the prisoner and ran away. He followed, struck her with his fist, kicked her on the leg, and pulled savagely at her hair. A Mrs. O'Brien coming on the scene the prisoner made off with the shawls:in his possession. Half an hour later, Inspector Berry received a complaint from a female of the prisoner's con- duct, who he found in Buttermarket-street in a very drunken condition. He was consequently locked up, and explained that he had had a few words with his wife, who had left the shawl in his possession. They were subsequently dis- covered to belong to the prosecutrix.—ln extenuation of the offence, the prisoner put forward the plea of drunkenness.— Major Cartwright said women must be protected from such men as the prisoner, who was sentenced to four months' im- prisonment with hard labour. SERIOUS AGGRAVATED ASSAULT: A DANGEROUS FELLOW. —John McCarty, a country-looking fellow, was charged with committing an aggravated assault on Priscilla Roberts, domestic servant to Mr. Benjamin Grimshana Folly Farm, and also with using threatening language to James Kilcan- non, teamsman to the same gentleman.—The Chief Con- stable said Miss Roberts was 23 years of age. The prisoner had been cowman for Mr. Grimshaw for the last two months. On Wednesday last the prisoner attempted to take certain familiarities with Miss Roberts, which she resented, and in defending herself she broke a stone jar. The prisoner then "took to his heels and ran." Mr. and Mrs. Grimshaw left home on Saturday evening, leaving Miss Roberts in charge of the farm; and on Sunday the prisoner was seen peeping through the front window. Some time afterwards she went into the back yard to empty some ashes. when the prisoner "jumped upon her "from behind the rain tub. She eluded his grasp and ran into the kitchen, the door of which she bolted. The prisoner made use of some disgraceful language, and Miss Roberts sent the poker at him. It struck him on the neck. He caught hold of her, and putting his head under her chin, struck her across the face and behaved indecently. Miss Roberts screamed loudly, and Captain Herbert, who lived in the house adjoining, came upon the scene.—The prisoner, Mr. Hunt observed, was well known at the court, having served two terms of imprisonment for assaulting a girl named Agnes Holt, who had had to leave a good situation through his conduct. Miss Roberts said she had been com- pelled, to leave home through the prisoner's conduct.—The Prisoner: She called me foul names, and I catched hold of her and kissed her. That was all I did. I wouldn't hurt a hair of her head.—Mr. White: They don't generally kiss them for calling them foul names.—Mary Jane Roberts con(b)rated her sister's statement. and Jas. Kilcannon proved the threatening language. He stated that prisoner brandished a knife when he came on the scene.—P.S. Bowen deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who admitted the offence, and said he had been courting Miss Roberts for ten years.—The Bench commented strongly upon the pri- soner's conduct, and sentenced him to six month's hard labour.
TUESDAY.—Before Major CArtwright and Mr. Frcd. Monks.

A PRECOCIOUS DRUNKARD.— Edward Sauce, who was described in the charge sheet as being sixteen years of age, and a forge labourer, residing at 10, Town-hill, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street the previous night.—P.C. Crickett, who proved the case, said the prisoner, who was cursing and acting in a disorderly manner, stretched out his arms and knocked the people off the footpath. It required three officers to carry the prisoner to the police station.—Major Cartwright: He has been here before.—The Chief Constable: He has; for being drunk, and he is only 17 years of age,P.C. Crickett : His con- duct was most disgrac2ful, sir.—The Chief Constable: His conduct since he has been locked up has been very disgrace- ful, indeed. He howled and yelled for a long time, and knocked and kicked shamefully.—P.C. Chantler : He had to have his clogs taken off. The prisoner was sent to gaol for fourteen days with hard labour. :31TEFT BY A lawirEn.—Patrick Cahill, a hawker, residing in Bay Horse-yard, was charged with stealing from the per- son of Mary Dolan, whilst in the Higher Angel, on Monday night, two neck shawls, value 2s. 61., her property.—The complainant, a girl 18 years of age, had been out charring on Monday, and about nine o'clock at night when in Butter- market-street, she met a female friend who asked her to go into the Higher Angel and have a bottle of cider. She agreed and they went, and were about to drink the beverage when the prisoner entered, and asked the complainant for " his shilling." The complainant, who had not seen the pr'soner previously that night, said she had not got a shil- ling, but prisoner maintained that he had given her one, and said if she did not return it he would take her shawls. He carried out his threat, and on getting outside com- plainant called the attention of P.C. Evans, who was passing, to the matter, and in the end the prisoner was locked up.— Prisoner still maintained that he gave the complainant is. for an immoral purpose, but this she denied, stating that another young woman was with the prisoner. It having been proved that the complainant could not have seen the prisoner previously at the time he stated, the prisoner was fined ss. and costs, .£1 63., or in default 14 days' imprison- ment.
THURSDAIY.—Before Giptain hitton and Alderman Webster.

INHUMAN HUSBANDS : DESERVED PUNISHINIEWS.—Chas. Clark, an underhand puddler, was charged with running away and leaving his wife and two children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. Harbourne said on the 4:h February the prisoner's wife appealed to him. He investigated the matter, and found the family in a very destitute condition, being in want of food, clothes, and shoes. The Guardians in consequence allowed her 4s. per week. Before paying the money, witness saw the prisoner, and asked him to make some arrangement with his wife. He offered her 4s. per week, which she refused, as she considered it insufficient to maintain her.—Sarah Davies, mother-in- law of the prisoner, said her daughter during the last nine , weeks bad only received 15s. from the prisoner, who, al- though he could get emploval/mi, would not work.—P.S. , James deposed to apprehending the prisoner at Bursiem, where he was working at an iron works.—Mr. Sutton lasked on behalf of the Guardians that where a Case cif neglect and cruelty was fully proved, as in this case, the Bench would severely punish the offender.—Mr. Hunt said he had 50 warrants in his possession for the apprehension of persons who had left their families.—The prisoner was sentenced to two months' hard labour.--James Gleave, a wire forger, employed at Messrs. Jolley's ironworks, and living at 20, Erwood-street, was charged with allowing his wife and children to become chargeable to the Union.—lt appeared that on Saturday night last the prisoner smashed the furniture in is house, and turned his wife and three children into the street. The Guardians, after considering the case, admitted the family into the workhouse, and on Wednesday Mr. Harbourne had an interview with the prisoner, and informed him that he had better remcve them from the morkhouse. He .replied "No, she can stop there a hundred years."—A witness was called to prove the destitution of the family, who stated there was not a chair to sit upon in the house.—Alderman NiCetster said he considered the prisoner's conduct shameful. —After some deliberation the Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for 14 days with hard labour' FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Alderman Davies, and Mr. John White.

DAMAGE IN nig )racE CELL.—Joseph Marsh,a young man, was charged with beln drunk and disorderly in San-1 key-street, at 11-30 last night; and also I'd wilful damage doing damage to the amount of 3s ad in the police cell by rollting a utensil.—The prisoncr was fined is and costs for beitig drunk, or in default seven days' imprisonment ; and his was ordered to pay the damage, or a fuitl.er term of 14 dayg' im- prisonment. FELONY BY A YOUNG Womor.—Margard §ig-gailey, young woman, living at 22, •Dolman's-lane, Vers clrd with stealing a woollen shawl, of the value of 10s', Ore ' dwelling-house of John McCormick, 23, Dolinan's-igsi.-= Whilst the prosecutor's wife was absent a few minutes froth her house, the prisoner entered and abstracted the shawl, afterwards pirening it at Mr. Jackson's for 4s.—The prisoner had been previously convicted for felony, and she was cDm• mitted to gaol for a month. A DISHONEST SERVANT.—Abraham Mercer, journeyman hamper tinker, was charged with stealing from his employer, Mr. James Chantler, Wilderspool-road, a new market basket, of the value of 39.—0 n the previous evening the prisoner was seen to cirry the basket from the warehGnbe, and conceal it behind a quantity of willows. Thomas Millington watched the place, and half an hour afterwards the prisover fetched it and gave it to his young son Subsequently the prisoner was apprehended by P.C. McLaren with the basket in his possession.—Prisoner maintained his innoceuce, and st.,ited he had had the basket for six months.—He was committed to gaol- for 14 days With hard labour. of Old-road, Laarytehafonrdd, Ewlelreen Hughes, charged yfainthd Annie Salmon,

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 4, 1882. WORKINGMEN'S IISS lON CHAPEL. ST. HELENS TRAMWAYS COMPANY.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 4, 1882. WORKINGMEN'S IISS lON CHAPEL. ST. HELENS TRAMWAYS COMPANY.

assaulting Catherine O'Brien, of the same neighbourhood.— Hearing a scream of murder in Old-road at about 11 o'clock on Saturday night, the complainant went to discover the cause. The defendants were illtreating a woman, and when complainant attempted to help her, they attacked her, and "all got in her hair pulling it out by the roots." Complain- ant produced a large quantity of hair.—After hearing the evidence, the defendants were ordered to pay the costs 4s 63 each.—Elizabeth Hill and Henrietta Wade, married women, were charged with having, on the 25th February, used language to Mary Anderson calculated to provoke a breach of the peace.—The parties are neighbours, living in Wakefield-street, and It was stated there was some illfeeling with regard to pigeon flying. It was shown that a series of retaliotary annoyances had taken place between the com- plainant and the defendants, and the cases were dismissed, each party to pay their own costs. MAINTENANCE OF A CHILD. - Henry Archer, wire drawer, 9, Rogers-street, was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute towards the maintenance of his child, Sarah Ellen.—Mr. Shearer asked for an order for 4s 10d per week, and the Bench acceded to the application.—lt was stated that the defend- ant's wife was also in the workhouse, but in consequence of the defendant being able to prove that she had been un- faithful to him, the Guardians could not ask for an order in respect to her.

ANNUAL TEA MEETING. Over 200 persons sat down to tea in the schoolroom of the Workingmen's Mission Chapel, Bank Quay, Warrington, on Monday evening, on the occasion of the annual grithering of the members of the church. The tables were decorated with plants, &c., and the trays were given by the following : Mrs. Long, Mrs. Monks, Mrs. Williamson, Mrs. Ashley. Mrs. Hough, Mrs. Grant, Mrs. Hill, Mrs. Hassall, Miss Wood- ward, Mrs. Middleton, Mrs. Summerfield, Mrs. Turton, Mrs. Osborne, Mrs. Dasvber, and Mr. Bolton. The usual enter- tainment was afterwards held. It proved a most successful one, and was the source of much pleasure to the large audience. Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., presided, and there were also present Messrs. E. Bolton, N. Legge, H. Roberts, J. Monks, J. Long, T. Ashley, F. Williams (lion. secretary), eec. The CHAIRMAN, in his address, said these annual parties were calculated to do them a great deal of good, and they gave la great deal of pleasure. He thought it was exceedingly kind of the teachers of the school, that they not only gave their services every Sunday in teaching the children, but had contributed out of their own small means 10s. each to- wards the trays for the tea. (Applause.) He thought that was exceedingly liberal on their part, and be had no doubt whatever of the success of a Sunday school like this when therewere teacher T who would practice such self denial. But the success of a place like that depended, of course, more upon the teachers and the superintendent than upon any- thing else; and if the superintendent and the teachers entered upon their work in a true spirit, with the sole ob- ject of doing good to those who were wound them, and not for the sake of self-glorification and self-importance, they were sure to succeed. When Sunday schools broke down it generally arose through the people who undertook the management of them, having in view some object other than the true object of a Sunday school—that was, the good of the children. (Hear. , hear.) It was now ten years since the Mission chapel was built, and the good it had been since then to the Sun- ' day school must be very great indeed. He was sure the chapel had been like a ray tif light in the midst of a dark cloud—(hear, hear),—for before then the children were running about Bank Quay as utterly uncared for as if they had been in the middle of Africa. They might have been heathens, and the parents who lived around there must be thankful, he was sure, to the teachers of that school for their devotion to the children every Sunday. He must also say there was credit due to the parents for the way in which they sent their children to schocl, because their at- tendance was remarkably good and regular. He also thought there was great credit due to the Mission Chapel, for when the census was taken of the attendance at the different places of worship in Warrington, there was no place that had such a large attendance in proportion as the Slission Chapel. (Applause.) Out of 300 sittings he found there were 280 persons present—(hear, hear) ;—ard he was told by his friends around him that there were many Sunday nights when the chapel was filled to overflowing, and many.had to go away because they could not get seats. All this was very encouraging, and very hopeful for the future. They had gone through troubles as every place of worship had to go through troubles, but he could say with truth that day that the chapel and the Sunday school were stronger, healthier, better, and more prosperous than ever they had been since they were opened. (Hear, hear.) This was very encouraging, and he looked forward to the future of the Mission chapel and school with the greatest pleasure. He concluded with expressing his indebtedness to the teachers for the admirable manner in which they conducted their classes. (Applause.) The SECRETARY read the annual report, which, after speaking of the spiritual prcress made during the past year, stated they had every reason to hope for, nay to expect still greater things, because the congregation consisted largely of young men and women who had been or were scholars in the Sunday school. They were glad to report a large increase in the number of members. They had on the books 60 members; at the commencement of last year they had only 20; thus showing an increase of 40. This number, they believed, would soon be augmented as they had several friends who were about to join them. It was gratifying to be able to say that of the number quoted the greater portion were young people. The class, which had been put in thorough working order, was of great benefit to the church, and was well attended. During the past year the school's history had been made memorable by the most successful anniversary ever held. They believed it was through this that their services since had been so largely attended. The Sunday services were never so largely attended, and they believed theirs was one of the best attended chapels in War- rington, the chapel being filled every Sunday evening, people having on several occasions to go away for want of room. During the year they had had two series of special services, and much good had resulted. The school was steadily increasing ; and they bad found it necessary to extend- their borders. They were building two vestries which they hoped would be.ready for occupation about the end of March. It was intended to hold a conversazione, and to adopt other means to defray the cost of the work, but Mr. Crosfield, with his usual generosity, stepped forward and met the whole cost, (Applause.) This had enabled them to devote their energies towards raising funds for the purchase of new banners, and satisfactory progress had been made. They had at present on the books 420 scholars, with an average attendance of 160 in the morning, and 350 in the afternoon. There were also on the books 18 male and 10 female teachers, with an average attendance of 16 males and 10 females. The expenditure during the year had been £65 195., and the income £6l Be., leaving a balance of £4 11s, due to the treasurer. The CHAIRMAN here stated that be was sorry Mrs. Cros- field was not present, but she had had to go away for the benefit of her health. Had she been at home, she would have been very glad lobe with them. (Applause.) During the evening Mr. A. Crosfield gave two well executed pianoforte solos, and the enthusiasm with which he was greeted showed that hi a efforts had been greatly ap- preciated. Recitations were given by Mr. G. Aspinall and Mr. John Taylor, both of whom were listened to with great interest, and the spirited delivery of Mr. Aspinall's pieces calls for special remark, A dialogue was also well rendered by Masters Alfred Long, Joseph Williams, James Lawton, Joseph Monks, and William Foster, who were warmly ap- plauded at its close. Miss J. Burrows met with a cordial reception for her capital vocalisation of "The nightingale," and she appeared to even greater advantage in the duet, "Home to our mountains," with her brother Mr. J. Burrows. " When we were boys together" was ably sung by Mr. H. Roberts, who secured an encore by his rendition of "The dumb wife," which was provocative of much laughter. Besides discharging the duties of accompanist, Mr. Thomas Ford gave two concertina solos in masterly style, and ob- tained the deserved applause of the audience. Mr. N. LEGGE proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding. Mr. E. BOLTON seconded the motion, and referred. to his long acglaint4nceship witb the Crosfield family, who had contributed much to the welfare of those around them. • Mr. 8.. Wirto.aorsors supported the motion, which was car- ried with enthusiasm, and Ihe meeting terminated with the Benediction being pro- nounced. General regret and sympathy was felt by the committee and friends at the absence of Mrs. Crosfield through indis- position, and hopes were entertained that she would soon be amongst them again.

The annual general meeting of this company was held on Monday afternoon, at the Fleece Hotel, Mr. Busby pre- siding. There were present Messrs. J. Riley, Spencely, Pen- nington, H. L. Riley, Slater, Lewis, Gaskin, R Coop, J. C. Wolfenden, Harrison, Speight, Beloe (engineer), Dromgoole, Hammill (secretary), ar.d others. The Secretary's report was read as follows :

It is the duty of your directors to meet you here to-day to give an account of their stewardship, and this duty is ren- dered very agreeable by the statement which we are able to make to you, and which will confirm your belief that we have embarked in a desirable undertaking. The first section of the tramways was completed and opened for public traffic in November last, and we are happy to inform you that so far the traffic on this section was quite equal to, and in fact exceeded the original estimate of your directors. This line from Present to St. Helens will give better accommodation when it is opened through the town to the railway station, and a good increase of the traffic may be safely looked for when passengers from Pres- cot and St. Ann's can be taken to the railway station. With the view of securing as much of the summer traffic as possible we have entered into a contract with Messrs. Chas. Phillips and Co., of London. They are substantial tramway contractors, who, in addition to making a cash payment to the company (which was needed for the due completion of the Prescot sec- tion), have undertaken the laying of the lines from Denton's Green by the Cricket Ground through the town and on to Peasley Cross; from Haydock into the heart of the town (six miles in all); and to erect substantial and commodious stabling, car sheds, manager's house and office on land which we have fortunately been able to secure close to Corporation-street, and very near the railway station. The contract also provides for the equipment of these lines with a sufficient number of horses, cars, harness, and other requisites. The' consideration for this contract was the allotment to Messrs. Phillips and Co., or their nominees, of 3,746 shares in the company, and 1,750 of mortgage bonds, which the Company's Act entitle to be issued, which prac- tically complete the entire capital of the company both in shares and mortgages; and while the nominal value of this consideration is undoubtedly higher than would have been paid on a cash con- tract, your directors had met with so much difficulty in at- tempting to float their shares, and had been put to so much expense in connection with their :successive prospectuses, that they thought it better at once to dispose of their capital in ex- change for the desired works, and leave to their contractors the burthen of outlay and delay in connnection with the ulti- mate placing of the shares and bonds. It is satisfactory to re- member that within the money powers created by Parliament in favour of the company all the estimates laid before it, the un- dertaking of the company will be completed in all its essential features, and as well equ'pped as any lines in the country possibly can be. It is also a matter of congt atulation for the original : abet eholders that the nett profits for the first two years' working' have been practically reserved for them, Messrs. Phillips and Co., who are also pur- chasers of a very considerable holding in the, first issue having undertaken that their second issue of shares shall not 1 rank for dividend for iWo years, and as has doubtless been ob- served have offered investors in the shares issued by them a guaranteed interest at the rate of 6 per cent. No time has been lost by Messrs; Philips & Co. over these additional lines, and already they have been laid through the main streets of this town to the cricket field on the one side, and to Peasley Cross on the other; and completed with the exception of a few rails to be put in on the railway bridge, which we expect will be I finished off during the next fortnight. Good progress has also been made with the tiamway to -Haydock, so much so that we expect being ab'e to get the lines in the town and to Black- brook on the Haydock route inspected and opened during next month, and the remainder by the first of May. Prescot line is doing exceedingly well, but the directors fully expect to get even better results from the Peasley Cross and the Hay- dock route; from the former because it suns hrough the long main streets of the town and along the thickly populated dis- tricts of Peasley Cross; and from the other because the whole route from St. Helens to Blackbrook and along to Haydock is wholly without railway ace immodation. As you are aware the directors have,entered into working arrangement for the leasiug and management of the line for two years, during which the line will have full time to develop. The arrange- ment made secures to the shareholders of the first issue a minimum dividend of 5 per cent. during this period with in- crease of dividends as baffle receipts increase above a minimum sum as has been agreed upoe ; while the shareholders of the second issue receives a guaranteed interest at the rate of 6 per cent. during the first two years, after which date the shares will tank equally for divided against the earnings of the com- pany. Judging from the results of working the fist section, your directors havereason to believe that when all the lines are open for traffic the arrangements made will ensure for the orig,inal shareholders dividends considerably in excess of 5 per cent. I may mention that very good arrangements have been made for the advertising in the car • under which we get an asinual ren'al of £3O per car, and as we shall prebably have filteen to twenty ears it will be seen that our ren:als for adver- tising will form a g od increvse to a dividend upon capital. The first section having been op •ned so recently as Nov. last and only one menth's revenue having been obtained at the end of the year it is set proposed to make any distribution to the original shareholders, but the amount will be brought into and dealt with this year's account. The books will be made up to the end of June next, and at a subseque it meeting we trust that we shall be enabled to make a substantial distribui ion to our shareholders,

The CITAIR3IAN said he had been over the lines that morning, and had visited the horses and rolling stock, and work: and all was being conducted in a very good fashion. The SECRETARY read the balance sheet, some of the prin- cipal items of which were as follows:
CAPITAL AND LIABILITIES.
Capital subscribed Amount paid up Other Liabilities
BRUNNER, MOND, Sc CO., LIMITED,
WINNINGTON, NORTiIWICII.

The second half-yearly ordinary general meeting cf the shareholders of the above company was held at the Law Association Char.thers, Liverpool, on Monday last. Mr. John Crosfield presided, and there was a fair attendance of share- holders.

Mr. T. H. FORGAN (secretary to the company), read the notice convening the meetinz. The directors' report of the operations of the company, which had been printed and circulated amongst the share- holders, was taken as read. In it the directors stated, that nothwithstanding the continuance of the extremely low market prices which had now ruled so long, they could heartily congratulate the shareholders:upon the continued prosperity of their business': The profit for the half-year ended the' 30th June last, £12,927 4s 7d, was dis- posed of as follows :—The sum of £1.234 2s 81 was paid to the preference shareholders, and £lO,BOO to the ordinary shareholders, leaving £923 is 11d, which was carried for- ward. The balance sheet and profit and loss account showed a profit on the working of the half-year ended 31st Decem- ber, 1881, after charging income-tax for the year, of the sum of £17,032 10s 2d, which, with the amount brought for- ward, made a total of £17,955 12s id available for dividend. The amount payable on the preference capital was £2,916 198 sd, and the directors recommended the payment of a dividend upon the ordinary share capital at the rate of 19 per cent, per annum, which would absorb £14,250, leaving £7BB 12s Si to be carried forward. The re- port added : " One half of the new works at Winnington have been successfully started and are now in full operation. Mr. Edward Milner retires from the board of directors and is recommended for re-election. The auditor also retires but is eligible for re-election." The CHAIRMAN moved the following resolution :—" That the directors' report and statement of accounts, taken as read, be adopted, and that a dividend be paid to the holders of preference shares at the rate of 7 per cent per annum, on the amount paid up or credited on such shares, regard being had to the period for which such amount has been paid up or credited, and that a dividend be paid the holders of the ordinary shares at the rate of 19 pr cent per annum for the half year free of income tax, according to the amount paid up or credited on such shares." Mr. Crosfield said it was very satisfactory to the direc- tors that they had been able to pay even more than what was stated in the original prospectus. When they consi- dered that the alkali trade had been as bad as it could be during the past lZmonths, he thought that great credit was due to their managin2; directors who had put the company in a position to pay an average of 17 per cent, for the past year. (Hear, hear.) As far as he could see there was every prospect of the dividend for 1882 being as good or better.

Mr. H. COGHILL seconded the resolution, which was put to the meeting and unanimously carried. Mr. W. LONG, of Warrington, moved that Mr. Edward Milner be re-elected a director of the company. Mr. JAMES SimrsoN (Liverpool) seconded the motion, which was unanimously agreed to. On the motion of Mr. GEORGE HOLT, seconded by Mr. RODERICK RAYNER, Mr. T. W. Read, chartered accountant, 30, Castle-street, Liverpool, was re-appointed auditor. The CHAIRMAN: I may state, gentlemen, that I spent some hours one afternoon at Winnington with Mr. Read, and went into the accounts as thoroughly as I could. I searched them and cross-examined them as much as pos- sible in order to see that they were thoroughly correct and that nothing was charged to capital that ought to be paid out of revenue, and I may tell you that I believe that the dividend is honestly and truly earned. (Hear, hear.) Mr. COGHILL : When do you propose to call upon the remainder of the ordinary share capital. The CHAIRMAN: I believe the Ist of July is the time fixed for the last call.

Mr. MOND said there was nothing absolutely settled about it, but the probability was that the ordinary share capital would be called up on the Ist of July. It was, however, doubtful whether any further call would be made at present on the preference capital. Mr. J. I'. BRUNNER proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfield for his conduct in the chair.
Mr. G. JONES, of Liverpool, seconded the proposition, which was carried with acclamation.

The CHAIRMAN : I am very much obliged to you, gentle. men, for the vote of thanks. It has been a great pleasure to me to meet you here to-day, and to. declare such a good dividend. I hope we may never have a leas. (Hear, hear.) The meeting then terminated.

div.head: WARRINGTON PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall and T. J. Gillespie.
div.p: WARRINGTON PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall and T. J. Gillespie.

BREACHES OF THE ELE'DIENTARY EDUCATION ACT.—Jas. Hankinson, publican, Croft, was charged with neglecting to send his child to.school as required by the Elementary Edu- cation Act.—Mr. Alfred Dixon, school attendance'officer for Southworth-with-Croft, proved the case and an order was made for the child's attendance at school.—A similar charge was made against Richard Moss, farm labourer, Croft, in regard to his children, Henry James John, and Kate. The school fees were paid by the Board of Guar- dians, and Henry James (10) bad made only 40, John (8) 73, and Kate (6) 90 attendances out of a possible 116.—A fine of ss. was imposed.—Neglect under similar conditions was proved against Joseph Houghton, labourer, Croft, with regard to his children Thomas (12) and Alfred (10), and he was fined ss.—Geo. Lyon labourer, Croft, was mulettd in a similar penalty, his daughter Ellen only having attended school 69 times out of a possible 110. Edward, son of John Lynch, labourer. Croft, was proved to have been ab- sent from school 46 times, and his father was fined 53. John Rowles, teamsman, of Croft, was fined ss. for neglect- ing to send his children James, Elizabeth, and Mary.—The defendant's wife said the children had to walk almost two mites to schciol, and sometimes she could not give them anything to eat in a morning, and she kept them at home. Her husband only received 178 per week, and there were 7 to be kept out of it.—The Bench advised her to apply to the guardians for the school fees. Mr. Sut- ton. clerk to the Guardians, appeared to prosecute. Francis Beddall, of Liverpool-road, for neglecting to send his children to school, and he was fined ss. -A similar Penalty was also imposed upon the following persons, on the evidence of Mr. Hobson :—John Abby. labourer, Middleton; Phcebe Wadsworth widow, Hollins Green • George Travis, hampermaker, Hollins Green; John Tongue, Edward Lathom, Charles Harrison, and James Durnbell, all of Hollins Green.

SERIOUS CHARGE OF HIGHWAY HORBERY.—Dennis Niland, a farm labourer, at Bold, was charged with assault- ing Richard Cash, living at Sankey.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the complainant, and Mr. G. T. Moore for the defendant. —From Mr. Davies's statement it appeared the defendant and his father, also a farm labourer at Bold, left Warrington Central Station for Sankey at 9-10 on Saturday night, the 4th February. They were very drunk, and on arriving at Sankey they entered the Chapel House Inn, where they were drinking from a gallon jug until closing time. They then proceeded on their way to Bold, along Liverpool-road. Plaintiff, accompanied by a friend called Jackson, when walking towards Sankey, met the defendant, who kicked the plaintiff's terrier dog, and threatened to do the same to the plaintiff. He pulled from his pocket an open clasp knife and attempted to stab the plaintiff, who, however, had a stick in his possession ; and with this he struck the defendant a heavy blow on the hand, causing him to drop the knife. Defendant "like a frantic maniac, kicked up.a great row," and went to the house of a person named Goulding and asked for the master, saying "I will take somebody's life before morning." Nothing further was heard of the matter until the following Monday, when Cash, Jackson, and a young man called Appleton were arrested on a charge of assault and robbery. —Complainant, Jackson, and Mrs. Goulding confirmed this statement. The latter said the defendant and his father were so beastly drunk they could scarcely walk—The three young men, Richard Cash, Joseph Jackson, and Thomas Appleton, were then charged with assaulting John Niland, father of the defendant in the last case, and with stealing 9s. 61 in silver from his person.—Mr. Davies defended, and pleaded not guilty. Mr. Meore prosecuted, and said the prosecutor and his son left the Chapel House Inn, Sankey, on Saturday night, the 4th ult., at about 11 o'clock, and they had only proceeded a short distance, when the prisoners jumped through the hedge, one of whom struck him a violent blow on the head felling him to th a ground. Whilst in a stunned condition the prisoners brutally kicked him, and extracted 9s. 6.1. from his pocket. The son, seeing his father was being nearly murdered, ran to his help, but had no knife in his hand. Cash and Jackson struck him savagely on the arm with a stick. Another man named Harrison came on the scene, and they ran away.—The wit- nesses for the prosecution gave their evidence in a most unsatisfactory manner, and one named Wall, a tramp, was proved to have told an untruth.—The Bench, without hearing the defence, dismissed the charges against the prisoners, and also the one against Dennis Niland. • TRESPASS IN PURSUIT OF GAME.—Patrick Murray, chemi- cal labourer, Widnes; Patrick Kennedy, and John Smith, were charged with trespassing in pursuit of game at Cuerdley, on the 19th February.—Kennedy and Smith did not appear, and warrants were granted for their apprehen- sion.—Murray was fined 2s. Gd. and costs. A COVETED SEAT.—On a case being called in which Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the complainant, and Mr. G. T. Moore for the defendant, Mr. Moore said he had been an advocate for 30 years, and he had always occupied the seat which Mr. Davies now occupied. The only reason was be- cause he had an affection of the eyes, which was increasing, and that was the only place where he could see. When Mr. Bretherton was there, his (Mr. Moore's) brethren in the pro- fession.always allowed him the seat. He simply wished to be able to do justice to his client, and if he could not see to read be should be unable to do so. For no other reason whatever did he wish for the seat. and he asked their worshins to give him permission to occupy it. He had sent his clerk to the court before the business commenced to place a book there and occupy the seat, but he was turned from it. He would not trouble their worships were he not suffering from an affec- tion of the eye.—Mr. Greenall : It is not a question that the magistrates can decide.—Mr. Moore : No. sir.—Mr. Davies said he was put in a false and wrong position. Mr. Moore ordered him to leave the seat, as be had ordered him before when he had appeared there. It was the defendant's side, and—Dlr. Greenall interrupted, and said the Bench could have nothing to do with the matter.]—Mr. Moore: I ask my friend Mr. Davies to--Mr. Greenall : You must not put the question. If Mr. Davies accedes to the request it will be all right. —Mr. Davies: I gave way—Mr. Green- all : Let the case go on.—Mr. Moore: I cannot take the case. I ask Mr. Jackson and Mr. Buckton to take it.—Mr. Davies: Rather than you shall retire, I will give up the place —The case then proceeded; and after Mr. Moore had made his speech for the defence he transferred the case to Mr. Buckton.—Mr. Davies remarked that be never knew Mr. Moore so" thinsliinned " before.

div.head: 'IFIE LORDS' COMMITTEE ON TIIE LAND ACT,
div.p: 'IFIE LORDS' COMMITTEE ON TIIE LAND ACT,

The first meeting of the Committee appointed by House of Lords to inquire into the operation of the Land Act was held on Tuesday afternoon. The proceedings were conducted in private, and occupied little more than half an hour. Earl Cairns was appointed chairman of the Commit- tee, and all the members were present with exception of the Duke of Somerset and the Eirl of Clarendon. Although the Committee adjourned without fixing any date for the next meeting, it is understood that they assemble again next Tuesday, and will probably then call some evidence. The Committee sent a communication to the Chief Secretary and the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland inviting them to attend and give evidence. In their invitation to Mr. Forster, the Committee made an important statement with respect to the scope of their inquiry, which was obviously designed as the basis of an agreement on the issue raised between the House of Lords and House of Commons. A Cabinet Council was immediately summoned to consider the matter. The Daily News understands the conclusion arrived at by her Majesty's Ministers was that neither the form•nor substance of the communication justified them in accepting it as a settlement of the question raised by the vote of the Hous of Lords.

div.head: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.
div.p: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.

The other evening the members of the Winsford Fire Brigade had a knife-and-fork tea at the new fire engine station, to celebrate the opening of the station. Mr. John Stubbs was in the chair. Toasts appropriate to the occasion were proposed and suitably responded to.

A iw.morial having been presented to the Loc.il Govern- ment B9ard asklng for the severance of Bickerton from the Nantwicli Union, the Clerk has. been instructed to write to the Local Government Board, and say that the Guardians were of opinion that there were not sufficient grounds for entertaining the memorial.

CATTLE iIStABE 114 CHESHIRE.—Major ilarnersiey, cMet constable 'fat Cheshire, reports that during the past week there has been no case of pleurb-pneumonia in the county of Chester. There has ben a fresh out-bremk of foot-and- mouth disease, two animals having been attacked. Four beasts aff,cted with the disease have died; six have recovered, and 47 remain under treatment. 'There have been no fresh cases of swine fever.

An important case as affecting the rights of farmers to keep unlicensed dogs was heard at the Altrincham Sessions on Mondny morning. Samuel Timperley, farmer, Dunham Massey, was summoned for keeping a do.- without a license. Defendant stated that it was a sheep dog, and that he did not know a license was necessary. The magistrates' clerk said he ought to have applied for an exemption to the Ex- cise.—Defendant, who subsequently obtained an exemption, was ordered to pay the costs.

Mr. HAMMILL was about to read a copy of the auditor's report when Mr. REID, one of the auditors, said that he would prefer to read his own report, which he had in his hand, and which was the original. He thought it was stated in the Act that the auditor should read his own report. The CHAIRMAN thought they would find it different. Mr. RILEY referred to the Act and said it was clearly stated that the report be presented by the directors. The Secretary then read the auditors' report, which com- plained of the preliminary expenses incurred in floating the shares, and the cost of advertising. It further stated that Mr. Belot's services as engineer had been dispensed with, so that practically the work of laving the tramways was actually being accomplished without a clerk of the works; and be (Mr. Reid) understood that Mr. Moe was preferring a claim against the company for wrongful dismissal. He also condemned the mode of raising the capital by allowing Messrs. Philips and Co., of London, tramway contractors, to take shares in mortgage bonds (Z 17,500 a thing which was wrong, as snch a mode of raising the capital did not appear in the prospectus. He complained that the hooks were not kept in proper order. The CHAIRMAN moved and Mr. Spencely seconded the reception and adoption of the report, and this was carried. Mr. GASKIN thought it would be far better for the share- holders if the report and balance sheet had been printed, as there appeared to be some extraordinary sums paid. He moved that they be even now printed. £5,000 per mile was estimated for, but it appeared to him that the mileage had been more like £9,000, or £5O per cent. more than it ought to be.

Mr. BUSBY said he had intended to move the printing of tha reports if adopLed. In reply to the other remarks of Mr. Gaskin, he should state that the directors tried various ways to get the capital up, but failed, and they were put to great cost in consequence. But he might say that the amount per mile included the full equipment—rolling stock, horses, harness, and evecything else necessary to carry on the busi- ness. There had, moreover, been over £lOOO paid in ad- vertising. Some mention being made that the report should be printed also, _ _

Mr. Sr cur objected to that, because it was not a proper report. The auditor had taken upan himself the duty of censor to that Board; instead of contbing himself to his pro Pe'r vAttion. The directors had done their best, at least he had, and if they tirmight others cculd have done better, so far as he was concerned, he should be willing for them to do it. The report of the auditor was simply ridiculous, going into the question of the dismissal of Mr. Beloe, and going into the question that Mr. Beloe was bringing an action agiinst them for certain claims. They all desired that Mr. Beloe should be paid what was due to him, but it was a matter upon whic'r the directcrs and Mr. Beloe were not agreed, and certainly if they assented to every claim without in- quiry, the shareholders would consider the directors were not doing their duty. With respect to the cost of the line, it had clearly nothing whatever to do with the auditor. The difficulties and labour that the directors had had to contend with he could not state, and it was a piece of gross im- pertinence for Mr. Reid to attack the policy and management of the directors.

Mr. H. L. RILEY said that although he was the solicitor he had a substantial interest in the company as a shareholder. It was only in the later days of last week that the engineer altered the form of his claim. He (Mr. Riley) had not com- municated it to Mr. Reid, and he should like to know how the auditor had got to know about Mr. Belo e altering his tactie, Mr. REID said he heard that from a solicitor at Liverpool. As auditors they had a right to criticise items which were not stated with the prospectus. The prospectus said nothing about £17,000 of mortgages. Mr. SPENCELY said Mr. Reid had apparently been hearing a lot of gossip at Liverpool. Mr. DROMGOOLE and Mr. SPEIGFIT protested against the report of the auditor, the latter remarking that he could ap- peal t.o the Government Inspector, and Mr. Hart, the borough engineer, as well as the chairman of the Prescot Local Board, as to whether the line between St Helens and Prescot was not well done.

It was decided not to print the auditor's report. HARRI,SQN expressed his determination not to it as a director, as h found thatilosition and the one he occupied in the Town Council conflicting, It was decided to have three directon, co that two might form a quorum. Mr. J. Riley was re-elected, stti on the mo. tion of Mr. SPETGHT, seconded by Mr. PENNINGTON, it was resolved that 500 guineas te given to' the directors for their services during the past thine years, to be divided between them. Mr. BELOE asked if this was going to be paid out of the capital or revenue. The CHAIRMAN said he, supposed it would be paid out of the revenue. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: ST. HELENS LITERARY & SCIENTIFIC
div.p: ST. HELENS LITERARY & SCIENTIFIC
ASSOCIATION.

The Rev. J. Brown presided at the fortnightly meeting of this association on Tuesday evening, and there were about 30 members present to hear a paper by the Rev. J. P. Ritchie, on "The theory of human progress." Mr. RITCHIE, in his opening remarks, referred to the fossil remains found in dif- ferent strata of the earth's crust, showing the advancement from lower to higher forms of life. He quoted the fact that there was first the stone age, followed by the iron age, and that whilst man was at one time content to live in caves dug out of the earth, he eventually proceeded to erect for himself habi- tations of stone. Man gradually advanced until he attained the intellectual power essential to the exercise of self-control, and the establishment and maintenance of law and order in society. In-looking at these things we were confronted by a variety of curious facts. There could be no doubt that the size and splendour of the public buildings of the ancient capitals of Greece and Rome, surpassed anything that could be found in the wealthiest European cities. The lecturer went on to speak of several of these buildings, mentioning the Great Circus, Amphitheatre, the Colliseum, and the In- penal Palace on Palatine Hill, which was capable of shelter- ing an army under its walls. Speaking of the wisdom of the Egyptians, he said they were bound to admit, that in at I least something of human culture and skill, the world might possible have gone backward instead of forward. Having spoken in terms of praise of the Aneid of Virgil, the hietories of Herodotus, and the works of Xenophen, Mr. Ritchie said he had to allow that among the ancients, there were indivi- dual men of genius who were not below the level of the most distinguished men of modern times. Men of ancient times had attained a degree of excellence in works of art,literature and religion, which had never been surpassed in later ages; and whilst they could not maintain that there had been an advancement of the race in every range of culture, yet the sum total of intelligence of to-day was perhaps greater than ever it was before. The whole resources of ancient empires were then exhausted in building the chief seats of royalty, but in modern times wealth was more equally distributed amongst the different parts of the community. In ancient cities there were some beautiful palaces, but the great mass of the people continued in most abject poverty, and the out- ward show of greatness and glory was only a covering to the social degradation and corruption that prevailed within. The introduction of Christianity found the nations of the earth in a state of chronic antagonism to each other, and proclaimed its message of peace on earth and good will towards men. It lighted the darkness of the world's despair, and to it we owed all the benevolent and philanthropic in- I stitutions now flourishing amongst us, the innumerable agencies for the relief of human suffering, and the correction of human perversity. He then compared the architecture of modern times with that of the ancients, and said that he was still forced back upon the consideration that it was rather from the lack of means than the lack of ability that we were now hindered in the erection of such buildings as were seen in Rome and Greece. With regard to sculpture we had done nothing to boast of, and as to painting there could be no question that strides of advancement had been made in that branch of art. Still, for loftiness of concep- tion, gracefulness of style, and loveliness of colouring, no recent modern painting could surpass the sublime creations of some of the immortal masters of the old Italian school. Pre-eminence, however, must be given to the present age over the precedin, ages in regard to scientific knowledge, and the lecturer here instanced the printing press, the steam engine, the hydraulic press, the microscope and the tele- graph. Whatever might be said in favour of Mr. Ruskin's teaehings, therc was 139 degbt that machinery had been an important ?actor in the progress of. civilisation. In his mind there were two great underlying principles upon which human progress had proceeded; the first was the truth of proving what was true, or the inductive method of reason- ing, which was first shown to the world in Bacon's Nowt ni Ort jonu ;A. The other principle was the agreement of nun's conduct with his knowledge of the truth. This was the principle of righteousness, which was the embodiment of the truth. He then referred to the late prophecies by Mr. Proctor as to the earth coming into collision with the sun, and he gave his opinion that the world had still a great and glorious career of progress before it.—Comments were made upon the lecture by Dr. McNicell, Mr. Riley, and the chair- man. A vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, and a similar compliment was paid to the chairman.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

ENTERTAINMENT.---A humorous and dramatic recital was given at the Winsford Town Hall on Walnesday last, in con- nection with the Intellectual Company which existed actively two years ago, now all but dormantly. Mr. Inglis gave a series of the most telling pieces chiefly from the humorous writers of the Artemus Ward and Barnham class, with a few of the best from Dickens, Shirley Brooks, Shakespeare, &c. The company was not sufficiently large to pay well, but amply so to appreciate a good recitation.

OVER CRICKET CLUB—We understand this club is beginning to show fresh signs of vitality, and has at the commencement of its season secured pod flaws in the vicinity as honorary subscribers. Amongst the patrons the chief are Lord Delamere, T. Knowles, Esq., M.P., Captain Turner, J.P., J. D. Kay, Esq., J.P., Mr. John Knowles, Rev. Canon Hayhurst, Messrs. Hughes, Leigh, Hornby, &c.. The secretary, Mr. H. Greenhalgh, is expecting many to join as active members.
