div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. WEDN7SDAY.—BC for e Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, sour., (chairman) and Mr. George Pilkington. A SraEuT FIGHT.—John Hughes was convicted, on the evidence of P.C. Brydges, of having, on the 19th ult., caused a great disturbance in the street by fighting with another man. Defendant was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment in default of entering into sureties to keep the peace three months, himself in £lO and two in £5 each. WHEELING A BARROW ON THE FOOTPATH—Joseph High- land, an old man, was charged with obstructing the footpath, ii Waterloo-road by wheeling a barrow upon it.—Defendant was discharged on agreeing to pay ss. towards the costs, and promising not to offend again. SHOOTING A DRAGON PIGEON.—A middle-aged, respect- ably Oiessed man, was charged with having, on the 20thult., unlawfully killed a tame pigeon value 101, the property of Mr. Henry Baker, under circumstances which did not amount to larceny at common law. Complainant said he was a farmer at Lipton, and whilst he was in one of his fields he heard defendant firing in an adjoining field, and immediately afterwards found that a valuable dragon pigeon had been killed by him. He noticed defendant making off as fast as he could.—W. R. Horner, defendant's son, said he was with —his father on the day in question. His parent went out for the purpose of shooting linnets, and, so far as he (witness) knew, he did not kill any pigeon.—Homer, in reply to the Bench, denied having killed the bird.—The Chairman: Well, it was a very audacious thing of you to shoot your neighbour's pigeon.—Defendant: I never did so.—The Chairman: And so we shall fine you 203., the costs 103. GI, and you will have to pay 103., the value of the pigeon. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—A number of people were summoned by the Widnes School Board for not sending their children to school. Mr". G. H. Danby conducted the cases, which were proved by the attendance officers, and each of the following defendants were ordered to pay 55., including tests :—Michael Kelly, Peter Riley, Honora Cannon, Patrick McLoughlin, Stephen White, and Ellen Jones. A FOWL THIEF CAUGHT.—James Keating., labourer, was ,charged with stealing, on the previous Monday' a fowl, the property of Mrs. Maly Ann Gill, landlady of a beerhouse in Wellington-street.—The evidence was to the effect that on Sunday night, the prosecutiix,who keeps a number of fowl, saw the cock safe, but on the following morning in was missing. The same morning, Thomas Coupe, an errand boy employed by Mr. Read, chemist, Waterloo-road, was work- ing in the yard behind his master's shop, when he saw the prisoner walk into an entry near Mrs. Gill's, put the cock under his arm, and walk away with it. Shortly after the prisoner was arrested, but denied having seen the bird.—He was sentenced to one month's imprisonment with hard labour. • ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Martin Weir, who had given himself up to the police, knowing that there was a warrant out for his apprehension, was charged with assaulting Sabina Keenan, on the 23rd January last.—Complainant said the prisoner was in drink at the time he assaulted her, and she was willing to forgive him. She wished to withdraw the case, and the magistrates consented to this course being adopted on complainant paying 6s 6d costs. NEW Moon RATE.—Mr. Rigby, assistant overseer, applied to the magistrates to sanctiqn a new poor rate of 3s in the E for Widnes.—ln reply to Mr. Lewin (clerk), Mr. Rigby said that only £126 of arrears remained to be collected. Of this amount £36 Be was placed to the account of John Knight's bankruptcy, and £46 15s 8d to another local failure. The sum of £22 3s lid was owing by the London and North- -Western Railway, and its collection had stood over until their Appeal had been decided; £2O 183 5d was owing by cottage property owners. The present rate would be for eight months only.—The Bench granted the application.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. William Banks and R. M. Brooke.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. William Banks and R. M. Brooke.

DIRTY CHIMNEYS.—SeveraI-persons were summoned for permitting the chimneys of their dwelling houses to be on fire, and were each fined as follows :—Mr. William Mellor, grocer, Church-street, 6d., and 93. 6d. costs; Mr. Walter Timmins, Halton, 6d. and costs, 123. 6d.; William Harring- ton, Peel-street, 6d. and 9s. 61. costs; Mirgaret Morris, High-street, 6d., and 93. 6d. costs; and Robert Gibson, Poole-street, a similar sum and costs. A CARELESS PARENT.—Richard Seymour was sumcnonell by the Runcorn School Board for not sending his child to school.—Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer, proved the case, and defendant was ordered to pay 53. including costs. POOR RATE DEFAULTERS.—Eighty-five people were sum- moned by Mr. Sutton, assistant overseer, for non-payment of poor rates. Sixty-four of the cases were settled, and twenty-one summonses were heard, and orders made for payment. 'SAD CHARGE AGAINST A DRUNKEN BOATMAN. —Richard Taylor, a boatman, was brought up on a warrant, charged -with stealing Ll 2s. 9d., the money of his employer, Mr. William Bate, coal and salt merchant. The prisoner had been in the employ of the prosecutor for some months, his duty being to take charge of a narrow boat. On Saturday week, he was told to take a cargo to Bury. Mr. Forrester. Bate, son of the prosecutor, paid the prisoner the freight, and gave him the sum of Ll 23. 9d. with which to pay cer- tain canal dues. On the following Wednesday, Taylor went to the office and stated that instead of going away with the boat, he had been drinking, and spent the money that had been entrusted to him. He told Mr. Bate that if he would let him have a little more money, he would go away with the boat at once. On that understanding, he gave him 10s., but the fellow merely went off and spent it. A warrant was then issued against him, and he was taken into custody by Sergeant Walley.—Prisoner now ,pleaded guilty, and was sent to gaol one month. IVEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Wm. Bankes (chairman) and John Brundrit.

DISTURBING THE SALVATION ARMY.—William Peck, a young man who has for some time been living at a fast rate, and who is the son of Mr. Peck, station omnibus proprietor, was charged firstly, with having, on the let instant, been guilty of riotous and violent behaviour, in a place of wor- ship known as the Foresters' Hall, which is registered in accordance with the 18 and 19 Vic., as a place in which to hold divine service ; secondly, with assaulting P.C. J. P. Clarke in the execution of his duty; and thirdly, with damaging that officer's-coat to the amount of 10s.—Thomas Wood, lieutenant in the Salvation Army, said that on the night named, at about half-past nine, he was holding a religious service in the Foresters' Hall, when the prisoner, who was under the influence of drink, entered the building, and when the doorkeeper spoke to him, he raised his fist to strike him. He (witness) knew that it was useless to talk to the ycung fellow, as the result of previous encounters with him, so he picked him up, and carried him out of the building. This, however, did not have the desired effect, for Peck kicked the door in so savage a manner that they had to open it in order to prevent it being broken. On again entering the halt, the prisoner struck and kicked any one •evhom he could seize. For two or three weeks the young man had proved a great nuisance, and when h had met him in the street, had told him "he would do for him."—P.C. -Clarke said he was on duty near the hall when he was called in, and found Peck kicking several of the people and '-behaving in a most violent manner. The lieutenant asked lira to go out quietly, on which he gave him a blow in the face. He (witness) then forcibly put the prisoner out, but in so doing he was struck on the face and kicked several times. He had obtain the assistance of P.C. Noden in order to take the yonag man to the police station.—Robert Phillips, known as "Sailor Boy," corroborated the statement of Lieu- tenant Wood.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and said that on the afternoon of the day named on which the offence was com- mitted, he fell in with a friend who treated him with drink. He was under the influence of this when he went to the hall. He was very sorry for what he bad done, and he hoped the magistrates would deal leniently with him, as lie would behave better in the future.—Superintendent Williamson re- marked that he was not anxious to press the case against the prisoner, and, with the permission of the Bench, he would withdraw the one in which Peck was charged with damaging the policeman's coat.—The Bench consented.—The Chair- man said the prisoner bad pleaded guilty to a tery serious offence, viz., that of being guilty of violent behaviour in a place of worship. Even if he was under the influence of liquor at the time, he ought to have known better than go to the hall. He would be tined 40e. and G. 41 costs for the first offence, or, in default, one month's imprisonment, without hard labour ; and for the assault on the officer he would be sentenced to one month's imprisonment without the option of a tine.—Superintendent Williamson observed that for some time he had noticed a number of young men, se:erne of whom he saw in the court that morning, doing all they could to annoy the people in the Salvation Army proces- sions, by brawling, shouting, and attempting to sing, if he could dignify the noises they made by snch a term. He wished these young men to understand that if they con- tinued such a course of conduct, they would be summoned. He thought that a fit opportunity to give them a warning that their disorderly behaviour in the public streets would n ,t be tolerated any longer. A FOUL-TONGUED WOMAN.—Matilda Shaw was brought up under a warrant for not appearing to a summone on te 13th ult. charging her with haying used threats to Sarah Lowe, on the 1101 January.—Evidence was given by Lowe and three witnesses to the effect that the prisoner formerly lodged with her about six months, and on the dae- in ques- tion met her in Bridge-street, made use of very bad language and threats, and also charged her with having ueen guilty of misconduct with a certain man belornei ng to one of Messrs. Kenworthy's fiats, in consequeece of which she had not had much peace at home since.—Prisoner denied the truthful- nes; of Lowe's statement, and added that on the 11th Jan. nary she merely asked complainant for some things which she had left at her house. She also called her husband, who corroborated this statement.—The Bench ordered the prisoner to find one surety in £lO to keep the peace for six months, and pay 245. 6.1. costs, or in detault, be sent to gaol one month. A YOUTH TIRED OF WORKHOUSE LlFE.—Thomas James Lloyll, a youth who said he was 18 years of age, but looked several years younger, was charged with running away from Dutton Workhouse on the 28th ult., and taking with him a suit of clothes belonging to the Gaardiians.—Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, enquired of Loyd how he knew his exact age, to which he replied that he was born in 18e4. In answer to a further question as to what data be bad for saying this, the prisoner said "he had thought on, which caused much amusement in court.—Mr. Jone.s. svoris- house master, said the prisoner first came to the workhouse with his own mother, some years ago. He wns afterwards taken out, and, for some reason or other, was committed to an industrial school at Chester, where he remained SOMG years. He was next dismissed from the school, and again taken to the workhouse, where he had been up to within a

few days. Several times recently he had had to complain of the prisoner's misconduct, and a few days ago he was sent ' to the post office with some letters, and given fourpence to buy stamp, which money he spent. On the 28th ult. he left the house in the suit of clothes belonging to the Guar- dians.—The Chairman extracted a promise from the youth that he would behave better in future, and return to the workhouse, on which he was discharged.

RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. OPENING OF NEW PREMISES. On Monday, the members of the Young Men's Christian Association entered upon their new premises, in the com- modious rooms belonging to the Coffee and Cocoa Rooms' Co., and the event was celebrated by the holding of a free tea, the cost of which was defrayed by several gentlemen. Nearly one hundred members were present at the repast, which was creditably got up by Mr. William Moore, the manager to the company. After tea a public meeting was held. Dr. Steele, the president, occupied the chair, and there were also present the Revs. Canon Barclay Wm. Preston, and Messrs. John Simpson, Thomas Norman, S. C. Becket, and B. Kniveton (secretary.) The proceedings having been opened by prayer by the Rev. W. Preston, The CHAIRMAN, who was very well received, congratu- lated the members of the association upon having obtained possession of the rooms. He remarked that he was pleased to hear that their financial prospect was new very hopeful. From the facts which had been supplied to him by the secretary, he felt that there was a prosperous future before the association, and it was quite likely that before long they would be able to carry on without the aid of outside subscriptions. At the close of last year they had only 64 Members, in addition to being burdened with a deficit of £49 6s. 7d.. whilst they had now 115 n-embers—(applause) —and a balance in hand. The amount of their yearly sub- scriptions was £46. The present rental, which include gas, firing, and lighting, was £32 per year. The cost of news- papers and periodicals would be about £l2, and say for sundries about £lO, which would make their expenditure about £54. This left about £8 to be provided, which sum, he thought, would be easy to obtain. He need hardly re- mind them that the association had been kept alive, year after year, by the generosity of Mr. Robert Shaw—(ap- plause); but now the teaccess of it depended upon the individual exertions of its members. He hoped that the necessary energy would not be lackins, on the part of each of them. (Hear, hear, and applause.)' The Rev. CANON BARCLAY delivered an address of con- siderable length. He thought it would be a great shame and disgrace to a rising. community like Runcorn, if an in- stitution like that could not be supported. He contended that ought and must be a place in the town where where young men—and for that matter middle-aged men— might periodically meet together. It might be said that clubs of that kind were a great enemy to domestic peace, and that wives and daughters did not like them. He did not believe very much in the truth of such allegation, be- cause if men were inclined to leave their homes, they would find some place to go there, even if there was no such asso- ciation as that in existence. The question arose whether it was not better they should meet there, where there was no inducement to partake of intoxicating liquors, rather than at a public-house. He was not condemning public•houses in the abstract. He had never done so, for he had always found that those who conducted them were honourable and gocd members of society. At the same time, though there was ne sn in going to a public-house, there was a great deal of danger; and he thought they ought to do what they could to avoid temptation, and keep their fellow creatures out of it, especially in Runcorn, where, in his ministerial capacity, he was constantly seeing ems of illness which had been brought on by a too great indulgence in intoxi- cants. Many of the cases to which he referred might be described as alcoholic poisoning. The best way to remove such an evil was to put a counter attraction in its place. He contended that man was a social animal, and that however comfortable his home might be, there were times when he, very naturally, wished to meet with his social compeers. They were just at that moment in a political crisis, and he thought it was quite as natural that people like them should meet together and discuss these matters, even as gentlemen did at their clubs. He was very glad that the society had been able to keep on its legs, and that it had a better pros- pect of usefulness before it. It was important it should do so, if only for the purpose of carrying on the mental im- provement- of the young. Education WAS advancing very rapidly in the present day, and now-a-days children at 13 years of age left school with very much more knowledge on any given subject than they did when some of those present were juveniles. What, however, was the good of laying this foundation of knowledge unless there was some means of carrying it on. The acquisition of knowledge gave a thirst for information, and if they did not provide proper and wholesome literature for the new generation, they were ' sure to find something which was bad. The other day he was required to make a return in reference to what was termed "the social evil" in the town, and one of the ques- tions he had to answer was, "Is there much improper litera- ture circulated ?'' He consulted the Superintendent of Police, who said he was not aware that there was. He did not hesitate to say that the moral condition of Runcorn was very much improved during the last few years, as was proved by the number of cases brought up at the police court on Mondays, especially when they considered that this was a seaport population. He attributed this partly to the spread of education. There was only one similar institution to that in the town, as far as he knew, and that was the Working Men's Club, which was a class affair, and, therefore, did not supply the want which was felt. What they really required was a place where the high and the low could meet together on common ground; wherein, if a gentleman desired, he could come and play a game of chess with his foreman or workman. Any- thing which would tend to do away with that clan distinc- tion which prevailed in this country would be a great bene- fit. Political alarmists told them that the danger which threatened England arose from the fact that the rich formed one class, and those who were lower down in the scale another class, and there was a mutual antagonism between the two. Surely it was well that such meetings between the two classes should take place, as the rich man then saw that his poorer workman might be as much a gentleman as he was, because it was not the "guinea stamp" which made the gentleman, but gentlemanly feelings. There was many a rich man who was a great snob, and many a poor man clad in fustian who was quite worthy of the name of gentleman. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The bringing together of different classes would conduce to mutual respect, as the man in the lower rank of the social scale who had not so many advantages, either of time, money, or opportunity, would be led to see that his richer brother, whom he was inclined to envy, was not such a bad fellow after all. All the great improvements of the present generation had come from the upper classes of society. Who was it that emanci- pated the slaves? Was it not William Wilberforce, the member for the grand Yorkshire constituency? Who was it that emancipated the factory workers from their thraldom of immense labour? Was it not Lord Shaftesbury, who was then Lord Ashley? Let them even take the Reform Bill of 1832, which was the first extension of the constitution, was it not brought forward by a nobleman who was almost sob- bing when he submitted it to the House, at the thought of the enormous change he was bringing about? He was also glad to see that the association carried on work for the im- provement of the spiritual condition of young men. He did not think that those who took an interest in such an institu- tion as that should be called upon to put their hands into their pockets, as their late president had done. He saw from the report that but for the kindness of Mr. Robert Shaw the body would have come to grief. (Applause.) The speaker hoped that if the members found themselves in difficulty at the end of the financial year they would not object to give an extra contribution in order to relieve it. Mr. S. C. BeeKETT, the treasurer, said the total amount of bills which the Association had to meet was £35 15s. 2d., the amotiat of cash in hand was £l6 125., and towards this they had subscriptions amounting to £4663., including the following :—Mr. Wigg, £4 45.; Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst, £4 45.; Mr. Shaw £lO, and honorary subscription £4 45., and ordinary members' subscriptions £2. This would leave a balance of £7 10s. 10d. at the end of June. It was esti- mated that they would receive £5 from members' subscrip- tions; and there would be £8 to pay for rent, and £2 for papers; so that at the end of June it was supposed they would have a small balance in band. Mr. Joule SIMPSON congratulated the Association upon having secured Dr. Steele as president, as he thought this would show the people of the town that the Association was not sectarian in its character. He referred, in an humorous manner, to the various reports which had been in circulation in the way of predictions of the speedy death of the Associa- tion, fellowing upon the decease of the Literary and Mechanics' Institute; and concluded with a graphic pictnre of the great improvements which bad taken place in regard to the newspaper and periodical press since he was a lad. On the motion of Mr. SnortE, seconded by Mr. J. D. JONES, the vacancies on the committee were supplied, after which the procetelings terminated. he I see

div.head: PENKETIT.
div.p: PENKETIT.

In connection with the Penketh Band of Hope, a very successful service of song, entitled "Her Benny," was given in the Elementary Schoolroom, on Thursday evening, by the choir of the Wesleyan chapel, Sankey Bridges, to a crowded and ovetflowidg audience. The connected readings were given by Mrs. R. Garnett, Brookside, in a very effec- tive manner, and was highly appreciated by the audience. Mr. George presided at the harmonium. A vote of thanks le to thOse who had taken part in the entertainment was heartily proposed by Mr. R. Garnett, Brookside, Penketh, and ably seconded by Mr. Dodd, Hale Nook, and carried with acclamation. The meeting concluded by the choir singing the hymn, "God moves in a mysterious world." This was one .of the best entertainmtnts which have been held in the schoolroom for a long period; and the frequent applause testifld to it being much appreciated.

INQUEST AT ST. HELENS ON A COLLIER. —An inquest Ws held on Saturday, at the Talbot Hotel, in Duke-street, before Mr. Barker, on the body of Peter Harrison, 27 years of age, who lived with his mother at 43 York-street. Da- ce ised was employed at the Ravenhead collieries, and on the 11th January he pulled a rope to signal to the top, when a prop fell and knoesed him down. He complained of a pain in his aide by falling on a stone, but worked all night. After- wards he did not return to work.—Evidence was given to the effect that deceased was not strong, and that the accident, Which would not have proved fatal to one in better health, might have accelerated his death. A verdict was returned accordingly.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 4, 1-882. RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 4, 1-882. RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.

The half-yearly meeting of this company was held on Monday, at the offices, the Public Hall, Runcoru. Mr. John Brundrit (chairman of directors) presided, and there were also present Messrs. William Hayes, Thomas Bankes, John Simpson, William Whittaker (directors), Thomas Norman, James Shaw, James Collier, Peter Smith, John Ashton (solicitor), and W. F. &likeld (secretary). The report, which was taken as read, stated The revenue account shows a balance of £620 13s 11d. includ- ing the amount brought forward from the previous half-year, out of which the directors recommend a dividend to be paid of 4 per cent, per annum, free of inc ,me tax, payable on and after the let day of March. This will absorb £463 3s, leaving a balance of £157 103 lid to be carried forward The directors I wish to inform the shareholders that they have been able to obtain all the money required during the past year at 4} per cent. (according to the res)luin passed at the meeting held on the 28th day of February. 1881), which has reduced the Interest paid on lcans from £667 Os 2d in June to £630 153 in December. The directors regret that the depression still con- tinues in one of the great staple industries of the town. and only a very limited quantity of water has been wanted at these manufactories recently. There has been, however, a much greater demand for water to shops and houses in the neizh- bourho -d of Bridge-street, owing to the water from the Foun- tain belonging to the town and near to the public offices becom- ing so impure that the authorities have published a caution to the inhabitants not to use it for domestic purposes. Our revenue will thereby be considerably increased. An extension of the mains will be required to Leinster-street, Duke's Field, to supply houses recently built there (and constantly added to), and the oacupiers have no other source of supply for edible use than that which can be obtained from this company. The directors have the satisfaction of stating that the water in the well continues pure and abundant, that all the plant stands good and firm, and the boilers and machinery are In excellent working order. The report of the auditors (Messrs. R. Toft and Ralph Forrester) was next read. . The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the report and balance sheet, and remarked that he had great pleasure in meeting the shareholders, and seeing laid before them a report which allowed the directors to recommend a little larger dividend than was the case last half-year, when it was only 21- per cent., as against 4 this six months They would observe from the report that the receipts for water had not been so large as during previous half-years, but this was to be attributed to the fact that lesser quanti- ties had been required at the works, but there was now a somewhat brighter prospect in this respect. The statement of accounts showed that whereas in the quarter ending Sept. they only received £t345 10s. 44. for water, in that ending December 31st the sum thus received was .£386 03. 7d. It was also encouraging that the receipts for fittings during the last six months had been much larger. In the last half- year but one there had beenl£9s, and in the past six months £135, which showed that a considerable number of houses which had not been supplied with water in the past were now having one. Since the accounts had been published the public fountain near the Town Hall had been closed, and this has proved a source of increased revenue, as many householders who had in the past obtained water from the fountain had been reluctantly, compelled to apply to the company for it. Thus the truth of the old adage was proved—" It is an ill wind that blows nobody any good." I Before sitting down he wished to draw the attention of the directors to the operations of the Mersey Brine and Salt Co. It appeared that they were constructing a reservoir in a field adjoining Runcorn Heath, and in close proximity to the well belonging to the Waterworks Company. A line of pipes was also being laid across the heath within a distance Of between 900 and 1000 yards of the well. A tunnel was likewise being driven through the sandstone rock to enable the Brine Company to carry their pipes on to Weston Point. The progress of these works would need careful watching, for if the pipes were not properly made, or if there happened to be any leakage through the porous sandstone, from the pipes in the tunnel, or from the reservoir into the well, there was no telling what would be the effect upon the water sup- ply of the inhabitants of Runcorn. The directors, thinking it very desirable that something should be done to prevent any such possible interference, wrote to the Mersey Salt and Brine Company in London, who very courteous- ly sent down plans and specifications tin- bracing all the proposed works from the reser- voir to Weston Point. These they intended to for- ward to their own engineer, leaving it to him to adopt such measures as would be sufficient to protect the interests of the shareholders. They were not taking these steps with the object of opposing, in any sense, the brine scheme, but simply for self-protection. He might mention that he had heard it stated that the directors of the Waterworke' Com- pany were proceeding in an acrimonious spirit, but there was not the slightest foundation for such a statement. No doubt their shareholders would naturally be very indignant if they found that the directors did not look after their interests in every possible way. Mr. T. BANKES seconded the resolution, which was passed. Mr. Taos. NORMAN moved a vote thanks to the directors for the ability they had brought to bear on the work of the company in the past. They had had to grapple with many difficulties, but from the inception of the company to the present time they had never wearied in their work. The prospect certainly did seem brighter, and as the town in- creased in size and population he had hopes that the com- pany would yet be a great success. The resolution was seconded by Mr. JaarPs SHAW, and carried. The CHAIRMAN, in responding, assured the meeting that the directors, as they had always done, would in future endeavour to do all they could for the good of the company. He might mention, though it was outside the business of that meeting, that since the fountain had been closed they had put water into 102 houses and stables. That was not entered in the present half year's accounts, but it was very satisfactory to know that there had been such an increase. Mr. NORMAN also moved that a resolution of thanks be accorded to the secretary. In doing so he eulogised Mr. Sal keld's efforts to promote the success of the company. Mr. Jas. COLLIER seconded the motion, which was sup- supported by the Cam mare, who said that no one knew the value of Mr. Salkeld more thars the directors, who in busi- ness contact with him found his services to be inestimable. Mr. SALKELD briefly replied, assuring the meeting that it would always be his chief aim to promote the prosperity of the company. The proceedings then terminated.

Clare, jun., lOs ; and Mrs. Chadwick (Greenway Vaults), 10s. The total sum raised was. £353 lie. Gd., besides which contributions of mapdttrikiheen,promised from Mr. Thos!Norman atd other friqudS. The cast of the land, which was • freehold, would be 4111, and the contract for the building of the house was £,3tY which With/d .net,'"howt3ver;e Include, a boundary twall and other matters. The member S-of the church and-Congre- gation were very thankful to all that had helped them in this good work. The Rev. H. W. PRICE remarked that they seemed to be setting about the matter in hand, in right good earnest. Let them never forget that in all their church work, that the real strength would Oe found in frequent appeals at the throne of God. It did not follow that because they had got a good minister, and a good building and schools, or that because they had a few strong and loyal-hearted min and women associated with the society, that God would bless the church, for sometimes all these thiugs were gathered together, and yet the efforts put forth were not crowned with the success they reasonably anticipated. Very often this was the case, bee muse those engaged in the work were tempted to rely upon their own efforts, whereas the spiritual blessing could only come as the direct action of the Holy Spirit. They were, at times, led to say, "We have got the net, and we can catch the fish," whereas it was not until they heard the Heavenly voice, saying " Let doe n the net" that they could hope to (cure any impot tint spiritual results. In conclusion, he urged them to be frequent in the use of the battle-axe of all prayer. The Rey. H. SIMSON (Toxteth Liverpool), was glad to see the spirit of activity and loyally to Christ which seemed to pervade them as a church. He was also pleased to know that they were busily engaged in providing a manse for their minister, for in some of the small places where Con- grevational churches whre in existence, it was sometimes difficult for the pastor to find an appropriate home. Let them be sure they put the study on the sunny side of the building, and that it was a large, well-lighted, and airy room--such a room, in fact, as would tered to influence the composition of Mr. Thomas's sermons. (Hear. hear, and a Voice: We have done so.) Let them never forget that a minister was very much influenced by the surroundings in his study. They must not be sparing in connection with so geo4 a work remembering that they were labouring for genera- tions to come, and for the ministers who would probahty have charge of the church in far off years. He also heartily howd that their united action on this question would to rewarded by a great spiritual 'blessing. At the present day, they heard many complaints about their prayer meetings being plorly attended, and he was afraid that this fact arose owing to their not always meeting in the name of Christ. Certainly they met in the name of custom, in the name of duty; but if they looked to it that they gathered together in the name of Him whose name was above every name, . _

they would have meetings which would attract those who were fond of prayer, which "linked the world with golden chains about the throne of God." He would sooner have a dozen men who were united with him in supplication at a prayer meeting, than a thousand who merely attended as a matter of custom. The battle was not won merely by one or two great guns, but by the rank and file; and just in proportion as they were loyal to Christ in connection with that church, would they be blessed. Above all things, let every one amongst them find something to do, for without Christian activity they could not grow. They might hear the best sermons, but until they began to work for Christ they would know comparatively little of the blessedness of true religion. Let them not forget that it was the man who put his talent in a napkin and buried it in the earth, who had such dis- torted views of God, calling him, parabolically, a hard master, and an austere man. Another thing they must do was to cheer each other in the work. In conclusion, the speaker whilst advising the members of the church and con- gregation to criticis3 the sermons of the pastor, urged them to be exceedingly careful not to indulge in personal criticism before titeir children, which pract.ce, he believel, had in many places led to most sad results in the case of young men, who would, under other influences, have been led to re- gard their ministers with that respect which their sacred calling demanded. The Rev. THOMAS COLE urged those present to See to it thai they did not attend divine service merely to receive I spiritual food, but to be actual as well as receptive, letting thought develop itself into action. In other words, he would say to them, with the apostle, "Be ye doers of the Word, and not hearers only." On the motion of Mr. BECK, seconded by Mr. SS iLLIAer HANDLEY, and supported by the CHAIRMAN, a vote of thanks was given to the ladies, the speakers, and the decorators. During the evening, the choir sang several anthems, which were given with commendable effect. We may add that the following are the names of ladies who had the management of the sale of work and tea : Mesdames J. D. Thomas, W. Handley, F. Fairhurst, Chad- wick, Hazlehurst, Rutter, Mcßryde, Dobson, Corf, 'l'. Hand- ley, Lacey, and Misses Williams, Lydiate, Littler, Chadwick, Hardley, Edwards, and Morris. Those who assisted the ladies in the decorations, which were of a very chaste des- cription, were Messrs. W. H. Chadwick, T. E. 'Canna, W. Handley, F. Fairhurst, G. Rutter, Hazlehurst, W. Dobson, W. Gowanloch, A. Stanway, W. Cringle, J. Streets, T. Lunt, J. Corf, P. Ainswor th, S. Watson, G. J. Percival, and W. Roach. The total amount realised by the sale was £33.
BEWSEY DISTRICT BAND OF HOPEI

The annual tea party in conncction with this temperance mission was held in the Workmen's Club Hall, Warrington, _on Tuesday evening. Tea was partaken of by 200 persons, and thelablea were presided over by the following ladies:— Nl'. Dodds, Mrs. D. Garnett, Miss Naylor, Mrs. J. Naylor, ,Mrs. and Miss H6rton, Mrs. Jenkins, Miss Plinston, Mrs. Gaest, Mrs. Bonnell, Mrs. Price, Mrs. Bea- man, and Mrs. Goulden. Subsequently a suc- cessful meeting and entertainment was held under the pre- sidency of Mr. Charles Parker, of Penketh. He was eup- ported by Messrs. John Paton, of the Irish Temperance 'League, R. A. Naylor, Robert Garnett, and C. Plinston. The following programme was creditably gone through in the course of the evening :—Glee, "Lightly tread," by the Choir; song, "Far away yet ever near," Miss Daniels ; duet, harp and piano, Miss Hettie and Miss Florrie Toft ; song, "Angels ever bright and fair," Miss Bonnell ; duet, "The land without a storm," Miss Waterfield and Miss Hedgcock ; harp solo, Miss Hettie Toft; glee, " Pic-nic," Choir; recitation, "The little mother," by Miss Whalley ; duet, " Shells of the ocean," Miss Bonnell and Miss Water- field. The entertainment concluded with a harp solo by Miss Hettie Toft, whose performances had been greatly enjoyed. For one so young she showed great skill in the manipulation of her instrument. Miss Turley efficiently accompanied the vocalists on the piano. The CHAIRMAN observed that he occupied that post that night in ccnsequence of the position of 'lris mother, who had, in the face of much opposition from friends and relatives whose opinions she much esteemed, obeyed the call of duty in regard to the temperance question, and on more than one occasion had addressed a meeting at Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He was glad the sacrifice she had made was acknow- ledged in this way. After a few remarks upon the staleness of the different phases of the Temperance question, there was, he concluded, one thing new about it, viz., that the victims perishing through intemperance were ever new ones. The old drunkards died and entered the dark unseen, and their places were being filled from our sisters and brothers and children; and this fact ought to warn them to join themselves together in bands of hope and love and faith round the little ones, so that they might be guarded from following so many who had gone to the "drunkard's here- after."

Mr. PLINSTON read the following report : In presenting their report before the attention of the public the committee desire very earnestly to express their gratitude that they have been enabled, through the blessing of Almighty God, to do some little in ineaticating the principles of total ab- stinence in the minds of the children entrusted to their care. During the twelve months that this society has been estab- lished we have taken 320 pledges, and enrolled 240 members. The average attendance at the weekly meetings has been from 150 to 180. Unlike many kisdred societies these meetings have been continued all though the year, the committee feeling that it has a very deteriorating effect to make a pause in the work during the summer months. We have been amply re- paid by the large number of children who regularly attended these summer meetings, which were thoroughly appreciated, and we trust, made not only attractive, but useful and beneficial. Through the kind liberality of James Dodds, Esq., the mem- bers to the number of 220 spent a most enjoyable and happy afternoon, and partook of tea, on the Ist Monday in August, in a field kindly lent by Mr. Kershaw, of Sankey. The entertain- ments and meetings, nine of which have been held, have, on the whole, been successful, and encouraged us to still continue them. The thanks of the committee are due to Mr. Windsor, whom, we regret to say, has removed to another town, for the very able manner in which he trained so large a number el children to render, in such an efficient manner, a service of song, "The desire of all nations," which was thoroughly ap- preciated by a large audience. The time when such principles, as are advocated by this society, were unusual and laugi,e 1 at as being foolish, has passed, and it has been proved by the actual experience of many thousands of young people, that when they are brought up in the practice of total abstinence, they are, in a great measure, secured against the temptations that beset those who partake even moderately of intoxicating drinks. There are surely no parents who do not sometimes reflect uporr t e temptations with which their boys and girls will soon have to contend. The appetite for strong drink completely leads astray those who are weak and unfortunate enough to be under its control. Our reformato ies, workhouses, and prisons are led, not with teetotalers, but, in nearly every instance, with those who, from want of early training, have given way to the temptations connected with strong oxink. No one becomes a criminal suddenly and at one bind, and it is also certa n that no man or woman tccomes a drunkard without having firbt been a moderate drinker. Drink sways bis 'cepire almost over the entire race, and fi'ls this fair land with its terrible influence. Like stars In the blackness of a stormy night tteae es stand serene and radiant, the hope of the rising genera- tion. This sociely is, however humbly, trying to help on this great temperance reformation. It is our aim to get firm hold on the mines of the children before their habits are formed and their taste vitiated; and to train them so that they may never become drinkers of intoxicants. This surely is a right aim, and the committee of the society feel that they can eon- fidently ask you to entrust your children to their care. They ask you to give your prayerful sympathy, and active sapport ,and encouragement to the work, b-lieving that neither parents nor children will have reason to regret, but rather to rejoice, that they have given their adhesion to the Band of Hope, Mr. J. PATON addressed some encouraging remarks to those who had taken the pledge of total abstinence, observ- ing that a pledge that was not kept after being taken was a moral curse, and just in proportion as they adhered to it were they blessed. He had kept the pledge for 23 years, and his physical health was unabated, and his mental vigour was in harmony with his physical health. (Hear, hear.) Father Matthers in his day had pledged thousands, perhaps millions of Irishmen. When he commenced his work, the people of Ireland were drinking eleven million gallons of whiskey every year, but he succeeded so com- pletely that the consumption of the Spirit fell down to six millions. It would thus seem that half the people of Ire- land had taken the pledge; but Ireland to-day, notwith- standing her poverty, was spending 13 millions of money on drink, and only 11 millions in rent for her land. What an amount of pledge breaking there must be in Ireland! He had lately had a map of the drink cursed districts of Liver- pool, and he found that in those districts the death rate was fifty or sixty per thousand, and in those not so cursed only ten in the thousand. (Hear, hear.) It was a well established fact that the faithful keeper of the pledge, lived longer and better than the drunkard, and to a working mu, health meant domestic happiness in far higher degree than it did to the rich man. It was Isis duty to keep his health for his offspring, who had a greater in- terest in that than anythinz else. If they took the pledge to be rich they would be disappointed; it only promised sobriety. Suppose a man with 255. per week, which might be placed as the a-rerage wages of a workingman, with a wife and six children, taking the pledge to grow rich. (Laughter.) He would be cheated; and if he did grow rich he ought to be thrashed. (Laughter.) Mr. Paton called attention to the great increase of wife beating, and said he concurred in the opinion expressed by so many editors of newspapers, that the husband who beat his wife, should have the lash. In conclusion, he explained the objects of the Ijrnted King- dom Alliance. The proceedings terminated with the usual votes of thanks. On Wednesday evening, 250 children connected with the band of hope, partook of a good tea in the samettrilding, and afterwards spent an enjoyable evening in varioua amuse- ments.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL TEA PARTY AT
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL TEA PARTY AT
RUNCORN.

en Tuesday afternoon, a sale of work was opened at Bethes la Corgregational Chapel, on behalf of the fund for erecting a pastor's manse. The sale was not of a pretentious character, but the friends considered that the day being that upon which the annual Congregational tea party took place, It would be a good oPportun ty of raising a small sum to- wards the good object which is at present engaging the attention of the Church, which, weave pleased to notice, ap- pears to be working with much harmony under the gentle- man who fills the pulpit. Many prediction& of a doleful character were indulged in when Mr. Thomas came to Runcorn, under chcumstances of a somewhat depressing character, but these have all been falsified. The ladies who had charge of the stalls were Misses Williams, M. H. Chad- wick, Handley, Lydiate, Edwards, Littler, and Morris. During the afternoon the annual tea meeting was held in the same room, and proved very successful. The Rev. J. D. Thomas presided, and there were also pre- sent :—The Rev. '.F. Peters. Widnes; F. Carter, lforthwich F. Simon, Liverpool; H. W. Price, Chester; H. E. Lewis, ; Buckley; and Thomas Cole, Garstoa. The CHAIRMAN said he did not intend to detain them that evening by any observations, further than saying he was very glad to see so good an attendance, and to state that he took that opportunity of thanking the friends from the different congregations in the town for their patronage. The Rev. H. E. LEWIS remarked that he, came there to show his interest in the work which Mr. Thomas, who was his predecessor at Buckley, was doing in Runcorn. They would no doubt be glad to hear that the people at Buckley were still considerably interested in their old pastor's wel- fare. He urged them to persevere in the good work of pro- viding their poster with a manse. Perseverance had helped many a church to ccntinue until they obtained the guerdon of success. They were no doubt aware that there was a class of people who could never be anything bat obstruc- tions. They found this to be the case in Parliament ; and it was quite as necessary that they should have some change in this course of procedure on the part of some connected with their churches, as it was in the Commons, if they were to carry on their labours with unanimity and success. He hoped there was no obstructionist in connection with Bethesda, but that they were all working together for the advancement of the cause of Christ. A certain minister when he took charge of a particular society found a deacon, who one night waited upon him and said, "I cannot do much, for I have very few talents, and what I possess, don't shine. The only thing I can do is to put a stone to the wheel as it is going up the hill." " FrienA," said the minister, "do you put the stone before or behind the wheel 2" (Laughter). Let it b 3 their en- deavour as members of the church at Bethesda, to put the stone behind the wheel. Mr. FAIRHURST said he should like to give the audience some idea of what had been done in regard to providing Mr. Thomas, the pastor, with a house. He might state that the movement arose with their good friends the ladies. When Mr. Thomas accepted their invitation to be their pastor, it was considered that it would be well to put things in order before he took the position. There were several things which required to be done, in the way of renovating, painting, and so forth ; and the ladies decided that the best thing they could do would be to get up a sale of work, and put the proceeds on one side for the purpose. When they made their preparations for the sale which was afterwards held, they they aimed at getting £l5O, but they were pleasantly sur- prised by obtaining £133 odd above that sum. (Ap ;louse). It was then decided to provide a manse for the new minister, and he (the speaker) received a sum from the Ladies' Sew- ing Society, which raised the total receipts from the sale to £l4O. This money was put on one side for this specific purpose, and in 1380 they got up an entertainment called "The Flower Queen," the profit upon which proved to be £35, and this was put to the fund, towards which the following had been received : the Rev. J. W. Thomas. £5; Mr. J. Bell (Garston), £5 55.; Mr. R. Shenhard, £5: Mr. John Williams, £5; Mr. William Handley, £5; Mr. J. J. Speakman, £5; Mr. James Wilson. ▪ ; Mr. Joseph Littler, £5; Mr. John Wilson, £5; Mr. Peter Ainsworth, £5 ; Mr. R. div.head: " GLADSTONE'S GAGGING BILL."
div.p: " GLADSTONE'S GAGGING BILL."

LECTURE AT WARRINGTON. In the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening. Mr. Robert Webster gave a lecture on the new rules of procedure in the House of Commons, but neither the popularity of the lecturer nor the satirical title of the lecture, " Gladstone's Gagging Bill," succeeded in drawing a large audience, and the Workmen's Club, where the lecture was first announced to be delivered, would haye afforded ample accommodation for those who attended. Mr. A. Mackie occupied the chair, and his frequent references, in the course of his address. to Mr. Gladstone, called forth loud cheers, which were repeated on his allusions to Mr. Bright and Mr. P. Rylands. He remarked that the attempt to "gag" the House of Com- mons at the present time was singularly unfortunate, and was altogether unnecessary. The House of Commons should be asked, before it passed a "gagging bill," to pass an "Example Bill "—a bill to give short pithy speeches, and of keeping to the point. He hoped they would express their deepest regret that Mr. Gladstone should have found it necessary to introduce a bill to gag the powers of speech in the British House of Commons; and they would be asked to express their opinion whether or not they should ask Mr. Gladstone to endeavour by some means to 'put an end to that proceeding, and not to let it go down to poste, ity that he, in his vigorous old age, the very heighth of his fame, had his unsulliedenatne associated with that which they must all deplore. The LECTURER, who was suffering from hoarseness, ex- plained that in speaking in defence of the right of speech, he had lost the power of speech himself. The British House of Commons, he said, had a glorious history, and had existed for hundreds of years. It was the pattern of assemblies of this description, and many times had liberties been defended be' minorities. But they were told to look at foreign coun- tries and see the great advantage of the cl6,ture. Let them examine how it worked Thcy had it in France, where they had had more revolutions than in any country in the world. They had it in Germany and Prussia, and did not they know that Prussia was probably the most arbitrarily ruled power in the world ? They were told they lead the clOture in America, but he had heard Americans say that had they not had the clOture in America they might hake had no civil war. This question of the cloture did not appear to him to be a question to put down obstruction in the House of Com- mons, but one to silence the Opposition. The Government wanted to have their say, and their say alone, and that the minority should not equally have a right to express their opinion. Sir Erskine May, on being askedin 1881, whether the present system of non-compulsion could be maintained by arrangements for getting through the business of the House mole easily, answered "It is my opinion that by judicious regulation it will be quite possible to go through the business without any interference with the rights of members." The House of Commons was a place of free debate, and as long as that was the case we must be content to pay to some extent for this freedom. Nobody denied that they must have some overhaul of the present system of procedure in Parliament. (Hear, hear.) The bitte Government put down obstruction against the intli- vidual, but they did not silence the rights of the minority. He thought those were the right lineseo go upon. If a man obstructed they should silence him,, and not silence the rights of the minority for his obstr. ction. Li the rule the late Government passed were not stringent enough they could easily make them more strong. Examining the pro - nosed rules, the lecturer said the first resolution which the -Conservatives strongly opposedattacked freedom of debate, the others simply attacked the opportunities for debate. If .they excluded the first and paseed the remainder the House of Commons would be able to conduct its business without any necessity for the gagging process which the first rule brought in. There were several rults with which he to a great extent agreed—that in regard to divisions, and the standing committee on matters pertaining to law, courts of justice, and trade. The great danger of the clOttrie ap- peared to be that they made the majority too powerful, but the Liberals must be aware that when the Conservatives 'became the majority again they might feel the rod on their . own hicks. If they gave absolute power to the majority they lost that responsibility now felt by the minority for the bills that passed through Parliament. They would find their voices closed, and they would say, "It is no business of ours," and they would go to the country and speak in regard to these measures out of deors. He then described the Government as a Government of surp!isee, anel went on to speak of the Irish Land Act, the conduct of the House of Lords, and local taxation, and remarked they had one principle left and that was the freedom of speech, which he trusted they would not lightly give up that freedom. He dared say at the present moment there might be no danger in allowing the cltitro.e to be passed.. They had an excellent Speaker, and he did not think Mr. Gladatone's majority would allow him arbitrarily to use the cloture. But could they alweys say it would be the same in the future? He therefore asked if the following would meet their views:— " That this public meeting whilst fully admitting the necessity for some change in the existing rules of procedure in the House of Commons, considers the proposed rule to close debate by the decision of the majority would prove dangerous to rights of freedom of speech in the House of Commons, and to the constitutional duty of the minority to guard against excessive public expenditure." (Applause.) '[he resolution, however, did not find a proposer, and a ! workingman, who made his way to the platform with the Object of moving an amendment, was thus prevented from doing so. ' The meeting terminated with the Chairtlian expressin the tbanki of the mooting to the lecturer.

div.head: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
INTERESTING PATER BY ALDERMAN DATIES.

The paper on "The Shakespearian characters of Richard 111. and Hamlet contrasted." which Alderman Davies read before the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, on Thursday evening, was listened to by the largest audience which has attended the meetings of the society this session. Besides the Alderman, there were present Mr. C. Btoadleent (chairman), the Mayor and Mayoress (Aid. and Mrs: Pick- mere), Mr. and Mrs. J. Dun, Mr. R. Davies, Mr. and Mrs. John Fairclough, Mr. and. Mrs. James Fairclough, Alderman Webster, Councillor Jeans, Councillor and Mrs. Pierpoint, Councillor and Mrs. M'onks, Major and Mrs. Cartwright, Messrs. J. Ellison, C. Twiss, D. W. Finney, J. Turner, J. Paterson, C. Chorley, T. Longdin, A. Perris, J. R. Young, P. Davies, W. Owen, Sec. The CHAIRMAN said he might tell Mr. Davies that they were all looking forward with great interest to hie paper that night, and heevas very pleased indeed to see so large an audience. He thought it was one of the largest meetings they had had for some considerable time. (Hear, hear.) He could also tell Mr. Davies that a great deal of curiosity had been excited by the announcement of his paper. They all knew that there•was a great deal of difference between Hamlet and Richard 111., and they were curious arra in- terested to hear exactly how Mr. Davies intended to draw his lines of contrast between the two. But they knew that Mr. Davies had always given a good deal of attention to the drama—and he was himself a very respectable performer on the stage—(applause);—and they were quite sure that he was very capable of dealing with the subject he had chosen. (Applause.) Mr. DAVIES, afeer some introductory observations, said he was satisfied in his own mind that in drawing the livee of Hamlet and Richard 111. Shakespeare intended to show the most opposite characters, both in body and mind, that could possibly exist in nature. In Hamlet Shakespeare intended to draw perfection of beauty in mind and body. In Richard 111. he intern-led to draw perfection of deformity in body and mind. Having, referred to the Richard of history, who, with an insatiable ambition and cruelty, hesitated at nothing, and yet withal was admitted to have been a re- uowned soldier, decisive, shrewd, clever, and brave ca a lion, Mr. Davies proceeqed to trace Richard's career as recorded in the drama and personified on the stage. He was deformed. His left leg was shorter than the right, the left arm withered or shrunk, and the left shoulder shrunk with it, which gave the right shoulder the appearance of a hump. It was al- ways so personified by Betterton, Garrick, and Kean, and he could not help remarking that the actors were after all the best commentators upon, and exponents of, the

_ characters of Shakespeare. A ccording to this theory there was evidently a great preponderance of strength and vitality on the right side. With copious quotations M.:. Davies showed Richard's consummate- dissimulation, cunning, and eloquence ; his ambition, wicked- ness, deceit, and cvaelty ; his decision, shrewdness, and self confidence; his bravery and prowess. But Shakespeare knew the weak point of his creature, and from his earliest youth it peeped out now and then through all the story of his life—he meant his superstition' of which Mr. Davies nave several illustratiow. Just before Bosworth battle, Richard said'.— Were will I tie tonight: Rut where to-morrow? well, all's one for that.

And when he was at last overcome with dangers and anxieties, be sought relief in the wine cup to drown his cares. Though vigilant to the last yet nature was overcome, and he fell asleep to dream the most terrible dream that ever entered into the heart of man to conceive. Not a single phantom to cast a gloom o'er him, but troops of victims— avenging ghosts—crowded upon and overwh%duled him with
the dreadful foreboding of defeat, despair, and death. In the midst of his dreaming terror he awoke and his first cry was—

Give me another horse. Bind up my wcunds ! No appeal to God or man, save that in a moment of delirium he gasped the popular phrase "Have mercy, Jesn," and then, half ashamed of his weakness, he exclaimed : " Soft ; I did but dream," and argued against fate until he was relieved by the presence of the devoted Ratcliffe, and confessed. Yes, the courageous, wicked, valiant yillian, who never feared friend or foe, confessed— Shadows to-night
Have struck more terror to tlie heart of Richard

Than could the substance of ten thousand soldiers. Being now fully awake, he reassumed his vigilance and order for the battle. Still his superstition hung about him, and, on referring to the kalendar, he was worried to find at dull morning afforded no sunshine on his enterprize. Not yet daunted, he laid out his order of battle with wonderful discretion, to a tittle. Notwithstanding disaffection and treason were everywhere rampant, he led on his forces in person, shouting and cheering. When all was lost, and Ratcliffe suggested the prudence of escape, he defied the superstitious auguries, and, with the reckless courage of a fatalist, shrieked: A horse ! a horse! my kinf.s.dom for a horse!.

- • Relying more upon his favourite "White Surrey " than upon eught else, human or divine, he rushed into the fight, achieving prodigies of valour, to fall at last by the hand of shallow Richmond. Wicked and hateful as Richard was, he had often thought that Shakespeare drew his opponent too puny to overcome this Dei—devil. There was a Miss Nancy air about Richard that ill-befitted him for the work be bad to do. Thus ended the life of Richard 111, whose body, brain, and mind were all awry and terribly revolting to sight, thought, and feeling, though grand and interesting to the utmost degree. (Applause.) —At this point the Mayor stated that he had received infor- mation that the Queen had been fired at that afternoon, but no one was hurt, and the would-be assassin was apprehended, a statement that was received with applause.— Considering next the character of Hamlet, that wonderful creation in every way original and natural, fresh and pure from , the mighty intellect of our Poet, Mr. Davies said he could fancy that Shakespeare was led to write this play after he had completed Richard, by way of comparison—a contrast. After stating that Richard 111. was printed six or seven years before Hamlet, he proceeded to analyse the character of Hamlet on the same lines as he did that of Richard. Could they for a moment tolerate an un- graceful Hamlet? Certainly not. He was of a goodly stock. and the play abounded with passages confirming this conclusion. As to his physique and strength, he broke away from Horatio and Marcellus on the beckoning of the ghost. He overcame Laertes in fencing. His education was vouched by his knowledge of and reciting Eucas' tale to Dido, and his philosophical reasoning, his gentle gracious- ness, his reception of the players, his caution to them not to mock Polonius made him a general favourite with the people. The grave-digger spoke of him with a quaint familiar loving regard as "Young Hamlet," though now 30 years of age. Mr. Davies then gave illustrations of Hamlet's loving memory of Yorick, his friendship, affection and love, his affectionate regard for his poor friend Horatio, his filial obedience to his mother's commands in the very heat of his passionate horror of her depravity, his love, his goodness and reliance on God's providence. He referred to the latter as an illustration of the opposite character of Hamlet to that of Richard, with his fatalism and supersti- tion. He would not say it profanely, but what human example in the Old Testament surpassed Hamlet? As to the weak point of Hamlet's character, assuming there were aught in his theory, so physically perfect was Hamlet that even the lobes of his brain were equal, and the reflective de- finite action of one was overcome by the reflective counter- action of the other. Indeed he was the victim of perfection, and so his youth, strength, beauty and accomplishments, his universal graciousness, his sterling friendship, unbounded affection and love, his goodness and reliance on Providence were all thus clouded and. eclipsed by indecision and inac- tion, fed by refined crotchets, and a morbid conscience. He himself suspected his infirmity and gave colour to his (Mr. Davies's) suggestion when he succumbed to his cross argu- ments and said, " Foh ! about my brains." But the soliloquy on death expressed all be would say. The killing of Polonius and the King were brought about by accidents and sudden frenzy, rather than through fixed desire and of eet purpose. And so the good, gentle, and loving Hamlet lived and died a victim, accomplishing nothing. Richard and Hamlet were now fully before them,—Deformity, devilry, and deeds,—Perfection, goodness, and inaction. Was there anything in his theory? There are more things in Heaven and earth, Horatio. Than are dreamt of in your philosophy. (Loud applause.) On the motion of the MAYOR,- seconded by Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, a hearty vote of thanks was tendered to Mr. Davies for his paper, and in the discussion wkich followed the general opinion was that Shakespeare did not write the characters as a contrast.

TIIE FORTHCOMING ELECTION OF GUARDIANS. REVISION OF THE REGISTER. Mr. James C. Sutton, revising officer, sat in the Over- seers' Office, Town Hall, on Monday, to revise the register of owners and proxies who claim to vote at the election of Guardians. There were also present Messrs. H. Roberts (Liberal agent), John England (Coneeryative agent), J. L. Tunstall (deputy assistant overseer), S. Sutton &,c. There were 169 objections, of which 90 were by the Sutton, and 79 by the Liberals. Mr. Alderman Davis was the first gentleman to appear, and on his stepping forward, Mr. Roberts said for many years past the register of owners in force in Warrington had been in a most awkward condition. The names of many persons who were dead, and of others who had ceased to be owners of property, had been retained upon it year after year, and scores of owners had not been represented upon it at all, and the consequence had been that there had not been anything like an accurate register in operation. Last year, after the election of Guardians, it was mutually agreed between the Conservative agent and himself, that they should thoroughly purify the register; and with this object in view they came tolhe understanding that both parties should see the rate book, and make out new claims for their friends; and it was understood on both sides that those Liberals or Conservatives who failed to make a new claim should be open to objection on either side. His reason for making the statement was simply to assare those gentlemen who had come that morning to meet these objections that it was owing to the fact that they had not made the new claims, and the register being in the con- dition stated, that they had been obliged to compel thereto attend.—The Revising Officer: I take it, if the gentlemen objected to who appear before me to-day had made a new claim, you would not have objected to then) ? What is your objection to Mr. Davies' right to appear on this list ?—Mr. Roberts: My objection is that Mr. Davies has not within the last few years made a bona Ale claim to appear on the register. Ido not want to act unfairly in this matter either to my own party or the ether.—The Revising Officer said he conic.' not go into a party question. He took it, from what Mr. Roberts said, if these gentlemen had signed a claim he would not have objected to them. He therefore took it that their appearance there that day would pretty well satisfy Mr. Roberts that they were entitled to their votes —Mr. Roberts said he was entitled to put another matter before the Revising Officer. Seeing what the law required before any gentleman should have his name on the register, and seeing also, as he was bound to suppose, Mr. Davies had not made a claim, he claimed to have his name struck off.—Mr. Aid. Webster remarked that he should rather think it lay with the party objecting to prove that they were not entitled to vote.—Mr. Roberts replied that it lay with the claimants to prove that they were entitled. He then asked for the origi- nal claim by Mr. Davies, but Mr. Tunstall was unable to produce it.—Mr. Roberts said, in the absence of the origi- nal claim, his objection held good.—The Revising Officer: No; there must have been an original claim, or the over- seers would not have made the entry on the list.—Mr. Roberts submitted all he had to do in thesecaseewas simply to put in the objection.—The Revising Officer: Seeing this record was made January 29, 1872, and no objection has hitherto been made to it, I should suppose it was made in due process of law.—Mr. Roberts said he would not press the objection any further, and the claim was allowed.—Mr. Roberts said he hoped Mr. Davies was satisfied with the explanation he had given.—Mr. Davies said he was quite satisfied, hot he thought it was a mistake because he never voted politically at the election of Guardians.—The cases of the gentlemen present having been dealt with, Mr. England was about to proceed with his objections, when Mr. Roberts asked for proof of service.—Mr. England said he sent them out in the ordinary way by post. He, however, had no Post office duplicates.—Mr. Sutton: But what evidence have I before me that Mr. Longshaw, of Lymm, has received the notice of objection ?—Mr. England: You have none, sir, under the circumstances.—Mr. Sutton said his duty was not to expunge the names from the register, but rather to retain them, presuming they were fairly qualified; but it was incumbent upon the person objecting to show.to the revising officer that the notice had come ta the knowledge of the person objected to. The mere statement that the notice had been posted in the ordinary way, without the production of the duplicate, waa no evidence at all of service. It would I be impossNe for him to take off a, man's vote without having clear evidence that he had bad notice to appear- before-him. He therefore held that Mr. Roberts's objection was good.—The whole of the Consoreative objections were thus ruled to be invalid.—The revision has been highly satisfactory ta the Liberals, andlias resulted in a gala. to them of between 200 and C;00 votes.

St. Helens, 27th February, 1882. To MR. PETER STREET. 1 BEG TO APOLOGISE for the annoyance and disgrace you have been subjected to in consequence of your appre- hension and trial on a charge of appropriating money from my till on Thursday, the 23rd day of February, 1882. I deeply regret that you have suffered in any way, and desire to express my belief that you are entirely innocent of any such offence. I am desirous that this apology should be made public, and am quite willing that you shall make any tize of it that you may think proper. (Signed) RICHARD SEDDON, Alexandra Vaults, Thatto Heath, Near St. Helens. Witness—THOMAS GARNER, Clerk to Messrs. Swift and Son, Solicitors, St. Helens. ELLEN HOWARTH, Deceased.—Pursuant to an Act of Parliament cf the 22nd and 23rd Vitt., cap. 25, intituled "An Act to further amend the law of property and to relieve trustees." NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that all persons, being creditors or otherwise, having any CLAIMS upon or against tne estate of ELLEN HOWARIII, late of Mill Brow, Sutton, St. Helens, in the county of Lancaster, widow, deceased (who died on the 3rd day of February, 1862, and whose will was, on the 2ith day of February, 1882, proved in the Liverpool District Registry of she Probate Division of the High Court of Justice, by Noah Greenhough, of Sutton aforesaid, provision dealer, and William Gorton. of Bold, in the said county, farmer, the executors therein named), are hereby required, on or before the Ist day of May next, to send to us, the undersigned, solicitors to the said executors, the particulars of their Claims upon or against the said estate; and notice is hereby further given, that after the day last above mentioned the said executors will pro- ceed to distribute the whole of the assets of the said deceased among the parties entitled thereto, having regard only to the claims of which the said executors shall then have had notice; and that the said executors will not be liable for the as etc so distributed, or any part thereof, to any person of whose claim they shall not then have received notice. And notice is hereby further given to persors who are indebted to the estate of the said deceased, immediately to. pay the amount of their respec- tive debts to the said executors.—Dated this Ist day of March, 1882. ANSDELL AND SON, Solicitors, St. Helens.

S 0 N G 0 F A COA T . Air: "Song of a Shirt." As the beautiful spring comes on, 'Mid song and the scent of flowers, When the hedges bud with a tender green, Begem'd with the gleaming showers, Sweet, sweet, sweet, Is the song from the thrush s throat, And sweeter still is the song I sing— 'Tis a song of a Velvet Coat. Stitched, stitch'd, stiteh'd, Perfectly strong and neat, And work, work, work, Not the deftest band can beat! It's oh ! to be well dressed— • A duty that none should shirk— For nothing improves a man as much As the tailor's handiwork! Style, style, style, And finish smart and trim; Strength, strength, strength, And colour that ne'er grows dim.
